docs.title: Fusion HCI Multi-Architecture Integration
docs.text:
Welcome to the Fusion HCI Multi-Architecture Integration documentation. This project enables seamless integration of Fusion HCI x86 worker nodes into s390x/LinuxONE OpenShift clusters, creating true multi-architecture deployments.

Architecture Flexibility

While this project focuses on s390x/LinuxONE as the main cluster architecture, the solution is designed to be architecture-agnostic. The same principles and components can be adapted for ARM or Power-based main clusters. The network integration, VM provisioning, and configuration management patterns are applicable across different CPU architectures.

docs.title: What is This?
docs.text:
This integration solution allows you to:

  • Extend s390x clusters with x86 compute capacity from Fusion HCI
  • Run multi-architecture workloads in a single OpenShift cluster
  • Leverage both architectures for optimal workload placement
  • Maintain unified management across different CPU architectures

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
• Main Cluster: Your primary OpenShift cluster (s390x/LinuxONE, ARM, or Power)
  • HCI Cluster: Fusion HCI cluster providing x86 compute resources
  • Gateway VM: Network bridge providing DHCP, PXE, and routing
  • Worker VMs: x86 RHCOS nodes that join the main cluster

docs.title: Deployment Variants
docs.text: This solution supports two network topology variants:

docs.title: Mediated Topology (Private Network)
docs.text:
• Main cluster nodes in private network behind bastion
  • Bastion provides routing and DNS
  • Common in z/VM, LPAR, or highly secured environments

docs.title: Direct Topology (Public Network)
docs.text:
• Main cluster nodes on shared public network
  • Direct connectivity to HCI gateway
  • Requires static route on master nodes
  • Common in KVM, bare metal, or less restricted environments

See Deployment Variants for detailed comparison.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Prepare Main Cluster 

    oc adm upgrade --to-multiarch
oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

  2. Prepare HCI Cluster (cluster-admin, one-time) 

    oc apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml
oc label namespace <namespace> hci-gateway-enabled=true

  3. Set up credentials 

    ./operator/setup-provider-credentials.sh

  4. Apply a WorkerPool CR — the operators provision everything automatically: 

    oc apply -f operator/hci-consumer/config/samples/workerpool-sample.yaml
    The hci-consumer operator creates the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR for you. The hci-provisioner runs all bootstrap steps, then hci-consumer scales up.

See Getting Started for detailed instructions.

docs.title: Deployment Variants
docs.text: This document explains the two network topology variants supported by the Fusion HCI multi-architecture integration and helps you choose the right one for your environment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The integration supports two deployment variants based on your main cluster's network topology:

  • Mediated Topology: Main cluster nodes in private network behind bastion
  • Direct Topology: Main cluster nodes on public network with direct connectivity

The choice depends on how your main cluster is deployed and networked, not on the CPU architecture itself.

docs.title: Quick Comparison Table
docs.text: Aspect Mediated Topology Direct Topology Main Cluster Network Private (10.x.x.x) Public (172.16.x.x) Bastion Role Routes all traffic Routes only if needed Master Node Config Standard Requires static route S390x Worker Config Standard Requires static route Gateway VM Access Via bastion Direct DNS Bastion provides Bastion or direct Complexity Medium Low-Medium Common In z/VM environments KVM environments Setup Time ~30 min ~20 min

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Choose the Mediated Topology when:

  • ✅ Main cluster nodes are in a private network (e.g., 10.x.x.x)
  • ✅ Bastion host provides external connectivity
  • ✅ Main cluster nodes cannot directly access external networks
  • ✅ Common in z/VM, LPAR, or highly secured environments

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
Routing: - All cluster traffic goes through bastion - Bastion routes to HCI internal network: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 - Gateway VM connects to bastion's external IP

DNS: - Bastion provides DNS for entire cluster - HCI workers use bastion as DNS server - Forward and reverse zones on bastion

Security: - Private network provides isolation - Bastion is single point of entry/exit - Firewall rules on bastion control access

Configuration: - Apply: oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/ - Includes: MachineConfigPool + kernel args - No master node changes needed - No s390x worker changes needed

docs.title: Setup Steps
docs.text:
1. Configure Bastion Routing 

    # On bastion host
sudo ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100

# Make persistent
sudo tee /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/route-eth0 <<EOF
192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100
EOF

  2. Configure DNS on Bastion

  3. Add forward zone entries for HCI workers
  4. Add reverse zone for 192.168.100.0/24

  5. Ensure recursive queries allowed from HCI network

  6. Apply MachineConfigs 

    oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

  7. Deploy Gateway and Workers

  8. Gateway VM uses bastion IP for DNS and routing
  9. Workers automatically use bastion DNS

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# From bastion, verify route
ip route | grep 192.168.100

# Test connectivity to gateway
ping 172.16.1.100  # Gateway external IP
ping 192.168.100.1   # Gateway internal IP

# Test DNS
nslookup worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com
nslookup 192.168.100.10

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Choose the Direct Topology when:

  • ✅ Main cluster nodes are on public/shared network (e.g., 172.16.x.x)
  • ✅ Main cluster nodes can directly access external networks
  • ✅ Gateway VM will be on same network as main cluster
  • ✅ Common in KVM, bare metal, or less restricted environments

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
Routing: - Master nodes need static route to HCI internal network - S390x workers need static route to HCI internal network - Routes added via MachineConfigs: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 - HCI x86 workers route through gateway VM as usual

DNS: - Can use bastion DNS or direct DNS - More flexible DNS configuration - HCI workers can use bastion or external DNS

Security: - Public network requires careful firewall rules - Direct access means more exposure - Network segmentation via firewall policies

Configuration: - Apply: oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/ - Includes: MachineConfigPool + kernel args + master route + worker route - Master nodes will restart to apply route - S390x workers will restart to apply route

docs.title: What's Included
docs.text:
The direct overlay includes two additional MachineConfigs for routing:

  1. 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml
  2. Applies to: Master nodes
  3. Purpose: Cluster management (CSR approval, scheduling, health checks)

  4. Route: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 dev br-ex

  5. 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml

  6. Applies to: S390x worker nodes (via node-platform: s390x label)
  7. Purpose: Pod-to-pod communication across architectures
  8. Route: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100

docs.title: Setup Steps
docs.text:
1. Apply MachineConfigs (includes both routes) 

    oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

# This applies:
# - MachineConfigPool for HCI workers
# - Kernel args for HCI workers
# - 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route (for masters)
# - 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route (for s390x workers)

  2. Wait for MachineConfigPool Updates 

    # Masters will restart one by one
watch oc get mcp master

# S390x workers will also restart
watch oc get mcp worker

# Wait for all pools:
# - UPDATED: True
# - UPDATING: False
# - DEGRADED: False

  3. Verify Routes 

    # Check route on a master node
oc debug node/<master-node>
chroot /host
ip route | grep 192.168.100
# Should show: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 dev br-ex

# Check route on s390x worker
oc debug node/<s390x-worker-node>
chroot /host
ip route | grep 192.168.100
# Should show: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100

  4. Deploy Gateway and Workers

  5. Gateway VM on same network as cluster
  6. Workers route through gateway as usual

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# From any master node
oc debug node/<master-node>
chroot /host

# Verify route exists
ip route | grep 192.168.100

# Test connectivity to gateway
ping 172.16.1.100  # Gateway external IP
ping 192.168.100.1   # Gateway internal IP (via route)

# From s390x worker
oc debug node/<s390x-worker>
chroot /host
ip route | grep 192.168.100
ping 192.168.100.1

# Test from HCI worker node
oc debug node/worker-x86-1
chroot /host
ping api.cluster.example.com

docs.title: Why Both Routes Are Needed
docs.text:
Master Route: - Masters need to communicate with HCI workers for: - CSR approval - Node status updates - Pod scheduling decisions - Health checks

S390x Worker Route: - S390x workers need to communicate with HCI workers for: - Pod-to-pod communication across architectures - Service endpoints spanning both worker types - Network policies involving both architectures - Multi-architecture application deployments

docs.title: Choose Mediated Topology If:
docs.text:
• ✅ Your main cluster uses private networking (10.x.x.x)
  • ✅ You have a bastion host handling all external traffic
  • ✅ Your environment is z/VM, LPAR, or highly secured
  • ✅ You're comfortable with bastion-centric architecture
  • ✅ You want centralized traffic control

docs.title: Choose Direct Topology If:
docs.text:
• ✅ Your main cluster uses public/shared networking (172.16.x.x)
  • ✅ Cluster nodes can directly access external networks
  • ✅ Your environment is KVM, bare metal, or less restricted
  • ✅ You prefer direct connectivity over bastion routing
  • ✅ You're comfortable with master and worker node configuration changes

docs.title: Still Not Sure?
docs.text:
Ask yourself:

  1. Can my main cluster nodes ping 172.16.1.100 directly?
  2. Yes → Direct Topology

  3. No → Mediated Topology

  4. Does all my cluster traffic go through a bastion?

  5. Yes → Mediated Topology

  6. No → Direct Topology

  7. Are my cluster nodes on a 10.x.x.x network?

  8. Yes → Likely Mediated Topology
  9. No → Likely Direct Topology

docs.title: Registry Implications
docs.text: Both variants work with all registry strategies, but there are considerations:

docs.title: Bastion Registry Proxy
docs.text:
• Mediated: Natural fit, bastion already routes all traffic
  • Direct: Works fine, bastion proxies registry traffic

docs.title: Public Registry
docs.text:
• Mediated: Requires bastion to allow outbound internet
  • Direct: Direct internet access, no bastion dependency

docs.title: Internal Registry
docs.text:
• Mediated: Registry accessible via bastion
  • Direct: Registry directly accessible

See Prerequisites - Registry Strategy for details.

docs.title: Switching Between Variants
docs.text:
Not Recommended

Switching variants after deployment requires redeploying workers and reconfiguring the main cluster. Plan your variant choice carefully.

If you must switch:

  1. Remove existing workers 

    # Scale the WorkerPool to 0 and wait for drain + VM deletion
oc patch workerpool hci-workers \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":0}}}}'
# Then delete the WorkerPool CR — the operator cleans up remaining nodes
oc delete workerpool hci-workers

  2. Remove old MachineConfigs 

    oc delete mcp hci-vm
oc delete mc 99-hci-vm-kargs 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route --ignore-not-found

  3. Apply new variant 

    # Update integration-setup.yaml with the new topology and run:
./generate-setup

# Or apply manually via overlay:
# For Mediated Topology:
oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

# For Direct Topology:
oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

  4. Reconfigure networking (bastion routes, DNS, etc.)

  5. Redeploy workers by applying a new WorkerPool CR with the updated variant settings

docs.title: Mediated Topology Issues
docs.text:
Workers can't reach main cluster API: - Check bastion routing: ip route | grep 192.168.100 - Verify bastion firewall allows traffic - Test from bastion: ping 192.168.100.1

DNS resolution fails: - Check bastion DNS configuration - Verify recursive queries allowed from 192.168.100.0/24 - Test: nslookup worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com

docs.title: Direct Topology Issues
docs.text:
Masters can't reach workers: - Check master route: oc debug node/<master> -- chroot /host ip route | grep 192.168.100 - Verify MachineConfig applied: oc get mc 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route - Check master pool status: oc get mcp master

S390x workers can't reach HCI workers: - Check worker route: oc debug node/<s390x-worker> -- chroot /host ip route | grep 192.168.100 - Verify MachineConfig applied: oc get mc 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route - Check worker pool status: oc get mcp worker

Route not persisting: - Check systemd service: systemctl status hci-network-route.service - View logs: journalctl -u hci-network-route.service - For masters, verify br-ex interface exists: ip link show br-ex

Cross-architecture pod communication fails: - Verify routes on both master and s390x workers - Test connectivity: oc debug node/<s390x-worker> -- chroot /host ping 192.168.100.10 - Check network policies aren't blocking traffic

docs.title: Architecture Flexibility
docs.text:
Other Architectures

While this documentation focuses on s390x main clusters, both variants work with ARM or Power-based main clusters. The network topology (private vs public) is independent of CPU architecture.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Aspect Mediated Topology Direct Topology Best For Private networks, mediated access Public networks, direct access Bastion Role Central router Optional Master Changes None Static route added Worker Changes None Static route added (s390x) Complexity Medium Low-Medium Flexibility Less (bastion-dependent) More (direct access) Security Higher (isolated) Medium (exposed)

Recommendation: Choose based on your existing network topology, not on preference. The variant should match how your main cluster is already deployed.

docs.text:

  2. Follow Getting Started guide

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This guide walks you through the full lifecycle from a bare HCI cluster to a running multi-architecture integration. The process is organised in three independent tiers that have different cadences:

Tier Who How often A — HCI cluster-wide setup HCI admin Once per HCI cluster B — HCI per-integration setup HCI admin Once per main-cluster you want to connect C — Connect a main cluster Main-cluster admin Once per main cluster (re-run for re-connections)

Reconnecting an existing cluster?

If the bastion host is already configured and the main cluster has previously been integrated, tiers A and B are already done. Jump straight to Tier C and check each step against your existing state — several steps will be no-ops.

Prerequisites Required

Before starting, ensure you've completed all steps in Prerequisites, including setting up contexts named main-cluster and hci-cluster and choosing your registry strategy.

docs.title: Workspace Setup
docs.text:
If you have not done so already, complete the Environment Configuration section of the prerequisites: copy the example, fill in workspace/integration-setup.yaml, and run generate-setup once to produce all artifacts including setup_env.sh.

# If generate-setup has not been run yet:
mkdir -p workspace
cp templates/integration-setup.example.yaml workspace/integration-setup.yaml
vi workspace/integration-setup.yaml          # fill in your values
./generate-setup workspace/integration-setup.yaml

Source setup_env.sh to load the environment for this shell session:

# Source it (required for all commands in this guide)
source setup_env.sh

# Verify
echo "Main Cluster: ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}"
echo "HCI Cluster:  ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}"

Every new shell

Source setup_env.sh from the repo root in every new terminal — all commands in this guide use the ${VARIABLES} it provides.

docs.title: Tier A — HCI Cluster-Wide Setup
docs.text:
Run once per HCI cluster. Subsequent integrations skip this tier entirely.

These steps require HCI cluster-admin access. They create shared infrastructure that every main-cluster integration will use.

docs.title: A.1 — Enable the HCI Image Registry
docs.text:
The script configures the registry for external access. It is idempotent — safe to re-run.

What it does in one shot: - Configures ODF/NooBaa S3 storage and enables the external default route - Sets disableRedirect: true — required for cross-cluster push; without it the registry issues S3 pre-signed redirects that clients cannot follow across the bastion boundary

oc config use-context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
./hci-cluster/enable-image-registry-s3.sh

Verify:

oc get route default-route -n openshift-image-registry
curl -k https://$(oc get route default-route \
  -n openshift-image-registry -o jsonpath='{.spec.host}')/v2/
# UNAUTHORIZED = registry is up and reachable

oc get configs.imageregistry.operator.openshift.io/cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.disableRedirect}'
# true

docs.title: A.2 — Apply Cluster-Scoped Network Configuration
docs.text:
The ClusterUserDefinedNetwork provides the external network attachment that every gateway VM will use. Apply it once — it is cluster-scoped and integration-namespace agnostic.

oc config use-context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml

# Verify
oc get clusteruserdefinednetwork
# router-external-network    Active

docs.title: Tier B — HCI Per-Integration Setup
docs.text:
Run once per main cluster you connect. Reconnecting the same main cluster does not require re-running these steps unless the namespace or RBAC was deleted.

These steps create the HCI-side namespace, credentials, and RBAC for one specific main-cluster ↔ HCI pairing.

docs.title: B.1 — Create and Label the Integration Namespace
docs.text:
oc config use-context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}

oc create namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# Label enables the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork controller to create the NAD
oc label namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} hci-gateway-enabled=true

# Verify the NetworkAttachmentDefinition was created automatically
sleep 5
oc get network-attachment-definition -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
# router-external-network

NAD must exist before deploying VMs

If the NAD is absent after labeling, check the namespace label and the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork status before continuing.

docs.title: B.2 — Set Up Registry RBAC on the HCI Cluster
docs.text:
This script creates the registry-pusher ServiceAccount in ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} on the HCI cluster — the only credential that cannot be minted from the main cluster side. Its long-lived token is later read by setup-registry-access.sh (step C.6) to create the registry pull secret on the main cluster, without ever mutating the HCI cluster again.

# Run from the repo root with setup_env.sh already sourced
./hci-cluster/setup-consumer-rbac.sh

Recreating RBAC

If you need to rotate credentials or the SA was deleted, pass --delete first and then re-run: 

./hci-cluster/setup-consumer-rbac.sh --delete
./hci-cluster/setup-consumer-rbac.sh

docs.title: Tier C — Connect a Main Cluster
docs.text:
Run for each new main cluster, and again when reconnecting a previously integrated cluster.

Assumed execution context for Tier C

All commands in this tier are run on the bastion host of the main cluster as an unprivileged but sudo-capable user, with the repository cloned and setup_env.sh sourced. Commands that need elevated privileges call sudo explicitly — do not run an entire shell session as root.

Each step starts with a check command. Run the check first — if it passes, the step is already done and you move on.

docs.title: C.1 — Configure DNS on the Bastion
docs.text:
Check: all worker hostnames resolve correctly.

# Run for each planned worker name
nslookup worker-x86-1.<main-cluster-domain>
nslookup 192.168.100.10   # reverse lookup

If any lookup fails, add the missing forward (A) and reverse (PTR) entries on the bastion DNS server.

generate-setup automatically derives these zone files and writes them to the workspace/ directory:

  • workspace/<your-domain>.zone — forward zone section with A records for the gateway VM (hci-gateway.<domain>) and all worker nodes up to maxPoolSize
  • workspace/<subnet>.in-addr.arpa.zone — reverse zonefile with PTR records for worker nodes

Copy or append these entries on the bastion DNS server:

ssh user@${BASTION_HOST}

sudo vi /var/named/<your-domain>.zone
# Append contents from workspace/<your-domain>.zone:
# hci-gateway.cluster.example.com.           IN  A    172.16.1.100
# worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com.          IN  A    192.168.100.10
# worker-x86-2.cluster.example.com.          IN  A    192.168.100.11
# worker-x86-3.cluster.example.com.          IN  A    192.168.100.12

sudo vi /var/named/192.168.100.in-addr.arpa.zone
# Append/create with contents from workspace/<subnet>.in-addr.arpa.zone:
# 10    IN  PTR  worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com.
# 11    IN  PTR  worker-x86-2.cluster.example.com.
# 12    IN  PTR  worker-x86-3.cluster.example.com.

# Zone-file edits alone are picked up by a reload, but use stop/start whenever
# /etc/named.conf was touched (see the warning below)
sudo systemctl stop named-chroot
sudo systemctl start named-chroot

Use stop/start for named-chroot, not reload

On a chrooted BIND (named-chroot) the config file is bind-mounted into /var/named/chroot/etc/. An editor that saves by writing a new file gives /etc/named.conf a new inode, while the chroot keeps pointing at the old, unlinked one. systemctl reload then silently re-reads the stale config, so ACL changes have no effect and nothing in the log says so. A stop/start re-creates the mount. After editing named.conf, check that the copies match:

sudo ls -li /etc/named.conf /var/named/chroot/etc/named.conf   # same size and mtime, link count 1

DNS is critical

Without correct forward and reverse DNS, the csr-approver sidecar cannot validate worker node names and CSRs will not be approved.

Keep DNS in sync with your WorkerPool

The zone files are generated from the same integration-setup.yaml as the WorkerPool CR, so they stay in sync as long as you regenerate both.

DNS config integration-setup.yaml field Worker name prefix (worker-x86) consumer.workers.namePrefix Internal subnet (192.168.100.x) provider.networking.internalSubnet Number of entries pre-added up to provider.maxPoolSize Cluster domain consumer.domain

docs.title: Allow recursion for the gateway and the worker network
docs.text:
The bastion DNS server is not only authoritative for the cluster zone. It is also the only resolver the HCI components use, so it must resolve external names (for example mirror.openshift.com) on their behalf. The default BIND configuration only allows recursion for localhost and the bastion's own networks, so queries from the gateway VM and the worker VMs are refused.

Client Source address seen by the bastion Needs recursion for hci-gateway gateway external IP (provider.gateway.ip, e.g. 172.16.1.100) RHCOS boot file download (rhcos-sync) from mirror.openshift.com Worker VMs worker IPs in spec.provider.networking.internalSubnet (e.g. 192.168.100.0/24) Name resolution during first boot, before and after joining the cluster

Check: run this on the gateway VM (ssh core@<gateway-ip>).

dig @<dnsServer> mirror.openshift.com
# status: NOERROR with an ANSWER section  ← pass, nothing to do
# status: REFUSED, or no answer           ← recursion is not allowed, fix below

Test from the right host

A dig from the bastion or from any other host that is already allowed proves nothing. The ACL is evaluated against the source address, so the test must run on the gateway (and, for the worker network, from a host in the internal subnet).

If the lookup is refused, add both networks to the recursion ACL on the bastion (file and ACL name depend on your named.conf):

sudo vi /etc/named.conf
# acl "internal_nets" {
#     ...existing entries...;
#     172.16.1.100/32;       # hci-gateway external IP (provider.gateway.ip)
#     192.168.100.0/24;      # HCI internal worker subnet (provider.networking.internalSubnet)
# };
#
# options {
#     allow-query       { localhost; internal_nets; };
#     allow-recursion   { localhost; internal_nets; };
#     allow-query-cache { localhost; internal_nets; };   # set explicitly, do not rely on defaults
# };

sudo named-checkconf

# stop/start, NOT reload — see the warning above
sudo systemctl stop named-chroot
sudo systemctl start named-chroot
sudo ls -li /etc/named.conf /var/named/chroot/etc/named.conf   # must match

Where the refusal shows up

A refused recursive query is logged on the bastion as query (cache) '<name>/A/IN' denied for the client address. The denial is reported against the cache ACL, so allow-query-cache must include the gateway as well.

A missing entry fails silently

If the gateway is refused, rhcos-sync.service on the gateway fails every 5 minutes with curl: (6) Could not resolve host: mirror.openshift.com (see journalctl -u rhcos-sync.service). On the operator side this only shows up as the scale-up being deferred until the gateway syncs the boot files, and current-version.txt never appears under /rhcos/.

The gateway's DNS settings are applied once

The gateway VM receives its upstream DNS server (spec.consumer.networking.dnsServer) through cloud-init on first boot only. Changing the recursion ACL on the bastion takes effect immediately and needs no change on the gateway, but changing dnsServer in the WorkerPool afterwards does not update an already-running gateway.

docs.title: C.2 — Configure Bastion Routing and Firewall (Mediated Topology only)
docs.text:
Check: the route to the worker subnet exists on the bastion.

ip route show | grep "${INTERNAL_NETWORK}"
# 192.168.100.0/24 via <gateway-ip>  ← pass, nothing to do
# (no output)                        ← run the scripts below

If the route or firewall rules are missing, run the scripts with sudo (the scripts automatically locate and source setup_env.sh from the repository root):

sudo ./main-cluster/scripts/01-add-route.sh
sudo ./main-cluster/scripts/02-firewall-setup.sh

docs.title: C.3 — Enable Multi-Architecture Support
docs.text:
Check: the cluster payload already supports multiple architectures.

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} \
  get clusterversion -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.desired.image}' | grep -i multi \
  && echo "Multi-arch already enabled — nothing to do"

If the check produces no output:

oc adm --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} upgrade --to-multi-arch=true

# Wait for completion (30–60 minutes)
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get clusterversion -w

docs.title: C.4 — Apply MachineConfigs
docs.text:
Check: the hci-vm MachineConfigPool exists.

oc config use-context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc get mcp hci-vm 2>/dev/null && echo "MCP exists — nothing to do"

If absent, apply the overlay that matches your network topology (see Deployment Variants):

Mediated TopologyDirect Topology 
oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

oc get mc | grep hci
# machineconfig-pool-hci-vm
# machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs

oc get mcp hci-vm
# MACHINECOUNT: 0  (no workers yet — expected)

oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

oc get mc | grep hci
# machineconfig-pool-hci-vm
# machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs
# 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route

# Wait for master pool to finish rolling before continuing
oc get mcp master -w

docs.title: C.5 — Configure Bastion Registry Proxy
docs.text:
Check: the bastion is registered as an insecure registry on the main cluster.

oc config use-context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc get image.config.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.registrySources.insecureRegistries}' \
  | grep -o "${BASTION_HOST}:${REGISTRY_PROXY_PORT}" \
  && echo "Registry proxy configured — nothing to do"

If absent, run the setup script directly on the bastion as your normal user (not with sudo). It automatically sources setup_env.sh, wraps the HAProxy, firewall, and certificate commands in sudo itself, and runs all oc commands unprivileged with your own login against ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}:

./main-cluster/bastion-registry/setup-registry-proxy.sh

MachineConfigPool rollout

This triggers a cluster-wide MachineConfig update — all worker nodes restart in sequence. Allow 10–30 minutes.

Verify connectivity once the rollout is complete:

# From the bastion
curl -sk https://localhost:${REGISTRY_PROXY_PORT}/v2/ && echo ok

docs.title: C.6 — Create the Registry Access Secret
docs.text:
Check: the push/pull secret exists in the operator namespace.

oc config use-context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc get secret ${REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME} -n hci-node-manager 2>/dev/null \
  && echo "Secret exists — nothing to do"

If absent, run the setup script. It reads the long-lived token from the registry-pusher SA in ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} on the HCI cluster (created in Tier B step B.2 — this script is read-only on the HCI side) and stores it as a docker-registry Secret on the main cluster:

# Run from repo root with setup_env.sh sourced
./main-cluster/bastion-registry/setup-registry-access.sh

The script creates ${REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME} (default: hci-registry-push) in the hci-node-manager namespace.

docs.title: C.7 — Create Operator Credentials
docs.text:
The operators need their HCI-side credential Secrets to exist before they start reconciling. Create them now, before deploying.

Check: the credentials Secrets exist in the operator namespace.

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} \
  get secret hci-provisioner-credentials hci-provider-credentials \
  -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
# Both names listed without error → credentials exist, nothing to do
# Error: secrets "..." not found  → run the script below

If absent, run the script from the repo root with setup_env.sh sourced. It connects to both clusters using the contexts from setup_env.sh, creates the hci-consumer-operator and hci-provisioner-operator ServiceAccounts with their Roles on the HCI cluster, mints long-lived tokens, and writes two kubeconfig Secrets to the main cluster — all in one shot:

./operator/setup-provider-credentials.sh

Two Secrets are created in ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}:

Secret Consumed by Scope hci-provider-credentials hci-consumer operator VM + DataVolume CRUD in the HCI namespace — steady-state reconcile hci-provisioner-credentials hci-provisioner operator Gateway VM, UDN, SA/token management — bootstrap and teardown only

Rotating credentials

Re-run the script at any time to rotate tokens. Pass --consumer or --provisioner to rotate only one of the two.

docs.title: C.8 — Build and Deploy the Operators
docs.text:
Check: both operator pods are running.

oc config use-context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc get pods -n hci-node-manager
# hci-consumer-operator-xxxx    3/3  Running  ← pass
# hci-provisioner-operator-xxxx 1/1  Running  ← pass

Whether deploying for the first time or rebuilding after a code change, the steps are the same — see the dedicated page for the full workflow:

Building and Deploying the Operators →

Quick reference for the bastion-proxy registry case:

# REGISTRY_PUSH, REGISTRY_PULL, REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME are already exported
# from setup_env.sh — no config.env editing needed.

pushd operator
make apply-buildconfigs   # one-time: namespace, ImageStreams, BuildConfigs
                          # auto-selects external-registry overlay when REGISTRY_PUSH is set
make build                # builds both operator images in-cluster
make install              # applies WorkerPool and WorkerPoolProvisioning CRDs
make deploy               # generates active overlay from environment, runs oc apply -k
                          # MAIN_CLUSTER_DOMAIN is derived automatically — nothing to set
popd

oc get pods -n hci-node-manager
# hci-consumer-operator-xxxx    3/3  Running
# hci-provisioner-operator-xxxx 1/1  Running

docs.title: C.9 — Apply the WorkerPool CR
docs.text:
One CR — fully automated

Applying the WorkerPool CR is all that is needed. The operators handle everything: gateway VM, ignition, boot files, worker join, CSR approval, and node labeling.

generate-setup has already rendered an initial WorkerPool CR from integration-setup.yaml into workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml. It has workers.count: 0, so applying it provisions the HCI gateway only. Workers are added afterwards by editing the live resource.

oc config use-context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc apply -f workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml

# Once the pool is Ready, add workers:
oc -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} edit workerpool hci-workers   # set spec.consumer.workers.count

The generated file is a starting point and is overwritten on every generate-setup run. To keep the current state of a live pool, save it with oc get workerpool hci-workers -o yaml.

Watch both operators progress from a single terminal:

# WorkerPool: Provisioning → Ready → ScalingUp → Ready
oc get workerpool ${WORKERPOOL_NAME} -w

# WorkerPoolProvisioning: created automatically, shows per-step progress
oc get workerpoolprovisioning -w

The deployment is complete when PHASE=Ready and WORKERS, DEPLOYED, and READY are all equal with PENDING=0:

oc get workerpool
# NAME         PHASE   WORKERS   DEPLOYED   READY   PENDING   AGE
# hci-workers  Ready   3         3          3       0         12m

If the pool does not reach Ready, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Scaling the Worker Pool
docs.text: Once the pool is Ready, scaling is a single-field edit — the operator handles cordon, drain, and VM lifecycle automatically.

docs.title: Scale Up
docs.text:
oc patch workerpool ${WORKERPOOL_NAME} \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count": 5}}}}'

oc get workerpool ${WORKERPOOL_NAME} -w
# Transitions: ScalingUp → Ready

Ensure DNS entries exist for every new worker IP before scaling up.

docs.title: Scale Down
docs.text:
Scale down by reducing workers.count:

oc patch workerpool ${WORKERPOOL_NAME} \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count": 2}}}}'

The operator cordons and drains removed nodes before deleting their VMs. Watch progress:

oc get workerpool ${WORKERPOOL_NAME} -w
# Transitions: ScalingDown → Ready

docs.title: Check Node Status
docs.text:
oc get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm=""
# All HCI worker nodes should be Ready

Note: If the x86 workers are Ready but missing from this list, and the WorkerPool stays in ScalingUp with readyWorkers: 0, see Troubleshooting: WorkerPool Stuck in ScalingUp.

docs.title: Verify MachineConfigPool
docs.text:
oc get mcp hci-vm
# MACHINECOUNT and READYMACHINECOUNT should match workers.count
# DEGRADED: False

docs.title: Verify Network Configuration
docs.text:
# Check routes on a worker node (Mediated Topology)
oc debug node/<hci-worker-node> -- chroot /host ip route
# 192.168.100.0/24 via <gateway-ip>

# Check UDN on HCI cluster
oc config use-context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc get userdefinednetwork -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

docs.title: Test Workload Scheduling
docs.text:
# Schedule a test pod on an HCI worker
oc run test-pod --image=registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi-minimal:latest \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm":""}}}' \
  --restart=Never --command -- sleep 60

oc get pod test-pod -o wide
# Should show an HCI worker node in the NODE column

oc delete pod test-pod

docs.title: Registry Proxy Issues
docs.text:
# Verify HAProxy is running on bastion
ssh user@${BASTION_HOST} systemctl status haproxy

# Check insecure-registries in cluster config
oc get image.config.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.registrySources.insecureRegistries}' | tr ',' '\n'

# Test push/pull secret
oc get secret ${REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME} -n hci-node-manager -o yaml

docs.title: Gateway VM Not Starting
docs.text:
# Check provisioner logs
oc logs deployment/hci-provisioner-operator -c operator -n hci-node-manager | tail -40

# Check VM status on HCI cluster
oc config use-context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}
oc get vm -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
oc describe vm gateway-vm -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

docs.title: Workers Not Booting
docs.text:
# Check that DNS resolves
nslookup worker-x86-1.${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}

# Check DHCP/PXE logs on gateway
ssh -J user@${BASTION_HOST} cloud-user@<gateway-ip>
sudo journalctl -u dhcpd -f
sudo journalctl -u tftp -f

docs.title: CSRs Not Being Approved
docs.text:
# Check csr-approver sidecar logs
oc logs deployment/hci-consumer-operator -c csr-approver -n hci-node-manager | tail -20

# List pending CSRs
oc get csr | grep Pending

docs.title: Workers Not Joining Cluster
docs.text:
# Check consumer operator logs
oc logs deployment/hci-consumer-operator -c operator -n hci-node-manager | tail -40

# Check node-labeler sidecar
oc logs deployment/hci-consumer-operator -c node-labeler -n hci-node-manager | tail -20

docs.title: Tear Down
docs.text:
# Delete all WorkerPool objects first (triggers drain + VM cleanup)
oc delete workerpool --all -n hci-node-manager
# Wait for finalizers to complete, then:

# Remove operators
cd operator/
make undeploy

# Remove CRDs (also deletes any remaining CRs)
make uninstall

# Remove namespace
oc delete namespace hci-node-manager

Uninstalling CRDs while WorkerPools exist

Running make uninstall while active WorkerPool CRs exist bypasses the finalizer that drains nodes and deletes VMs. Always delete all WorkerPool objects and wait for completion first.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This page outlines the requirements and preparation steps needed before deploying the Fusion HCI multi-architecture integration.

docs.title: Main Cluster (s390x/LinuxONE)
docs.text:
OpenShift Version: - OpenShift 4.20 or later (tested on 4.20+) - Multi-architecture support enabled

Cluster Configuration: - At least 3 control plane nodes - Existing s390x worker nodes (optional but recommended) - Cluster-admin access required

Network Requirements: - Routable network for cluster nodes - Bastion host with external connectivity - DNS server (typically on bastion) - Available IP addresses for HCI workers

Storage: - No persistent storage required on main cluster - Worker node data stored on HCI cluster VMs

docs.title: HCI Cluster (Fusion HCI)
docs.text:
OpenShift Version: - OpenShift 4.20 or later (tested on 4.20+) - OpenShift Virtualization operator installed

Cluster Configuration: - Worker nodes with virtualization capabilities - Sufficient compute resources for VMs - Cluster-admin access required

Network Requirements: - OVN-Kubernetes CNI (default) - Physical network access (localnet support) - Available IP addresses in physical network range

Storage: - Fusion Data Foundation (FDF) built-in with S3 storage (NooBaa) - Storage class for VM disks - Sufficient capacity for worker VMs (50GB+ per VM) - FDF provides persistent S3 storage for HCI cluster's image registry

docs.title: Network Connectivity
docs.text:
Between Clusters: - Network connectivity between HCI and main cluster - Routing configured (via bastion or direct) - Firewall rules allowing required traffic

Required Ports: - 6443: Kubernetes API server - 22623: Machine config server - 80/443: Application routes - 9000-9999: Node ports (if used) - DHCP (67/68): For PXE boot - TFTP (69): For PXE boot - HTTP (8080): For ignition files

docs.title: Kubernetes Context Setup
docs.text:
Context Management

Using named contexts makes it easy to switch between clusters. We recommend naming your contexts main-cluster and hci-cluster for consistency with documentation examples and helper scripts.

docs.title: Main Cluster Access
docs.text:
1. Login and Create Context 

    # Login to main cluster
oc login https://api.cluster.example.com:6443

# Get the current context name
oc config current-context
# Output: default/api-cluster-example-com:6443/admin

# Rename context for easy reference
oc config rename-context $(oc config current-context) main-cluster

# Verify
oc config get-contexts
# Should show 'main-cluster' with a '*' indicating it's active

# Test access
oc whoami
# Should show your username

oc auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces
# Should return "yes"

  2. Bastion Host Access 

    # SSH access to bastion
ssh user@bastion.cluster.example.com

# On bastion, also setup context (if using oc there)
oc login https://api.cluster.example.com:6443
oc config rename-context $(oc config current-context) main-cluster

# Verify DNS service
systemctl status named

# Verify routing capability
ip route show

docs.title: HCI Cluster Access
docs.text:
1. Login and Create Context 

    # Login to HCI cluster
oc login https://api.hci-cluster.example.com:6443

# Rename context for easy reference
oc config rename-context $(oc config current-context) hci-cluster

# Verify
oc config get-contexts
# Should show both 'main-cluster' and 'hci-cluster'

# Test access
oc whoami

oc auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces
# Should return "yes"

  2. OpenShift Virtualization 

    # Ensure you're using HCI cluster context
oc config use-context hci-cluster

# Verify virtualization operator
oc get csv -n openshift-cnv

# Check for HyperConverged CR
oc get hyperconverged -n openshift-cnv

docs.title: Switching Between Clusters
docs.text:
Once contexts are configured, switching is simple:

# Switch to main cluster
oc config use-context main-cluster
oc get nodes

# Switch to HCI cluster
oc config use-context hci-cluster
oc get nodes

# View all contexts
oc config get-contexts

# View current context
oc config current-context

Context in Scripts

The helper scripts in main-cluster/scripts/ use the centralized setup_env.sh configuration which allows you to specify context names. Update setup_env.sh with your context names: 

MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT="main-cluster"
HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT="hci-cluster"

docs.title: Environment Configuration
docs.text: Before starting deployment, capture all cluster-pair decisions in a single configuration file — workspace/integration-setup.yaml. This is the only file you edit by hand. The generate-setup script derives every other environment artifact from it: shell environment variables, operator config, kustomize overlays, DNS zone files, and the initial WorkerPool CR. All integration-specific assets land in workspace/; setup_env.sh is written to the repo root so every script in the repository can source it with a relative path.

docs.title: Setting Up workspace/integration-setup.yaml
docs.text:
# 1. Create the workspace directory (skip if it already exists)
mkdir -p workspace

# 2. Copy the annotated example into the workspace
cp templates/integration-setup.example.yaml workspace/integration-setup.yaml

# 3. Open it in your editor — every field has an inline comment explaining
#    what it is and how to find the right value
vi workspace/integration-setup.yaml

The file has three top-level sections with clear ownership:

Section Owner What goes here consumer.* Main cluster (s390x/LinuxONE) admin Cluster context, domain, operator namespace, bastion, topology, DNS server provider.* HCI cluster admin Cluster context, HCI namespace, gateway IP, MAC prefix, internal subnet registry.* Both admins (agreed once) Registry model (local-s2i, cross-cluster, external) and model-specific fields

Two-admin handover

In a two-team setup the main cluster admin fills in consumer.* and the HCI admin fills in provider.*. The finished file is the negotiated record of the cluster-pair relationship — keep it alongside your Ansible inventory.

All fields have inline comments in the example file. The required fields are:

# ── Consumer cluster (s390x / LinuxONE) ──────────────────────────────────────
consumer:
  context: main-cluster              # oc config get-contexts
  domain: cluster.example.com        # oc get dns cluster -o jsonpath='{.spec.baseDomain}'
  operatorNamespace: hci-node-manager
  bastion:
    host: bastion.cluster.example.com
    user: root
  networking:
    topology: mediated               # direct | mediated
    dnsServer: 172.16.0.1            # main cluster bastion IP
    # mediated topology only:
    internalNetwork: 10.0.0.0/24    # main cluster's internal network
    internalGateway: 172.16.0.1     # HCI-side gateway to that network

# ── Provider cluster (x86 / Fusion HCI) ──────────────────────────────────────
provider:
  context: hci-cluster               # oc config get-contexts
  apiEndpoint: https://api.hci.example.com:6443
  registryHostname: default-route-openshift-image-registry.apps.hci.example.com
  namespace: main-cluster-workers    # one namespace per main cluster on this HCI
  maxPoolSize: 10                    # optional, default: 10; also sizes DNS zones
  gateway:
    ip: 172.16.1.100                 # assigned from HCI physical network
    prefixLength: 16
    defaultRouter: 172.16.0.1
  networking:
    macPrefix: "52:54:01"            # unique per pool on this HCI; optional, default: 52:54:00
    internalSubnet: 192.168.100.0/24

# ── Image registry ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
registry:
  model: cross-cluster               # local-s2i | cross-cluster | external
  # cross-cluster model only:
  proxyPort: 5443
  saName: registry-pusher
  secretName: hci-registry-push

docs.title: Generating All Configuration Artifacts
docs.text:
Once workspace/integration-setup.yaml is complete, run the generator from the repo root:

./generate-setup workspace/integration-setup.yaml

This writes every derived artifact in one shot:

Output Purpose setup_env.sh Shell environment — source this in every terminal session workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml Initial WorkerPool CR (workers.count: 0) operator/build/config.env Makefile variables for make build / make deploy main-cluster/configuration/overlays/<topology>/ Kustomize overlays (direct topology only) workspace/<domain>.zone Forward DNS zone section (A records for gateway + workers) workspace/<subnet>.in-addr.arpa.zone Reverse DNS zone (PTR records) 
# After generating, source the environment in your current shell
source setup_env.sh

Re-run after any change

generate-setup is idempotent — re-running it after editing workspace/integration-setup.yaml regenerates all artifacts consistently. The WorkerPool CR in workspace/ is overwritten on every run; to preserve the live state of a running pool use oc get workerpool hci-workers -o yaml instead.

docs.title: DNS Configuration
docs.text:
DNS zone files are generated automatically

Once you have run ./generate-setup workspace/integration-setup.yaml, ready-to-use zone file sections are written into workspace/:

  • workspace/<domain>.zone — forward A records for the gateway VM and all worker nodes up to provider.maxPoolSize
  • workspace/<subnet>.in-addr.arpa.zone — reverse PTR records for worker nodes

Copy or append those files to your bastion DNS server instead of writing entries by hand. Re-run generate-setup after any change to workspace/integration-setup.yaml to keep the zone files in sync with the WorkerPool configuration. Step-by-step instructions for applying them are in the Getting Started guide — step C.1.

The generated forward zone section looks like this:

; Forward zone entries — produced by generate-setup
hci-gateway.cluster.example.com.     IN  A  172.16.1.100
worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com.    IN  A  192.168.100.10
worker-x86-2.cluster.example.com.    IN  A  192.168.100.11
worker-x86-3.cluster.example.com.    IN  A  192.168.100.12

Allow recursive queries from the gateway and worker subnet

The bastion DNS server is also the upstream resolver for the gateway VM and all worker VMs. By default a BIND server only allows recursion from localhost and its own networks, so queries from those VMs are refused. Add the gateway's external IP (provider.gateway.ip) and the worker subnet (provider.networking.internalSubnet) to the recursion ACL — for example in a typical BIND configuration:

# /etc/named.conf
acl "internal_nets" {
    ...existing entries...;
    172.16.1.100/32;        # provider.gateway.ip
    192.168.100.0/24;       # provider.networking.internalSubnet
};
options {
    allow-query       { localhost; internal_nets; };
    allow-recursion   { localhost; internal_nets; };
    allow-query-cache { localhost; internal_nets; };
};

The Getting Started guide — step C.1 covers this in detail, including the stop/start requirement for named-chroot.

docs.title: Routing Configuration
docs.text:
Routing is handled by scripts driven by setup_env.sh

You do not set IP addresses or routes by hand. After running generate-setup (which writes setup_env.sh), the scripts and kustomize overlays in the Getting Started guide pick up all values automatically:

  • Mediated topology — main-cluster/scripts/01-add-route.sh and 02-firewall-setup.sh configure the bastion route and firewall rules (step C.2). Both scripts source setup_env.sh — no manual editing needed.
  • Direct topology — generate-setup writes a ready-to-apply route MachineConfig into main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/ (applied with oc apply -k in step C.4).

docs.title: Registry Strategy Selection
docs.text:
Record your choice in workspace/integration-setup.yaml, then follow the setup guide

Set registry.model to your chosen strategy before running generate-setup. The script wires the correct registry URLs and credentials into setup_env.sh and operator/build/config.env automatically. The actual HAProxy proxy and credential setup is then handled by scripts in the Getting Started guide (steps C.5 and C.6) that source setup_env.sh — no manual variable editing needed.

Choose your container image registry strategy:

docs.title: Option 1: Bastion Registry Proxy (Recommended) — registry.model: cross-cluster
docs.text:
Use when: - You want to build multi-architecture images - HCI workers on main cluster cannot directly access HCI cluster registry - You need a unified registry accessible from both clusters

Architecture: - HCI cluster has built-in Fusion Data Foundation (FDF) with S3 storage (NooBaa) - HCI cluster's image registry uses FDF S3 for persistent storage - HAProxy on main cluster's bastion proxies registry traffic to HCI cluster - Enables all workers (s390x and x86) to access HCI registry

Setup: Set registry.model: cross-cluster in workspace/integration-setup.yaml. The actual HAProxy and credential setup is handled by setup-registry-proxy.sh (step C.5) and setup-registry-access.sh (step C.6) — both source setup_env.sh.

Documentation: Bastion Registry README

Pros: - ✅ Persistent storage via HCI cluster's built-in FDF (no external S3 needed) - ✅ Works for all network topologies - ✅ Enables cross-cluster builds - ✅ Single registry for all architectures - ✅ No persistent storage required on main cluster

Cons: - ❌ Requires bastion HAProxy configuration - ❌ Additional infrastructure component (proxy) - ❌ Self-signed certificate (insecure registry config needed)

docs.title: Option 2: Public Registry (quay.io, ICR, etc.) — registry.model: external
docs.text:
Use when: - You have access to external registry - You don't want to manage internal registry infrastructure - Internet connectivity is reliable

Setup: Set registry.model: external and registry.pullSecretName in workspace/integration-setup.yaml. Pre-create the pull secret on the main cluster before following the setup guide.

Pros: - ✅ No infrastructure to manage - ✅ High availability - ✅ Valid SSL certificates - ✅ Often includes image scanning

Cons: - ❌ Requires internet connectivity - ❌ May have cost implications - ❌ Data egress from clusters - ❌ Dependency on external service

docs.title: Option 3: Main Cluster Internal Registry (Not Recommended) — registry.model: local-s2i
docs.text:
Use when: - Testing only - Temporary deployments - No persistent storage requirements

Setup: Set registry.model: local-s2i in workspace/integration-setup.yaml. No additional infrastructure needed — images are built and stored in the main cluster's internal ImageStream registry.

Pros: - ✅ No additional setup - ✅ Already available

Cons: - ❌ Ephemeral storage - images lost on pod restart - ❌ Not suitable for production - ❌ May not be accessible from HCI workers

docs.title: Decision Matrix
docs.text:
Requirement Bastion Proxy (cross-cluster) Public Registry (external) Internal Registry (local-s2i) Persistent Storage ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ❌ No (ephemeral) Multi-arch Builds ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ⚠️ Limited Production Ready ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ❌ No Setup Complexity Medium Low None External Dependency No Yes No Cost Infrastructure Service fees None

Recommendation: Use cross-cluster (bastion registry proxy) for production deployments, or external if you prefer a managed registry service.

docs.title: Deployment Variant Selection
docs.text:
Record your choice in workspace/integration-setup.yaml

Set consumer.networking.topology to mediated or direct. generate-setup uses this to generate the correct kustomize overlays and to include the mediated-topology fields (internalNetwork, internalGateway) in setup_env.sh. See Deployment Variants for a detailed comparison.

Choose your deployment variant based on your main cluster network topology:

docs.title: Mediated Topology
docs.text:
Use when: - Main cluster nodes are in a private network not directly reachable from the HCI cluster - Bastion host provides external connectivity

Requirements: - Bastion must route to HCI internal network - DNS provided by bastion - Gateway VM connects via bastion's public IP

docs.title: Direct Topology
docs.text:
Use when: - Main cluster nodes are on the same routable network as the HCI cluster - Direct connectivity between main cluster nodes and HCI

Requirements: - Master nodes need a static route to the HCI internal subnet — generated by generate-setup into main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/ - Gateway VM on same network as main cluster - Direct DNS resolution

See Deployment Variants for detailed comparison.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: This document provides a comprehensive overview of the Fusion HCI multi-architecture integration architecture, explaining how x86 worker nodes running on a Fusion HCI cluster can be integrated into a main OpenShift cluster running on a different architecture (s390x, ARM, or Power).

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The Fusion HCI multi-architecture integration enables:

  • Main cluster runs on one architecture (e.g., s390x/LinuxONE, ARM, or Power)
  • Additional x86 worker nodes provided as VMs from Fusion HCI via OpenShift Virtualization
  • VMs created in the HCI management cluster within a dedicated namespace
  • Single unified cluster with mixed architecture worker nodes

This architecture enables workloads requiring x86 architecture to run alongside the main cluster's native architecture workloads, with unified management and orchestration.

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Cluster
docs.text:
OpenShift supports running worker nodes with different CPU architectures in the same cluster:

  • Control plane must be single architecture (e.g., s390x, ARM, or Power)
  • Worker nodes can be mixed architectures (main + x86)
  • Container images must be multi-arch manifests or architecture-specific
  • Workload scheduling uses node selectors and tolerations for architecture targeting

docs.title: Why This Architecture?
docs.text:
Benefits:

  1. Unified Management: Single cluster for all workloads
  2. Resource Optimization: Use x86 hardware for x86-specific workloads
  3. Flexibility: Run workloads on optimal architecture
  4. Cost Efficiency: Leverage existing Fusion HCI investment
  5. Simplified Operations: One cluster to manage, monitor, and secure

Use Cases:

  • Legacy x86 applications that can't be recompiled for other architectures
  • Third-party software only available for x86
  • Development/testing of multi-arch applications
  • Gradual migration strategies
  • Workload-specific performance optimization

docs.title: 1. External Network (Localnet)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Connects gateway VM to main cluster network
  • Technology: OVN-Kubernetes ClusterUserDefinedNetwork with localnet topology
  • Configuration: Maps to physical network interface on HCI nodes
  • IP Assignment: Static IP on the gateway VM, set via cloud-init

docs.title: 2. Internal Network (Layer2)
docs.text:
• Purpose: Isolated network for HCI worker VMs
  • Technology: OVN-Kubernetes UserDefinedNetwork with Layer2 topology
  • Network: 192.168.100.0/24 (set by provider.networking.internalSubnet)
  • Gateway: 192.168.100.1 (network address + .1, the gateway VM)
  • IP Assignment: Gateway VM static (cloud-init); workers via static DHCP reservations on the gateway

docs.title: 3. Gateway VM
docs.text:
The gateway VM provides critical services:

  • Routing: Forwards traffic between internal and external networks
  • DHCP: Static reservations (MAC, IP, hostname) for the worker VMs
  • Network boot: iPXE (TFTP + HTTP) for RHCOS installation
  • DNS Forwarding: Resolves main cluster hostnames
  • NAT: Selective masquerading for internet traffic

Gateway VM Specifications (defaults; override with provider.gateway.resources): - OS: CentOS Stream 9 (or similar) - vCPU: 2 - Memory: 4GB - Storage: 30GB - Network Interfaces: 2 (external + internal)

docs.title: Routing Strategies
docs.text: The integration supports two routing variants based on main cluster network topology:

docs.title: Mediated Topology (Private Network)
docs.text:
• Main cluster nodes in a private network (e.g., 10.0.0.0/24, consumer.networking.internalNetwork)
  • Bastion host routes all traffic
  • Gateway VM connects to bastion's external IP
  • No changes to main cluster nodes

docs.title: Direct Topology (Public Network)
docs.text:
• Main cluster nodes on a public/shared network (e.g., 172.16.0.0/16)
  • Direct connectivity between nodes and gateway VM
  • Static routes added to master and worker nodes
  • More flexible but requires node configuration

See Deployment Variants for detailed comparison.

docs.title: 1. Cluster-Admin Resources (Cluster-Scoped)
docs.text:
Applied once by cluster administrator:

  • ClusterUserDefinedNetwork: External network definition
  • Namespace Labels: Enable network access per namespace

docs.title: 2. Integration Namespace Resources
docs.text:
Deployed per integration namespace:

  • UserDefinedNetwork: Internal worker network
  • Gateway VM: Routing and services
  • Worker VMs: x86 worker nodes
  • Secrets: Gateway cloud-init data, SSH keys
  • ConfigMaps: Network configuration

docs.title: 1. MachineConfigPool
docs.text:
Separate pool for HCI workers:

  • Name: hci-vm
  • Selector: node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""
  • Purpose: Isolate HCI worker configuration

docs.title: 2. MachineConfigs
docs.text:
Configuration for HCI workers:

  • Kernel Arguments: Boot parameters, multipath settings
  • Network Configuration: Interface management (variant-specific)
  • Kernel arguments: x86 VM-specific boot parameters (disable multipath, configure interfaces)

docs.title: 3. HCI Node Manager (sidecars)
docs.text:
Deployed as sidecar containers inside the hci-consumer-operator pod:

  • CSR Auto-Approval (csr-approver): stream-watch, millisecond reaction time
  • Node Labeling (node-labeler): applies node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: "" before MCO renders ignition
  • Permanent: re-reads config from hci-node-manager-config ConfigMap every ~30 s

docs.title: 4. hci-consumer Operator ✅ Complete
docs.text:
Kubernetes operator for steady-state worker VM lifecycle (Epics 1 and 2 complete, Epics 3–4 in backlog):

  • CRD: WorkerPool (hci-integration.openshift.io/v1alpha1) — declarative desired worker count
  • Scale-up: creates DataVolume + VirtualMachine on HCI when workers.count increases
  • Scale-down: deletes VM and node when workers.count decreases, gated on node NotReady state
  • Observe/diff/act: all API calls isolated in observe_world.yml; diff_desired_actual.yml is pure set arithmetic
  • maxPoolSize enforcement: CEL admission rule on CRD + runtime clamping with CR condition

See the hci-consumer operator README and the Operator Roadmap for full implementation status.

docs.title: Configuration Input
docs.text:
All cluster-pair decisions are captured once in a single file, workspace/integration-setup.yaml, filled in jointly by the HCI admin (provider.*) and the main cluster admin (consumer.*). The generate-setup script derives everything else from it: setup_env.sh, operator/build/config.env, the direct-topology route MachineConfigs, the DNS zone files and an initial WorkerPool CR with workers.count: 0. See Setup Concept for the design and Prerequisites for the how-to.

The concrete values shown as examples throughout the architecture pages map to these fields:

Example value in these pages integration-setup.yaml field mediated or direct routing consumer.networking.topology Main cluster domain cluster.example.com consumer.domain DNS server 172.16.0.1 (the bastion) consumer.networking.dnsServer Main cluster internal network 10.0.0.0/24 (mediated only) consumer.networking.internalNetwork Gateway towards that network 172.16.0.1 (mediated only) consumer.networking.internalGateway MachineConfigPool hci-vm consumer.machineConfigPool (default hci-vm) Operator namespace hci-node-manager consumer.operatorNamespace Worker name prefix worker-x86 consumer.workers.namePrefix Worker VM resources (4 vCPU, 8Gi, 50Gi) consumer.workers.resources (operator defaults) HCI namespace main-cluster-workers provider.namespace Gateway external IP 172.16.1.100, prefix 16, default router 172.16.0.1 provider.gateway.ip, .prefixLength, .defaultRouter Gateway VM resources (2 vCPU, 4Gi, 30Gi) provider.gateway.resources (operator defaults) Internal worker network 192.168.100.0/24 provider.networking.internalSubnet MAC address prefix 52:54:01 provider.networking.macPrefix (default 52:54:00) Maximum number of workers 10 provider.maxPoolSize Image registry strategy registry.model

docs.title: Phase 1: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Main cluster operational with OpenShift 4.20+
  2. HCI cluster operational with OpenShift Virtualization
  3. Network connectivity between clusters
  4. Registry strategy selected (registry.model)
  5. workspace/integration-setup.yaml completed and generate-setup run — this also produces the DNS zone files to be added on the bastion

docs.title: Phase 2: Main Cluster Preparation
docs.text:
1. Create MachineConfigPool for HCI workers
  2. Apply MachineConfigs (base + variant overlay; the direct-topology route MachineConfigs are generated by generate-setup)
  3. Deploy HCI node manager (optional but recommended)
  4. Configure registry access (if using bastion proxy)

docs.title: Phase 3: HCI Cluster Preparation
docs.text:
1. Cluster admin applies ClusterUserDefinedNetwork
  2. Create and label integration namespace
  3. Run setup-provider-credentials.sh to create operator credential Secrets

docs.title: Phase 4: Deployment
docs.text:
1. Apply the generated WorkerPool CR (workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml, workers.count: 0) — hci-consumer creates the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR automatically
  2. hci-provisioner creates UDN, gateway VM, ignition, and bootfiles; sets WorkerPool phase → Ready
  3. Set workers.count on the live WorkerPool; hci-consumer scales up and worker VMs network-boot (iPXE) and install RHCOS
  4. Workers join main cluster; CSRs approved automatically by the csr-approver sidecar; nodes become Ready

docs.title: Phase 5: Verification
docs.text:
1. Verify nodes appear in main cluster
  2. Check node labels and MachineConfigPool membership
  3. Test workload deployment on x86 workers
  4. Verify cross-architecture pod communication

docs.title: Namespace Isolation
docs.text:
• HCI workers deployed in dedicated namespace
  • Network policies control traffic flow
  • RBAC limits access to integration resources
  • Separate service accounts for components

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
• Internal worker network isolated from HCI pod network
  • Gateway VM controls all external access
  • Firewall rules on gateway VM
  • Optional network policies on main cluster

docs.title: Certificate Management
docs.text:
• Main cluster CA trusted by HCI workers
  • Node certificates issued by main cluster
  • TLS for all API communication
  • Automatic certificate rotation

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
• SSH keys managed via secrets
  • Ignition configuration secured
  • RBAC for HCI cluster resources
  • Audit logging enabled

docs.title: Network Latency
docs.text:
• Gateway VM overhead: ~0.5-1ms additional latency
  • Cross-cluster communication: Depends on physical network
  • Mitigation: Place gateway VM on low-latency nodes

docs.title: Nested Virtualization
docs.text:
• HCI workers are VMs: Some overhead vs bare metal
  • CPU performance: ~5-10% overhead
  • Memory: Direct mapping, minimal overhead
  • Storage: Depends on HCI storage backend

docs.title: Resource Allocation
docs.text:
Gateway VM: - 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM (minimal overhead) - Can be increased for high-throughput scenarios

Worker VMs: - Default: 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM, 50GB disk per worker (consumer.workers.resources) - Adjust based on workload requirements - Consider HCI node capacity

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling
docs.text:
• Add workers: Increase WorkerPool.spec.consumer.workers.count
  • Multiple namespaces: Support multiple integration namespaces
  • Gateway HA: Deploy multiple gateway VMs for redundancy

docs.title: Vertical Scaling
docs.text:
• Worker resources: Adjust vCPU/memory per worker
  • Gateway resources: Increase for high-throughput scenarios
  • Storage: Expand worker VM disks as needed

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Network bandwidth: Gateway VM is potential bottleneck
  • HCI capacity: Limited by physical HCI resources
  • IP address space: Internal network size (default /24 = 254 hosts)

docs.title: Gateway VM HA
docs.text:
Options for gateway VM redundancy:

  1. Active-Passive: Deploy backup gateway VM
  2. Active-Active: Multiple gateways with load balancing
  3. VM Live Migration: Leverage OpenShift Virtualization HA

docs.title: Worker VM HA
docs.text:
• Pod disruption budgets: Protect workloads during maintenance
  • Node affinity: Spread workers across HCI nodes
  • VM live migration: Move VMs without downtime

docs.title: Network HA
docs.text:
• Multiple gateway VMs: Eliminate single point of failure
  • Redundant routing: Multiple paths to main cluster
  • Monitoring: Detect and alert on network issues

docs.title: HCI Cluster-Level HA
docs.text:
The HA mechanisms above (live migration, node affinity, gateway redundancy) all operate within a single Fusion HCI cluster. They protect against individual HCI host failures but cannot protect against a full HCI cluster outage.

For deployments where loss of all x86 workers is unacceptable, the recommended approach is dual-HCI: two independent Fusion HCI units, each with its own WorkerPool CR on the main cluster. Worker VMs are spread across both units; if one HCI cluster goes down, the other continues to supply x86 capacity. This requires the main cluster workloads to tolerate reduced x86 capacity during a single-unit outage (e.g. via pod disruption budgets and appropriate replica counts).

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text:
Gateway VM: - Network throughput (in/out) - Packet loss rate - CPU and memory utilization - DHCP lease activity

Worker VMs: - Node status and readiness - Resource utilization - Network connectivity - Pod scheduling success rate

Integration Health: - CSR approval rate - Node join time - Cross-architecture pod communication latency

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
• Gateway VM logs (dnsmasq, firewalld, NetworkManager)
  • Worker VM console logs
  • Main cluster node logs
  • HCI cluster virtualization logs

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text:
• Gateway VM down
  • Worker VM failed to join
  • Network connectivity issues
  • Resource exhaustion

docs.title: Adding Workers
docs.text:
1. Increase WorkerPool.spec.consumer.workers.count
  2. The hci-consumer operator creates the additional VMs automatically
  3. Monitor CSR approval and node join via oc get workerpool -w
  4. Verify new nodes are Ready

docs.title: Removing Workers
docs.text:
1. Decrease WorkerPool.spec.consumer.workers.count
  2. The operator cordons and drains surplus nodes, then deletes the VMs
  3. WorkerPool.status.phase shows ScalingDown / ScalingDownBlocked until complete

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Main Cluster Upgrade: - HCI workers upgrade with main cluster - MachineConfigPool manages rolling updates - Workers reboot to apply new configuration

HCI Cluster Upgrade: - Gateway VM may need recreation - Worker VMs unaffected (run RHCOS from main cluster) - Plan maintenance window for gateway VM updates

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: See Troubleshooting Guide for detailed troubleshooting procedures.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
1. Start small: Deploy 1-2 workers initially
  2. Test thoroughly: Verify functionality before scaling
  3. CSR approval is automatic: the csr-approver sidecar in the operator handles it
  4. Document configuration: Keep WorkerPool and WorkerPoolProvisioning CR manifests in version control

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
1. Monitor continuously: Set up alerts for critical metrics
  2. Regular backups: Back up CR manifests and configurations
  3. Plan maintenance: Schedule updates during low-traffic periods
  4. Test disaster recovery: Verify recovery procedures work

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Least privilege: Use minimal RBAC permissions
  2. Network policies: Restrict traffic where possible
  3. Regular updates: Keep gateway VM OS updated
  4. Audit logs: Review logs regularly for anomalies

docs.title: Current Limitations
docs.text:
1. Single gateway VM: Potential single point of failure (HA possible but not default)
  2. Network bandwidth: Gateway VM throughput limited by VM resources
  3. IP address space: Internal network /24 limits to ~250 workers
  4. CSR approval and node labeling: Handled automatically by the csr-approver and node-labeler sidecars in the hci-consumer-operator Deployment
  5. HCI availability is a hard dependency for the main cluster: All x86 worker nodes run as VMs on the Fusion HCI box. If the HCI cluster becomes unavailable (hardware failure, maintenance, power loss), the main cluster loses those worker nodes and has no path to replace them until HCI recovers. Intra-HCI redundancy (VM live migration, node affinity across HCI hosts) mitigates individual host failures within the HCI box, but does not protect against a full HCI cluster outage. HA implication: deployments with strict availability requirements should operate two independent Fusion HCI units, each backing a separate WorkerPool CR, so that the main cluster retains x86 capacity if one HCI unit is lost.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text:
1. OVN IPAM with localnet: OVN IPAM is disabled; the gateway VM's IPs are set via cloud-init and the workers' IPs via DHCP reservations on the gateway
  2. Dual network conflict: Worker VMs must disable HCI pod network interface
  3. MachineConfig inheritance: Requires platform labeling to prevent conflicts

docs.title: Workarounds
docs.text: See Troubleshooting Guide for detailed workarounds.

docs.title: Short-term
docs.text:
• Gateway VM HA implementation
  • Enhanced monitoring dashboards
  • Automated testing framework
