docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The Fusion HCI multi-architecture integration provides a robust, scalable solution for extending OpenShift clusters with x86 worker nodes. By leveraging OpenShift Virtualization and OVN-Kubernetes networking, the integration maintains cloud-native principles while enabling multi-architecture workload deployment.

The architecture balances complexity, performance, and operational requirements, providing a production-ready solution for organizations needing multi-architecture capabilities.

docs.title: Network Design
docs.text: This document provides detailed information about the network architecture used in the Fusion HCI multi-architecture integration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The network design uses a dual-network approach with OVN-Kubernetes to provide:

  • External connectivity to the main cluster network
  • Internal isolation for HCI worker VMs
  • Gateway routing between networks
  • DHCP and network boot services for worker provisioning

Nothing on this page is configured by hand

The networks, gateway VM configuration (addressing, routing, NAT, firewall, dnsmasq) and worker NICs described here are created by the operators from the values in integration-setup.yaml. The snippets show what the operators set up so that you can understand and troubleshoot it; they are not steps to execute. The only manual network step is the one-time external network on the HCI cluster (see Localnet).

docs.title: OVN-Kubernetes Network Types
docs.text: The integration uses two OVN-Kubernetes network topologies:

docs.title: 1. Localnet (External Network)
docs.text:
Purpose: Connect gateway VM to physical network

Characteristics: - Maps directly to physical network interface - Provides external connectivity - No OVN overlay encapsulation - Direct Layer 2 access to physical network

Configuration: 

apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: ClusterUserDefinedNetwork
metadata:
  name: router-external-network
spec:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      hci-gateway-enabled: "true"
  network:
    topology: Localnet
    localnet:
      physicalNetworkName: localnet1
      role: Secondary
      mtu: 1500
      ipam:
        mode: Disabled  # no OVN IPAM; see IP Assignment Methods

Key Points: - Cluster-scoped resource (one per HCI cluster), created once by the HCI cluster admin with hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml (see Getting Started) - Each integration namespace on the HCI cluster must carry the label hci-gateway-enabled=true to attach to it - Requires physical network mapping on HCI nodes - IPAM disabled - IPs are set statically on the gateway VM and via DHCP reservations for workers - Multiple namespaces can use same network

docs.title: 2. Layer2 (Internal Network)
docs.text:
Purpose: Isolated network for HCI worker VMs

Characteristics: - Pure OVN logical switch - No physical network mapping - Isolated from HCI pod network - Gateway VM provides routing

Configuration: 

apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: UserDefinedNetwork
metadata:
  name: router-internal-network
  namespace: main-cluster-workers
spec:
  topology: Layer2
  layer2:
    role: Secondary
    ipam:
      mode: Disabled  # no OVN IPAM; see IP Assignment Methods

Key Points: - Namespace-scoped resource, created per integration by hci-provisioner in provider.namespace (UDN step) - Completely isolated from other networks - No MTU is set; the OVN-Kubernetes default applies (see MTU Considerations) - Gateway VM bridges to external network

docs.title: Address Allocation
docs.text:
All addresses, names and sizes on this page are the example values from templates/integration-setup.example.yaml. The real values are set once in integration-setup.yaml; see the field mapping in Architecture Overview.

External Network (varies by deployment):
├── Mediated Topology: main cluster 10.0.0.0/24 (consumer.networking.internalNetwork)
├── Direct Topology: 172.16.0.0/16 (derived from provider.gateway.ip / prefixLength)
├── Bastion / DNS server: 172.16.0.1 (consumer.networking.dnsServer)
└── Gateway VM: 172.16.1.100 (provider.gateway.ip)

Internal Network (provider.networking.internalSubnet):
├── Network: 192.168.100.0/24
├── Gateway: 192.168.100.1 (network address + .1)
├── Workers: 192.168.100.10-19 (network address + .10, one per slot up to provider.maxPoolSize = 10)
└── Remainder: unused

docs.title: IP Assignment Methods
docs.text: OVN IPAM is disabled on both networks. Addresses are assigned in two different ways:

docs.title: Gateway VM: static configuration via cloud-init
docs.text:
The hci-provisioner renders the gateway's NetworkManager connections into its cloud-init data. The external NIC gets the address from provider.gateway.ip:

# external connection (eth1), MAC 52:54:01:00:00:01
[ipv4]
method=manual
addresses=172.16.1.100/16        # provider.gateway.ip / prefixLength
gateway=172.16.0.1               # provider.gateway.defaultRouter
dns=172.16.0.1                   # consumer.networking.dnsServer
# mediated topology only:
route1=10.0.0.0/24,172.16.0.1    # consumer.networking.internalNetwork, internalGateway

The internal NIC (eth2) gets the first address of provider.networking.internalSubnet (192.168.100.1/24).

docs.title: Worker VMs: static DHCP reservations on the gateway
docs.text:
Worker VMs have no cloud-init. The gateway's dnsmasq runs DHCP in static-only mode, with one reservation per possible worker slot (up to provider.maxPoolSize):

# /etc/dnsmasq.d/pxe.conf (generated)
dhcp-range=192.168.100.0,static
dhcp-option=3,192.168.100.1                # default gateway = gateway VM
dhcp-option=6,172.16.0.1                   # DNS = consumer.networking.dnsServer

# one pair per slot: MAC -> IP, and the hostname for that slot
dhcp-host=52:54:01:00:00:10,192.168.100.10,set:host1
dhcp-option=tag:host1,12,worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com
dhcp-host=52:54:01:00:00:11,192.168.100.11,set:host2
dhcp-option=tag:host2,12,worker-x86-2.cluster.example.com
# ... up to slot 10 (192.168.100.19)

Advantages: - Predictable IP address and hostname per worker slot - No dynamic lease pool to manage; scaling within the pool limit needs no gateway change - No dependency on OVN IPAM - Supports network boot

docs.title: Routing Configuration
docs.text:
The gateway VM performs IP routing between networks:

# Enable IP forwarding
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# Route to main cluster (example)
ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.1

# Default route via external gateway
ip route add default via 172.16.0.1

docs.title: NAT Configuration
docs.text:
Selective NAT for different traffic types:

# Transparent routing (no NAT) for main cluster
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.100.0/24 \
  -d 10.0.0.0/24 -j ACCEPT

# Transparent routing (no NAT) for external network
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.100.0/24 \
  -d 172.16.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT

# Masquerading (NAT) for internet
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.100.0/24 \
  -o eth1 -j MASQUERADE

Why Selective NAT? - Main cluster needs to see real worker IPs for node management - External network may need real IPs for monitoring/logging - Internet traffic can use NAT for simplicity

docs.title: Mediated Topology (Private Network)
docs.text:
Main Cluster (10.0.0.0/24)
         ↓
    Bastion Host
    (internal side on 10.0.0.0/24)
    (172.16.0.1 external)
         ↓
   Route: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100
         ↓
    Gateway VM
    (172.16.1.100 external)
    (192.168.100.1 internal)
         ↓
    Worker VMs
    (192.168.100.10+)

Configuration: - Bastion routes to internal network - No changes to main cluster nodes - All traffic through bastion - Selected with consumer.networking.topology: mediated; the bastion route (main-cluster/scripts/01-add-route.sh) and firewall (02-firewall-setup.sh) are driven by the values generated from integration-setup.yaml (consumer.networking.internalNetwork, internalGateway, consumer.bastion.*)

docs.title: Direct Topology (Public Network)
docs.text:
Main Cluster (172.16.0.0/16)
    ├── Masters
    │   └── Route: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100
    └── Workers (s390x)
        └── Route: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100
         ↓
    Gateway VM
    (172.16.1.100 external)
    (192.168.100.1 internal)
         ↓
    Worker VMs
    (192.168.100.10+)

Configuration: - Direct connectivity to gateway VM - Static routes on master nodes - Static routes on s390x worker nodes - No bastion routing needed - Selected with consumer.networking.topology: direct (the default); the route MachineConfigs are generated by generate-setup from provider.gateway.ip and provider.networking.internalSubnet, and are created by the hci-consumer operator if absent

docs.title: DNS Resolution Flow
docs.text:
Workers receive the main cluster DNS server directly through DHCP (option 6). Their queries are routed through the gateway VM like any other traffic to the main cluster network:

Worker VM
    ↓ Query: api-int.cluster.example.com  (DNS server from DHCP)
Gateway VM (routes the packet)
    ↓
Main Cluster DNS (consumer.networking.dnsServer)
    ↓ Response, same path back
Worker VM

docs.title: Gateway VM DNS Configuration
docs.text:
The gateway's own dnsmasq also forwards to the main cluster DNS:

# /etc/dnsmasq.d/pxe.conf (generated)
no-resolv
server=172.16.0.1           # consumer.networking.dnsServer
domain=cluster.example.com  # consumer.domain

docs.title: Worker VM DNS Configuration
docs.text:
Worker VMs have no cloud-init. DNS server, search domain and hostname come from the gateway's DHCP reservation:

dhcp-option=6,172.16.0.1                   # DNS server
domain=cluster.example.com                 # DHCP option 15, search domain
dhcp-option=tag:host1,12,worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com   # hostname

docs.title: DHCP Configuration
docs.text: The gateway VM provides DHCP for worker VMs in static-only mode: there is no dynamic address pool, only one reservation per worker slot. See IP Assignment Methods for the generated configuration.

docs.title: Network Boot Configuration
docs.text:
Worker VMs boot via iPXE. dnsmasq serves the first-stage loader over TFTP and points iPXE to an HTTP boot script, nginx serves everything else:

# /etc/dnsmasq.d/pxe.conf (generated, excerpt)
enable-tftp
tftp-root=/var/lib/tftpboot
tftp-secure

# first request (native PXE firmware): iPXE loader over TFTP
# second request (iPXE announces itself with DHCP option 175): HTTP boot script
dhcp-match=set:ipxe,175
dhcp-boot=tag:!ipxe,undionly.kpxe
dhcp-boot=tag:ipxe,http://192.168.100.1/boot.ipxe

/var/lib/tftpboot/undionly.kpxe          iPXE loader (TFTP)
/var/www/html/boot.ipxe                  boot script (HTTP, port 80)
/var/www/html/rhcos/rhcos-live-*         RHCOS kernel, initramfs, rootfs (HTTP)
/var/www/html/rhcos/worker-hci.ign       ignition stub (HTTP)

The RHCOS files are downloaded by the gateway from the OpenShift mirror for the stream requested by the operator.

docs.title: Boot Process
docs.text:
1. Worker VM powers on and requests DHCP
  2. Gateway VM answers with the reserved IP, hostname and undionly.kpxe
  3. The firmware loads undionly.kpxe via TFTP and starts iPXE
  4. iPXE requests DHCP again and is pointed to http://192.168.100.1/boot.ipxe
  5. boot.ipxe shows a 10-second menu; with an empty disk it installs RHCOS
  6. iPXE loads the RHCOS live kernel and initramfs over HTTP
  7. The installer fetches worker-hci.ign and writes RHCOS to disk
  8. The worker reboots from disk and joins the cluster

The detailed sequence is in VM Provisioning.

docs.title: Firewall Rules
docs.text:
Gateway VM firewall configuration (set by the cloud-init data, excerpt):

# Interfaces and zones
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=external --add-interface=eth1
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-interface=eth2

# Forwarding between the internal and external side
firewall-cmd --permanent --direct --add-rule ipv4 filter FORWARD 0 -i eth2 -o eth1 -j ACCEPT
firewall-cmd --permanent --direct --add-rule ipv4 filter FORWARD 0 -i eth1 -o eth2 -j ACCEPT

# Services on the internal side: network boot and ignition
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-service=dhcp
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-service=tftp
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-service=http

# SSH (management)
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=external --add-service=ssh
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --add-service=ssh

The NAT rules shown under NAT Configuration are added the same way.

docs.title: Network Policies
docs.text:
Optional hardening, not created by the operators

The operators do not create any NetworkPolicy. The example below only shows what an administrator could add on top; adapt the labels (the gateway VM is named hci-gateway) before using it.

Standard Kubernetes network policies (enforced by OVN-Kubernetes) can restrict traffic:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-gateway-only
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: worker-vm
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: gateway-vm
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: gateway-vm

docs.title: MTU Sizing
docs.text:
Physical Network: 1500 (standard Ethernet)
    ↓
Localnet (external): 1500 (set in cluster-network-setup.yaml, no encapsulation)
    ↓
Layer2 (internal): OVN-Kubernetes default (no MTU set by the provisioner)

docs.title: Why the Internal Network May Need a Lower MTU
docs.text:
• OVN adds encapsulation headers (Geneve) on the internal Layer2 network
  • Typical overhead: 50-100 bytes
  • The operators neither set an MTU on the internal network nor send an MTU to the workers via DHCP

docs.title: MTU Configuration
docs.text:
The external network MTU is set once in hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml:

localnet:
  mtu: 1500

If your environment requires a specific MTU on the internal network, verify the effective value on the UserDefinedNetwork and inside a worker VM after the first worker is up.

docs.title: Network Throughput
docs.text:
Gateway VM as Bottleneck: - VM network throughput: ~10 Gbps typical - Physical network: 25-50 Gbps available - Gateway VM is limiting factor

Mitigation: - Increase gateway VM vCPU allocation - Use multiple gateway VMs for HA/load balancing - Enable virtio network drivers - Consider SR-IOV for high-performance scenarios

docs.title: Latency Optimization
docs.text:
Typical Latencies: - Physical network: <0.1ms - OVN overlay: +0.2-0.5ms - Gateway VM routing: +0.5-1ms - Total: ~1-2ms additional latency

Optimization: - Place gateway VM on low-latency nodes - Use CPU pinning for gateway VM - Enable NUMA awareness - Minimize network hops

docs.title: High Availability
docs.text:
Not implemented

The operators create exactly one gateway VM per integration (hci-gateway). The multi-gateway layout below is a design option; Gateway VM HA is listed under Future Enhancements in the Architecture Overview.

docs.title: Multiple Gateway VMs
docs.text:
A redundant design would use multiple gateway VMs:

# Gateway VM 1
external: 172.16.1.100
internal: 192.168.100.1

# Gateway VM 2
external: 172.16.1.101
internal: 192.168.100.2

Load Balancing Options: 1. Round-robin DNS 2. VRRP (keepalived) 3. BGP routing 4. External load balancer

docs.title: Failover Scenarios
docs.text:
Gateway VM Failure: 1. Detect failure (health check) 2. Promote backup gateway 3. Update routing tables 4. Workers reconnect automatically

Network Failure: 1. OVN detects link down 2. Reroutes traffic if alternate path exists 3. Alerts monitoring system

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text:
Gateway VM: - Network throughput (in/out) - Packet loss rate - NAT connection table size - CPU utilization - Memory utilization

Network Health: - Latency between networks - Packet loss percentage - MTU path discovery results - DNS resolution time

docs.title: Monitoring Tools
docs.text:
# Network throughput
iftop -i eth1

# Packet loss
ping -c 100 192.168.100.10 | grep loss

# NAT connections
conntrack -L | wc -l

# DNS performance
dig @192.168.100.1 api.cluster.example.com +stats

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
Workers can't reach main cluster: - Check gateway VM routing table - Verify NAT rules (should NOT NAT cluster traffic) - Test connectivity from gateway VM - Check firewall rules

DNS resolution fails: - Verify gateway VM DNS forwarder configuration - Check main cluster DNS server accessibility - Test DNS from gateway VM - Verify worker VM DNS configuration

Network boot fails: - Check dnsmasq (DHCP and TFTP) and nginx (HTTP) on the gateway VM - Check that the worker's MAC address has a dhcp-host reservation - Check undionly.kpxe in the TFTP root and boot.ipxe in the HTTP root - Check that the RHCOS boot files and current-version.txt exist under /var/www/html/rhcos/ - Verify network connectivity during boot

See Troubleshooting Guide for detailed solutions.

docs.title: Network Design
docs.text:
1. Use static IPs for gateway VM - Ensures consistent routing
  2. Document IP allocations - Maintain IP address inventory
  3. Plan for growth - Reserve IP ranges for future workers
  4. Monitor network performance - Establish baselines

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Minimize exposed services - Only open required ports
  2. Use network policies - Restrict traffic where possible
  3. Regular security audits - Review firewall rules
  4. Encrypt sensitive traffic - Use TLS for management

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
1. Automate configuration - Let the operators generate the gateway configuration from integration-setup.yaml
  2. Test failover scenarios - Verify HA works
  3. Monitor continuously - Set up alerts
  4. Document changes - Keep network diagrams updated

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document describes the provider/consumer architecture for the Fusion HCI integration, inspired by the ODF (OpenShift Data Foundation) Storage Provider/Client model. The goal is secure, operator-driven lifecycle management for multi-architecture worker nodes: x86 VMs running on a Fusion HCI cluster join an s390x (LinuxONE) OpenShift cluster as worker nodes.

docs.title: Three-Actor Model
docs.text:
The architecture separates concerns across three distinct actors, each with a strictly limited privilege scope:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HCI Cluster (provider)                                          │
│                                                                 │
│  [HCI Provider Operator] — Epic 3, planned                     │
│    Manages: ComputeConsumerRequest, namespaces, quotas,         │
│    onboarding tickets                                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ one-time ticket (24h, elevated) — Epic 3 future
                  ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Main (LO) Cluster                                               │
│                                                                 │
│  [HCI Provisioning Operator] — Epic 2, COMPLETE ✅             │
│    Drives WorkerPoolProvisioning CR steps: UDN, GatewayVM,     │
│    Credentials, Ignition, MachineConfig (bootstrap + teardown). │
│    Bootstrap and teardown confirmed end-to-end on live clusters.│
│                                                                 │
│  [HCI Consumer Operator] — Epic 1, COMPLETE ✅                 │
│    Permanent. Reconciles WorkerPool CR → HCI worker VMs.       │
│    Creates WorkerPoolProvisioning CRs on bootstrap/teardown.   │
│    Worker scale-up/scale-down confirmed on live clusters.       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key privilege-separation principle: the steady-state operator (which runs forever) never holds the elevated bootstrap credentials. The ticket exists only for the lifetime of the one-shot Bootstrap Job.

docs.title: WorkerPool CRD
docs.text:
The WorkerPool custom resource is the single control surface for the steady-state operator. It is installed on the main (LO) cluster.

API group: hci-integration.openshift.io/v1alpha1 Short name: wp Namespace-scoped

apiVersion: hci-integration.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkerPool
metadata:
  name: hci-workers
  namespace: hci-node-manager
spec:
  provider:
    apiEndpoint: "https://api.hci.example.com:6443"
    namespace: "main-cluster-workers"
    credentialsSecret: hci-provisioner-credentials
    maxPoolSize: 10
    gateway:
      ip: "172.16.1.100"
      prefixLength: 16
      defaultRouter: "172.16.0.1"
    networking:
      macPrefix: "52:54:01"
      internalSubnet: "192.168.100.0/24"

  consumer:
    networking:
      topology: direct    # or: mediated
      dnsServer: "172.16.0.1"
    workers:
      namePrefix: worker-x86
      count: 3          # desired number of HCI worker VMs / LO nodes
    machineConfigPool: hci-vm

status:
  phase: Ready          # Provisioning | Ready | Deprovisioning | Failed
  conditions:
    - type: ProviderCredentialsReady
      status: "True"
      reason: SecretFound
      message: "Provider credentials Secret found."
    - type: ScaleDownBlocked
      status: "False"
      reason: NoPendingDrain
      message: "No scale-down blocked."
    - type: CountExceedsMaxPoolSize
      status: "False"
      reason: CountWithinBounds
      message: "workers.count is within maxPoolSize."

docs.title: Reconciliation Logic
docs.text:
The operator follows a strict observe → diff → act pattern:

  1. Observe (observe_world.yml): reads the credentials Secret, lists all operator-owned VMs on HCI (by label), lists all matching nodes on the LO cluster, determines which nodes are Ready (have kubelet running). Zero decisions.

  2. Diff (diff_desired_actual.yml): pure set arithmetic.

  3. Computes vms_to_create = indices in 1..count not covered by an existing VM
  4. Computes vms_to_delete = existing VMs whose node is NotReady, capped at surplus

  5. Applies maxPoolSize clamping with a CountExceedsMaxPoolSize condition

  6. Act (scale_up.yml, scale_down.yml):

  7. Scale-up: create DataVolume + VirtualMachine on HCI for each missing name
  8. Scale-down: delete node object (LO) → delete VM (HCI) → delete DataVolume (HCI)

Scale-down safety gate: a VM is only eligible for deletion when its corresponding node's Ready condition is not True (kubelet has stopped). LOOps stops the VM it wants to remove; the operator observes the NotReady state and acts. No operator-side drain. The ScaleDownBlocked condition is set when workers.count is reduced but no NotReady node is yet available.

docs.title: Complementary Component: hci-node-manager
docs.text:
The node manager runs as sidecar containers (csr-approver, node-labeler) inside the hci-consumer-operator Deployment. Responsibilities are strictly separated:

Component Responsibility hci-consumer operator VM lifecycle: create, delete DataVolume + VM on HCI hci-node-manager sidecars Node join: CSR approval + node labeling (stream-watch, ms reaction time)

hci-node-manager owns the time-critical node-join path. The hci-vm role label must arrive before MCO renders ignition for the node — a polling-based operator cannot meet this window. The two components have non-overlapping responsibilities.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text:
The operator ServiceAccount (config/rbac/role.yaml) has minimal permissions on the main cluster only:

  • Nodes: get, list, watch, patch, update (for labeling and deletion)
  • CertificateSigningRequests: get, list, watch, update (for CSR approval, delegated to hci-node-manager)
  • MachineConfigPools: get, list, watch
  • Pods: get, list (for eviction check, future LO-09/LO-10)

HCI cluster access is via the narrow kubeconfig Secret (namespace-scoped to the consumer namespace on HCI, VirtualMachine/DataVolume/PVC write + Secret/ConfigMap read only).

docs.title: Implemented: HCI Provisioning Operator (Epic 2)
docs.text:
A dedicated operator managing the full infrastructure lifecycle via the WorkerPoolProvisioning CRD. Triggered by the WorkerPool operator when bootstrap or teardown is needed. See provisioning-model.md for the complete design.

Key design principle: the credential scope is the discriminant between the two operators. The steady-state operator holds only a narrow SA token scoped to one HCI namespace. The provisioning operator holds broader credentials: MachineConfig write on LO, SSH key access, topology awareness. These never cross the operator boundary.

WorkerPool phase state machine: - Provisioning — WorkerPoolProvisioning (mode=bootstrap) in progress; worker reconcile skipped - Ready — all bootstrap steps complete; worker reconcile runs normally - Deprovisioning — WorkerPoolProvisioning (mode=teardown) in progress; worker reconcile skipped

Step execution model: each bootstrap/teardown step is a Kubernetes Job owned by the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR (via ownerReference). The provisioning operator watches Job termination status and owns all status.steps transitions. Jobs are garbage-collected automatically when the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR is deleted.

Credentials handover: BS-05 (automated SA/Secret creation) was descoped; credentials are created with a script. The Secret is referenced by name in WorkerPool.spec.provider.credentialsSecret.

docs.title: Planned: HCI Provider Operator (Epic 3)
docs.text:
Runs on the HCI cluster. Automates what the HCI admin currently does manually.

Responsibilities (not yet implemented): 1. Watch ComputeConsumerRequest CRDs — process consumer onboarding requests 2. Provision consumer namespace, CUDN label, ResourceQuota on HCI 3. Generate onboarding ticket: privileged bootstrap ServiceAccount + time-limited token 4. Surface ticket in a Secret for the HCI admin to hand to the LO team 5. Monitor quota usage per consumer

docs.title: Deferred: Negotiation Flow (Epic 4)
docs.text: LO-initiated cross-cluster capacity requests. Design open — chicken-and-egg discovery problem (how does LO know the HCI API endpoint before any credentials exist?). Deferred to iteration 2. See the project operator backlog for NEG-01/02/03 story descriptions.

docs.title: Credentials Deployment
docs.text:
The one-time cross-domain credentials handover is done by script, run from the repo root with setup_env.sh sourced. See Getting Started (steps B.2 and C.8) for the authoritative procedure.

# On the HCI cluster (cluster-admin required once)
./hci-cluster/setup-consumer-rbac.sh
# Script prints the oc create secret command to run on the LO bastion

# Or create the operator Secrets directly (both clusters logged in)
./operator/setup-provider-credentials.sh

These create, in the consumer namespace on HCI: - ServiceAccount(s), a namespace-scoped Role (VM, DataVolume, PVC write; Secret/ConfigMap read) and RoleBinding - A 1-year ServiceAccount token, written as a kubeconfig Secret on the LO cluster

The Secret name is referenced by WorkerPool.spec.provider.credentialsSecret (CRD default: hci-provisioner-credentials).

Open inconsistency

The two scripts and the operator defaults do not agree on the Secret layout: setup-consumer-rbac.sh prints hci-provider-credentials; setup-provider-credentials.sh writes two Secrets (hci-provider-credentials and hci-provisioner-credentials); the CRD and role defaults use hci-provisioner-credentials only. To be resolved as part of the setup rework.

docs.title: What the Steady-State Operator Can and Cannot Do on HCI
docs.text:
The operator's kubeconfig is scoped to one namespace (e.g. main-cluster-workers) and can: - Create / delete VirtualMachine and VirtualMachineInstance - Create / delete DataVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim - Read Secret and ConfigMap

It cannot: - Access any other namespace on HCI - Create namespaces, RBAC, or network resources - Approve CSRs or label nodes on HCI

docs.title: HCI Provisioning Model — Lifecycle Operator Design
Overview
docs.text:
This document describes the architecture of the HCI Provisioning Operator (Epic 2), which manages the full lifecycle of a consumer relationship: bootstrap (create infrastructure) and teardown (remove infrastructure) triggered by the WorkerPool CR.

The steady-state operator (Epic 1) handles only the continuous worker VM reconcile loop. It deliberately knows nothing about how the infrastructure was set up. The provisioning operator is responsible for everything that must exist before the steady-state operator can function, and for removing it when the consumer relationship ends.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
The credential scope is the clean discriminant between the two operators:

Operator Credential Scope Runs HCI Consumer Operator (Epic 1) Narrow SA token on HCI — permanent HCI: VirtualMachine + DataVolume CRUD in one namespace. LO (in-cluster RBAC): Node patch/delete, CSR approve, MachineConfigPool + MachineConfig get/list/watch/create (create-if-absent, BS-02b); SSH key Secret read (for desired-version.txt management) Continuously HCI Provisioning Operator (Epic 2) Broader SA on HCI — permanent for lifecycle ops HCI: gateway VM + DataVolume, UserDefinedNetwork. LO (in-cluster RBAC): MachineConfig read-only (to read the 99-worker-ssh key); SSH key Secret create/read On CR create / delete

The steady-state operator never holds: - Topology-aware gateway configuration (direct vs mediated branching in cloud-init) - Knowledge of the gateway VM spec - UserDefinedNetwork or gateway VM permissions on the provider

These belong exclusively to the provisioning operator. MachineConfigPool / MachineConfig creation was moved to the consumer operator in BS-02b, because those are consumer-cluster resources the provisioner has no business owning. Source of truth for permissions: operator/deploy/base/rbac.yaml.

Design decision — bootfiles version management (BS-06b): The hci_consumer role owns desired-version.txt on the gateway and the scale-up gate, not the provisioning operator. Rationale: - The consumer runs every reconcile and is the actor that suffers if bootfiles are wrong — it is the natural owner of the "are workers bootable?" question. - The provisioner's responsibility ends when infrastructure is set up. Tracking OCP versions post-bootstrap is outside its scope. - The consumer reads WorkerPoolProvisioning.status.sshKeySecret to obtain the SSH key name, then uses the provisioner keypair to write desired-version.txt via SSH. The gateway's rhcos-sync.timer handles the download autonomously. - Scale-up gate: GET /rhcos/current-version.txt == ClusterVersion.status.desired.version. Non-200 or mismatch → defer scale-up to next reconcile (safe default). - There is no Bootfiles step in WorkerPoolProvisioning — the provisioner step list covers only one-time infrastructure setup.

docs.title: The WorkerPoolProvisioning CRD
docs.text:
The provisioning operator introduces a new CRD: WorkerPoolProvisioning. This resource is created by the WorkerPool operator when it detects that provisioning is needed (gateway VM absent, phase Pending). It is the coordination board for all bootstrap and teardown steps.

apiVersion: hci-integration.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkerPoolProvisioning
metadata:
  name: hci-workers-bootstrap
  namespace: hci-node-manager
  ownerReferences:
    - apiVersion: hci-integration.openshift.io/v1alpha1
      kind: WorkerPool
      name: hci-workers
      # ownerReference ensures GC when WorkerPool is deleted
spec:
  workerPoolRef: hci-workers
  mode: bootstrap         # bootstrap | teardown
  # providerAccess and infrastructure.{gateway,network,capacity} are copied
  # from WorkerPool.spec.provider / spec.consumer at creation time
status:
  phase: InProgress       # Pending | InProgress | Complete | Failed
  steps:
    - name: GatewayVM
      status: InProgress  # Pending | InProgress | Complete | Failed
      message: "Creating gateway VM and DataVolume on HCI."
    - name: UDN
      status: Pending
    - name: Ignition
      status: Pending
    - name: Credentials
      status: Pending

The ownerReference to WorkerPool means Kubernetes garbage-collects the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR automatically when the WorkerPool is deleted.

docs.title: Step Execution Model
docs.text:
All steps currently run directly in the Ansible reconcile loop (advance_steps.yml dispatches to step_<name>.yml task files). Each step is idempotent and re-checked on every reconcile until it reaches a terminal state. The provisioning operator is the sole owner of step status.

Job-based steps: designed, not used

The original design ran each step as a Kubernetes Job owned by the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR (with ownerReference garbage collection and exit-code-driven status). advance_steps.yml still contains the Job launcher, but its input list is an empty placeholder — no step uses it today. Steps are cheap synchronous API calls (or SSH/TCP probes), so the extra Job indirection was not needed.

docs.title: Ownership Chain
docs.text:
WorkerPool  →owns→  WorkerPoolProvisioning

Deleting WorkerPool removes WorkerPoolProvisioning via Kubernetes garbage collection.

docs.title: Status Protocol
docs.text:
Actor Transition Trigger Provisioning operator Pending → InProgress When the step's resources are created (or step re-check starts) Provisioning operator InProgress → Complete Step's completion condition confirmed (e.g. TCP reachability for GatewayVM, resource absent for teardown) Provisioning operator InProgress → Failed Step error, or timeout exceeded (GatewayVM) Provisioning operator Failed → propagate Patches WorkerPool phase to Failed with message Provisioning operator all Complete → phase Complete Patches WorkerPool phase to Ready (bootstrap) / Deprovisioned (teardown)

Step results are collected during the reconcile and written to status.steps once (consolidated write), because the operator-sdk proxy caches reads for the duration of a reconcile and per-step writes would clobber each other.

docs.title: GatewayVM Step Design
docs.text:
The GatewayVM step is handled directly by the Ansible reconcile loop, not a Job. Rationale: creating three Kubernetes resources on HCI (Secret, DataVolume, VirtualMachine) is fast and synchronous. The slow part — waiting for the VM to boot and become reachable — must not block a single reconcile; it is re-observed on every subsequent reconcile until the VM is up or the timeout expires.

State machine:

State Condition Action Pending No gateway VM exists on HCI Apply cloud-init Secret + DataVolume + VirtualMachine; set step InProgress + record lastTransitionTime InProgress Resources exist; VM not yet reachable Check TCP gateway.external_ip:22; if open → set Complete; if lastTransitionTime elapsed > gateway_vm_timeout_seconds → set Failed Complete SSH port reachable No-op (terminal) Failed Timeout reached No-op (terminal); WorkerPoolProvisioning phase → Failed; WorkerPool phase → Failed

Topology-dependent cloud-init (direct vs mediated):

Element Direct Mediated route1= in external nmconnection absent networking.linuxone_network, networking.linuxone_gateway Masquerade exception rules none ACCEPT for linuxone_network and gateway.external_subnet before the catch-all MASQUERADE rule Catch-all MASQUERADE rule present (all outbound eth1) present (catches everything not matched by exceptions)

In direct topology the gateway simply masquerades all outbound traffic from internal_subnet via eth1. In mediated topology worker VM traffic to the s390x cluster network must appear with its original source IP (transparent routing) — masquerading is suppressed only for those specific destinations. Both cases use firewalld direct rules with priority 0 (exceptions) and priority 1 (catch-all MASQUERADE).

Teardown: delete VirtualMachine, wait for VMI to disappear (async), delete DataVolume, delete cloud-init Secret. Set step Complete once all three resources are absent.

Idempotency: all kubernetes.core.k8s state: present/absent calls are idempotent. If the operator restarts mid-step the resources already exist; re-applying is a no-op. TCP check resumes on the next reconcile.

Timeout default: gateway_vm_timeout_seconds: 600 (10 minutes). Configurable in roles/hci_provisioner/defaults/main.yml.

docs.title: Dependency Graph (bootstrap)
docs.text:
The active bootstrap steps and their dependencies are defined in roles/hci_provisioner/defaults/main.yml (bootstrap_steps):

UDN ───────────────┐ (parallel, no deps)
GatewayVM ─────────┤
Credentials ───────┘ (no-op, auto-Complete)
        │
        └─ GatewayVM Complete ──→ Ignition
                                       │
                                       ▼  (all Complete)
                               WorkerPool phase = Ready
                                       │
                       (hci_consumer reconcile, every cycle)
                                       ▼
                      desired-version.txt written if drift
                      gateway rhcos-sync.timer downloads
                      scale-up gate: current-version.txt

UDN, GatewayVM and Credentials have no dependencies and run in the same reconcile. Ignition waits only on GatewayVM (SSH port must be open to distribute the file). Credentials is a placeholder that completes immediately — credential creation is done by script (BS-05 was descoped). There is no Bootfiles step in the provisioner — bootfiles version management is owned by hci_consumer (see design decision above).

MachineConfig is a consumer concern

The MachineConfigPool and MachineConfigs are created (if absent) by the hci_consumer role (ensure_machineconfig.yml, BS-02b) and the consumer gates creation of the WorkerPoolProvisioning on the pool being present and not Degraded (MachineConfigPoolReady condition on the WorkerPool). The provisioner has no visibility into consumer-cluster resources and has no MachineConfig step. The CRD enum still lists MachineConfig and Bootfiles, but neither is used.

GatewayVM does not depend on UDN: KubeVirt accepts the VirtualMachine object immediately; the NAD is resolved at VMI scheduling time, not at VM object creation time.

Key insight: worker-hci.ign is generated by rewriting the MCS endpoint in the base worker-user-data-managed Secret — that Secret always exists. The hci-vm MachineConfig is not consulted at ignition generation time; the node only contacts MCS at second boot. The target MCS path /config/<machineConfigPool> is taken from infrastructure.network.machineConfigPool.

docs.title: Dependency Graph (teardown)
docs.text:
Ignition, Credentials   →  no deps (no-op, auto-Complete)
GatewayVM               →  no deps  (parallel with Workers)
Workers                 →  no deps  (parallel with GatewayVM)
UDN                     →  GatewayVM + Workers

Workers (BS-08) lists and deletes all consumer-labelled worker VMs and DataVolumes on the provider, and confirms them absent before Complete. UDN must wait for both GatewayVM and Workers because worker VMs hold UDN attachments and the UDN controller finalizer will not complete deletion while any VMI is still attached. GatewayVM and Workers teardown each use a re-check loop (InProgress → confirmed absent → Complete).

Consumer cleanup after teardown: hci_consumer_cleanup runs once the WorkerPoolProvisioning teardown is Complete. By then all VMs are gone, so it deletes the corresponding node objects directly (ownership fingerprint: name prefix + MCP role label) instead of requiring cordon+drain first. This avoids the deadlock that would otherwise occur because the gateway VM is gone and the nodes go NotReady.

docs.title: Reconcile Loop (provisioning operator)
docs.text:
observe  (observe_world.yml):
  - WorkerPoolProvisioning spec (mode, step list)
  - current step statuses on WorkerPoolProvisioning.status.steps

diff  (diff_steps.yml):
  step Pending + all depends_on Complete           → launch (run the step task file)
  step Pending + dependencies not met              → no-op, wait
  step InProgress                                  → re-check (readiness / absence probe)

act  (advance_steps.yml):
  step results merged into steps[]                 → single consolidated status write
  step probe succeeded                             → set step Complete
  step error / timeout                             → set step Failed, set phase Failed
  all steps Complete                               → set phase Complete
                                                      patch WorkerPool phase Ready
  phase Failed                                     → patch WorkerPool phase Failed
                                                      surface failure message

This is a fully stateless, re-entrant reconcile. Every decision is derivable from observed Kubernetes state — the operator can restart at any point and resume correctly.

docs.title: WorkerPool Phase State Machine
docs.text:
The WorkerPool operator has a top-level phase gate. The worker reconcile loop only runs when phase == Ready.

                  CR created
                  credentials Secret present
                  gateway VM absent
                         │
                         ▼
                   [Provisioning]
              operator creates WorkerPoolProvisioning
              (mode=bootstrap)
              worker reconcile: SKIP
                         │
               WorkerPoolProvisioning phase=Complete
                         │
                         ▼
                     [Ready]  ◄──── normal worker reconcile loop
                  (workers.count reconciled continuously)
                         │
                  CR deletion requested
                         │
                         ▼
                  [Deprovisioning]
              operator creates WorkerPoolProvisioning
              (mode=teardown)
              worker reconcile: SKIP
                         │
               WorkerPoolProvisioning phase=Complete
                         │
                         ▼
               finalizer released → CR deleted

Provisioning and Deprovisioning are observable via oc get workerpool (or oc get wp) — LOOps and administrators can see exactly where the consumer is in its lifecycle.

docs.title: Step Implementations
docs.text:
Step Mode Task file Responsibility Key assets used UDN bootstrap / teardown step_udn.yml, step_udn_teardown.yml Pre-flight check that ClusterUserDefinedNetwork router-external-network exists; create / delete UserDefinedNetwork router-internal-network providerAccess.credentialsSecret kubeconfig GatewayVM bootstrap / teardown step_gateway_vm.yml, step_gateway_vm_readiness.yml, step_gateway_vm_teardown.yml Create cloud-init Secret + DataVolume + VirtualMachine; probe SSH; on teardown delete all three Provider kubeconfig, rendered cloud-init, provisioner SSH key Secret Ignition bootstrap only step_ignition.yml Rewrite MCS URL in worker-user-data-managed, SCP to gateway nginx root Provisioner SSH key, gateway internal IP Workers teardown only step_workers_teardown.yml Delete all consumer-labelled worker VMs + DataVolumes on the provider Provider kubeconfig Credentials both — No-op placeholder (auto-Complete) —

Note: There is no Bootfiles provisioning step. The consumer operator owns desired-version.txt management and the scale-up gate. See the separation of concerns decision above.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
The per-step design makes isolated testing natural:

  1. Unit test a single step: create a WorkerPoolProvisioning CR with only one step in Pending and all others Complete. Verify the step transitions correctly.
  2. Full bootstrap cycle: apply WorkerPool CR with credentials absent (or gateway absent) → observe WorkerPoolProvisioning created → observe each step advance → observe WorkerPool phase reach Ready → verify gateway VM running on HCI.
  3. Full teardown cycle: delete WorkerPool CR → observe teardown WorkerPoolProvisioning created → observe all assets removed → finalizer released.
  4. Create → delete → create: the canonical idempotency test. Validates that teardown leaves the cluster clean enough for a fresh bootstrap.

docs.title: Implementation Language
docs.text:
The provisioning operator controller is implemented as an Ansible operator — consistent with the steady-state operator and the rest of the project. The reconcile loop observes the step statuses, runs every step whose dependencies are satisfied, and writes the merged result once. Steps with no dependency between them run in the same reconcile pass; long waits (VM boot, resource deletion) are handled by re-checking on subsequent reconciles rather than blocking.

A migration to native Go operators (which would replace this loop with controller-runtime reconcilers) is tracked in Epic 6 — see Operator Optimization and Go Migration.

docs.title: Setup Concept — Direction C: integration-setup.yaml-Driven Day-0 Setup
Status
docs.text: Implemented — the generate-setup script and templates/integration-setup.example.yaml are the production realisation of this concept. The description below remains accurate as design rationale; refer to Prerequisites — Environment Configuration and the Getting Started guide for the operational how-to.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
The hci-consumer and hci-provisioner operators are happy once a WorkerPool CR exists and the prerequisites are in place. The CR is the right abstraction for runtime — it is the single source of truth the operators act on.

But getting to that first oc apply -f workerpool.yaml requires a non-trivial amount of day-0 setup that is currently manual:

  • Main cluster (s390x/LinuxONE): MachineConfigPool + MachineConfig manifests applied by the main cluster admin; hci-node-manager built and deployed; operator images available
  • HCI cluster: router-external-network CUDN exists; consumer namespace + quota created; hci-provisioner-credentials Secret produced by setup-consumer-rbac.sh
  • Joint: registry model chosen and configured; WorkerPool CR fields agreed between HCI admin and main cluster admin

These setup steps involve decisions that must be negotiated between two admins who own different clusters. Today that negotiation is implicit and the results are scattered across setup_env.sh, hardcoded values in kustomize overlays, and README instructions.

docs.title: The Concept: integration-setup.yaml
docs.text:
A single YAML file — the cluster-pair configuration — captures all the decisions that precede operator deployment. It is filled in jointly by the HCI admin (provider) and the main cluster admin (consumer) during the setup negotiation, and is the input to the generator script.

One file per HCI ↔ main cluster pair. Individual WorkerPools are instances within that relationship; their pool-specific parameters live in the WorkerPool CR, not here.

# integration-setup.yaml
# Cluster-pair configuration — negotiated once between HCI admin and main cluster admin.
# Captures the decisions that precede any operator deployment.
# Input to generate-setup.

provider:
  context: hci-cluster               # oc context for the HCI cluster
  apiEndpoint: https://api.hci.example.com:6443
  namespace: main-cluster-workers
  gateway:
    ip: 172.16.1.100
    prefixLength: 16
    defaultRouter: 172.16.0.1
  networking:
    macPrefix: "52:54:01"
    internalSubnet: 192.168.100.0/24

consumer:
  context: main-cluster              # oc context for the main cluster
  domain: cluster.example.com
  operatorNamespace: hci-node-manager
  bastion:
    host: bastion.cluster.example.com
    user: root
  networking:
    topology: mediated               # direct | mediated
    dnsServer: 172.16.0.1

registry:
  model: cross-cluster               # local-s2i | cross-cluster | external
  proxyPort: 5443
  saName: registry-pusher
  secretName: hci-registry-push

What belongs here vs in the WorkerPool CR:

Decision Where Which two clusters integration-setup.yaml Network topology (direct/mediated) integration-setup.yaml MachineConfigPool name integration-setup.yaml Image registry model integration-setup.yaml HCI namespace for this pool WorkerPool.spec.provider.namespace Internal subnet for this pool WorkerPool.spec.provider.networking.internalSubnet Gateway IP WorkerPool.spec.provider.gateway.ip Max pool size WorkerPool.spec.provider.maxPoolSize Worker name prefix WorkerPool.spec.consumer.workers.namePrefix Desired worker count WorkerPool.spec.consumer.workers.count

The rule: if it varies per WorkerPool, it belongs in the CR. If it is a cluster-pair-level decision made once, it belongs in integration-setup.yaml.

docs.title: generate-setup workspace/integration-setup.yaml
docs.text:
Produces all cluster-pair-level day-0 artifacts. Run once when establishing a new HCI ↔ main cluster relationship.

Outputs:

Artifact Description setup_env.sh Shell environment variables — sourced by all scripts and Makefiles. workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml Initial WorkerPool CR (workers.count: 0). Main cluster admin applies, then edits to scale workers. operator/build/config.env Makefile variables for make build / make deploy. main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/ Route MachineConfig YAMLs (direct topology only). Main cluster admin applies with oc apply -k. workspace/<domain>.zone Forward DNS zone section. Main cluster admin appends to bastion DNS. workspace/<subnet>.in-addr.arpa.zone Reverse DNS zonefile. Main cluster admin appends to bastion DNS.

The WorkerPool skeleton pre-fills: - spec.consumer.machineConfigPool ← from consumer.machineConfigPool - spec.consumer.networking.topology ← from consumer.networking.topology - spec.consumer.networking.dnsServer ← from consumer.networking.dnsServer - metadata.namespace ← from consumer.operatorNamespace - spec.provider.credentialsSecret ← default name

docs.title: generate-pool-setup (not yet implemented)
docs.text: A second generator for per-pool day-0 artifacts is planned but not yet implemented. When implemented it will consume an agreed WorkerPool CR and produce the HCI namespace + ResourceQuota manifest, CUDN manifest, and a pre-filled setup-consumer-rbac.sh invocation.

docs.title: Relationship to the Operator
docs.text:
The operators are unaffected by this concept. The hci-consumer operator is entirely happy with a WorkerPool CR — it does not know or care how the prerequisites were set up. The configuration file and generator are a developer experience layer that sits entirely outside the operator runtime.

workspace/integration-setup.yaml
        │
        └─ generate-setup ─────────────► setup_env.sh
                                         workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml
                                         operator/build/config.env
                                         main-cluster/configuration/overlays/<topology>/
                                         workspace/<domain>.zone
                                         workspace/<subnet>.in-addr.arpa.zone
                        │
                        ▼
              oc apply -f workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml
                        │
                        ▼
              hci-consumer + hci-provisioner operators
              (runtime — no knowledge of setup phase)

docs.title: Image Registry Models
docs.text:
Three models are supported, selected via registry.model:

Model Build Push Pull Day-0 setup local-s2i Main cluster S2I Main cluster ImageStream Main cluster buildconfig.yaml + S2I build script cross-cluster Main cluster S2I HCI registry via bastion proxy Main cluster pulling from HCI Registry proxy on bastion + cross-cluster push credentials external CI/CD or developer machine quay.io / Artifactory / … Both clusters Registry credentials, image mirror policy

All three models apply equally to: hci-node-manager, hci-consumer operator image, hci-provisioner operator image. generate-setup resolves the correct config.env variables and registry URLs from the chosen model.

docs.title: What This Is Not
docs.text:
• Not a runtime component — no new CRD, no new operator, no controller loop
  • Not a replacement for the WorkerPool CR — the CR remains the operator's single source of truth

docs.text:
1. Implement generate-pool-setup — per-pool HCI + main cluster artifacts (namespace+quota, CUDN, rbac script invocation)
  2. Formalise integration-setup.yaml schema with JSON Schema for validation
