docs.title: Solution Overview
docs.text: A generic, architecture-level map of the core concepts and components. No cluster names, IP addresses, or low-level configuration details.

docs.title: 1 · Problem This Solves
docs.text:
Two independently managed OpenShift clusters — each running a different CPU architecture — are combined into a single, unified cluster. Worker nodes are sourced as virtual machines from one cluster and automatically joined to the other as fully managed, architecture-aware workers.

The integration is fully declarative: an administrator describes the desired number of workers in a single Custom Resource; all infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management flows from that intent.

docs.title: 2 · The Two Clusters
docs.text: Main Cluster HCI Cluster Role Destination cluster. Runs the control plane and native worker nodes. Extended with additional architecture workers sourced from the HCI cluster. Infrastructure source cluster. Runs OpenShift Virtualization and hosts the Gateway VM and all Worker VMs. Requirements OpenShift 4.20+ with multi-architecture enabled. Separate MachineConfigPool for HCI-sourced workers. OpenShift 4.20+ with OpenShift Virtualization. Shared storage for VM boot volumes.

docs.title: Gateway VM
docs.text:
A dedicated virtual machine that acts as the network bridge between the two clusters. It is automatically created and managed by the provisioning operator and provides:

  • IP routing — forwards traffic between the isolated worker network and the main cluster
  • Selective NAT — masquerades traffic depending on destination (topology-dependent)
  • DHCP — static reservations (MAC, IP, hostname) for the worker VMs
  • Network boot — iPXE: loader via TFTP, boot script, RHCOS files and ignition via HTTP
  • DNS forwarding — resolves main-cluster hostnames for workers

docs.title: Worker VMs
docs.text: RHCOS virtual machines created on the HCI cluster. They boot via iPXE from the gateway VM, install RHCOS from an ignition configuration, then join the main cluster as worker nodes. Fully managed by the consumer operator (scale up / scale down).

docs.title: Dual OVN Networks
docs.text:
Two logical networks back the integration. They differ in scope:

  • External network (localnet) — maps to the physical underlay and carries the gateway VM's external interface. It is a cluster-scoped ClusterUserDefinedNetwork that exists once per HCI cluster and is shared by all integrations. It is created by the HCI cluster admin as part of the one-time cluster setup; each integration namespace gets access to it through the label hci-gateway-enabled=true.
  • Internal network (Layer 2 OVN overlay) — the isolated worker network. It is a namespace-scoped UserDefinedNetwork created per main-cluster integration, in that integration's namespace, with its own subnet (provider.networking.internalSubnet). The provisioning operator creates it during bootstrap and removes it on teardown.

docs.title: 4 · The Three-Operator Model
docs.text:
The solution is decomposed into three operators with separate responsibilities. Each operator handles one phase of the lifecycle.

Operator Runs on Responsibility Status HCI Consumer Operator Main cluster Steady-state worker lifecycle: scale VMs up/down, cordon/drain before removal. ✅ Complete HCI Provisioning Operator Main cluster Infrastructure bootstrap & teardown: creates the UDN and Gateway VM, generates the provisioner SSH key and distributes ignition to the gateway. ✅ Complete HCI Provider Operator HCI cluster HCI-side namespace & quota provisioning; generates time-limited onboarding tickets for new consumers. 🗓 Planned

Supporting Component: HCI Node Manager

A lightweight permanent process (not an operator) running on the main cluster. Uses a stream-watch (millisecond reaction time) to handle two time-sensitive operations that cannot wait for an operator reconcile cycle:

  • Automatic CSR approval for joining worker nodes
  • Immediate node labeling (assigns to the HCI MachineConfigPool)

docs.title: WorkerPool
docs.text:
The primary control surface. An administrator applies one CR specifying:

  • Desired worker count
  • Network topology variant
  • Target namespace on the HCI cluster

All provisioning and scaling flows from this single declaration.

docs.title: WorkerPoolProvisioning
docs.text: An internal coordination board, auto-created by the WorkerPool operator. Tracks per-step status for each bootstrap or teardown step (UDN, Gateway VM, MachineConfig, Ignition). Not managed by the administrator; short name wpp.

docs.title: 6 · Two Deployment Topologies
docs.text:
The topology choice is driven by how the main cluster is attached to the network — not by CPU architecture. It is set once at cluster-pair setup time.

Mediated TopologyDirect Topology

For main clusters on a private network. A bastion node acts as an additional routing hop between the main cluster and the gateway VM.

  • No changes to master or worker node routing tables
  • Bastion provides routing and DNS for the main cluster side
  • Simpler main-cluster configuration
Main Cluster → Bastion Node → Gateway VM → Worker VMs

For main clusters on a routable (public) network. Master and worker nodes have static routes applied via MachineConfig to reach the worker VM network directly through the gateway.

  • No bastion required as a routing middleman
  • Static routes pushed via MachineConfig (managed in Git)
  • Required on both master nodes and same-arch worker nodes
Main Cluster → Gateway VM → Worker VMs

docs.title: Bootstrap Flow (one-time per consumer)
docs.text:
WorkerPool CR applied
  → WorkerPoolProvisioning CR created
  → MachineConfig (MCP and routes) validated on the main cluster
  → Provisioner creates internal UDN
  → Gateway VM created & SSH-verified
  → Ignition distributed
  → Consumer phase → Ready

docs.title: VM Provisioning Flow (per worker node)
docs.text:
DataVolume created
  → VirtualMachine created
  → iPXE boot via Gateway DHCP/TFTP/HTTP
  → RHCOS install via Ignition
  → Kubelet starts, bootstrap + serving CSRs generated
  → csr-approver sidecar approves both CSRs
  → Node labeled → joins MachineConfigPool
  → MachineConfig applied → Ready  (~20–30 min)

docs.title: Scale-Down Flow
docs.text:
WorkerPool count reduced
  → Node cordoned & drained
  → Operator waits for NotReady
  → VM & DataVolume deleted

docs.title: 8 · Privilege & Credential Model
docs.text:
The operators on the main cluster reach the HCI cluster with a single ServiceAccount token. A setup script creates the ServiceAccount, its Role and RoleBinding on the HCI cluster and mints a token once per integration; the token is stored as a kubeconfig Secret on the main cluster. The script needs administrative access to the HCI integration namespace, which is why the operators never create credentials themselves.

Credential Scope Lifecycle HCI operator ServiceAccount token (Secret hci-provisioner-credentials) Namespace-scoped Role in the integration namespace on HCI: VMs, DataVolumes, PVCs, UDN, Secrets, ConfigMaps. Read-only access to the cluster-scoped ClusterUserDefinedNetwork. The Role also allows ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding management, reserved for a credentials step that is not implemented yet. Valid for 1 year, rotated by re-running the script. Stored in the operator namespace on the main cluster and used by both operators. Optional: registry push token (registry-pusher ServiceAccount) Push images to the HCI image registry from the integration namespace. Needed only for the bastion registry proxy (registry.model: cross-cluster). Non-expiring token created with the integration RBAC, read once and stored as a docker-registry Secret on the main cluster. HCI cluster-admin Full HCI admin: one-time cluster setup (network, registry), integration namespace, RBAC and token creation Human/admin only, never stored in-cluster

One Secret for both operators

WorkerPool.spec.provider.credentialsSecret is a single field, passed on to the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR, so the consumer and the provisioning operator read the same Secret. The setup script can also create a second, narrower consumer-only ServiceAccount and Secret (hci-provider-credentials), but the operators do not use it in the default configuration.

Planned: onboarding tickets

Short-lived, elevated onboarding tickets generated by the HCI Provider Operator are part of the planned design (backlog item HCI-04). They are not implemented.

docs.title: Kustomize Overlays
docs.text: Main-cluster MachineConfigs are managed as a base + overlay set. The base contains configuration common to all variants. Each topology overlay adds only what differs. New topologies can be added without touching the base.

docs.title: Cluster-Pair Setup File (integration-setup.yaml)
docs.text: A single YAML input file captures all cluster-pair decisions once: the two clusters, network topology, MachineConfigPool and image registry model. The generate-setup script derives all deployment artifacts from it — shell environment, build configuration, MachineConfigs, DNS zones and an initial WorkerPool skeleton — eliminating scattered hard-coded values. See Setup Concept for the design rationale.

docs.title: 10 · Guiding Design Principles
docs.text:
• Declarative intent — a single WorkerPool CR is the sole operational control surface.
  • Idempotent reconciliation — the operator can be restarted at any point and resume correctly; all state is derived from Kubernetes resources.
  • Least privilege on HCI — the operators reach the HCI cluster only through a namespace-scoped ServiceAccount; no HCI cluster-admin credential is ever stored in-cluster.
  • Observe → Diff → Act — the standard Kubernetes controller pattern applied consistently across all operator roles.
  • Topology abstraction — the same operator code handles mediated and direct deployments via configuration, not branching code paths.
  • Safe scale-down — a node must reach NotReady before its VM is deleted; no data loss or abrupt eviction.
  • Namespace isolation — each consumer gets a dedicated namespace and network on the HCI cluster; resources cannot leak across tenants.

docs.title: Closest Analogy in the OpenShift Ecosystem
docs.text: The solution mirrors the ODF Storage Provider / Consumer model: one cluster contributes a resource (storage / compute), another cluster consumes it, mediated by a pair of operators that manage the cross-cluster lifecycle. The difference here is that the resource is compute (virtual machines as worker nodes) rather than storage.

docs.title: VM Provisioning Architecture
docs.text:
This document describes how worker VMs are provisioned, configured, and integrated into the main OpenShift cluster.

All names, addresses and sizes are the example values from templates/integration-setup.example.yaml. The real values are set once in integration-setup.yaml; see the field mapping in Architecture Overview.

The resources and commands shown below describe what the operators create and what you can inspect when troubleshooting. They are not manual deployment steps: the hci-provisioner bootstraps the gateway VM and the ignition file, and the hci-consumer creates the worker VMs, once integration-setup.yaml has been turned into a WorkerPool by generate-setup.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The VM provisioning process involves:

  1. VM Creation - OpenShift Virtualization creates VMs on HCI cluster
  2. Network Boot - VMs boot via iPXE from the gateway VM
  3. OS Installation - RHCOS installs from ignition configuration
  4. Cluster Join - Workers register with main cluster
  5. Configuration - MachineConfig applies worker-specific settings

docs.title: 1. OpenShift Virtualization (KubeVirt)
docs.text:
Purpose: Provides VM infrastructure on HCI cluster

Key Resources: - VirtualMachine - VM definition and lifecycle - VirtualMachineInstance - Running VM instance - DataVolume - VM disk storage - UserDefinedNetwork - Network connectivity (router-internal-network)

VM definition created by the hci-consumer (abridged): 

apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachine
metadata:
  name: worker-x86-1
  namespace: main-cluster-workers
spec:
  running: true
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        k8s.v1.cni.cncf.io/networks: '[{"name":"router-internal-network","interface":"internal"}]'
    spec:
      domain:
        cpu:
          cores: 4
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: 8Gi
        devices:
          disks:
          - name: rootdisk
            disk:
              bus: virtio
            bootOrder: 2
          interfaces:
          - name: default            # pod network, not used for cluster traffic
            masquerade: {}
            bootOrder: 3
          - name: internal           # worker network, boots first
            bridge: {}
            bootOrder: 1
            macAddress: "52:54:01:00:00:10"
      networks:
      - name: default
        pod: {}
      - name: internal
        multus:
          networkName: router-internal-network
      volumes:
      - name: rootdisk
        dataVolume:
          name: worker-x86-1-rootdisk

docs.title: 2. Gateway VM
docs.text:
Purpose: Provides provisioning services

Services: - DHCP - IP address assignment - TFTP - Boot file serving - HTTP - Ignition config serving - DNS - Name resolution

Configuration: created by the hci-provisioner (GatewayVM step) from a cloud-init template filled with the provider.gateway.*, provider.networking.* and consumer.networking.* values of integration-setup.yaml. dnsmasq provides DHCP, TFTP and DNS; nginx serves the ignition file. Nothing is installed or enabled by hand.

docs.title: 3. Ignition Configuration
docs.text:
Purpose: Configures RHCOS during first boot

Source: Generated by the hci-provisioner (Ignition step) from the worker-user-data-managed Secret in openshift-machine-api on the main cluster. The result is a small stub that points the worker at the Machine Config Server of the configured MachineConfigPool (consumer.machineConfigPool, example hci-vm), and is copied to the gateway VM's HTTP server. It does not depend on the OpenShift version and is created once at bootstrap.

The worker hostname is not part of the ignition file. It is handed out by the gateway's DHCP server per worker slot (<namePrefix>-<index>.<domain>).

docs.title: Phase 1: VM Creation
docs.text:
WorkerPool CR (hci-consumer operator)
        ↓
hci-consumer: observe/diff/act reconcile
        ↓
Create VirtualMachine Resource on HCI
        ↓
Allocate Storage (DataVolume)
        ↓
Attach Networks (NADs from WorkerPoolProvisioning)
        ↓
Start VM (VirtualMachineInstance)

WorkerPool CR spec (excerpt): 

spec:
  consumer:
    workers:
      count: 3
      namePrefix: worker-x86
  provider:
    namespace: main-cluster-workers
    maxPoolSize: 10

docs.title: Phase 2: Network Boot (iPXE)
docs.text:
The gateway VM runs dnsmasq (DHCP and TFTP) and nginx (HTTP). The worker VM boots from its internal NIC first (bootOrder: 1), so the sequence below starts as soon as it is powered on.

VM Powers On
        ↓
PXE firmware requests DHCP on the internal network
        ↓
Gateway VM answers from its static reservation for this MAC
  - IP:        192.168.100.10   (fixed per worker slot)
  - Hostname:  worker-x86-1.cluster.example.com
  - Gateway:   192.168.100.1
  - DNS:       172.16.0.1       (consumer.networking.dnsServer)
  - Boot file: undionly.kpxe    (served via TFTP)
        ↓
Firmware downloads undionly.kpxe via TFTP and starts iPXE
        ↓
iPXE requests DHCP again (it announces itself with DHCP option 175)
        ↓
Gateway VM answers with an HTTP boot URL instead
  - http://192.168.100.1/boot.ipxe
        ↓
iPXE runs boot.ipxe: 10-second menu, default "Boot from local disk"
  - disk empty or not bootable → falls through to "Install RHCOS"
        ↓
iPXE loads the RHCOS live kernel and initramfs over HTTP

DHCP: the gateway does not hand out addresses from a dynamic range. It runs dnsmasq in static-only mode (dhcp-range=192.168.100.0,static) with one dhcp-host entry for every possible worker slot, up to provider.maxPoolSize. Each entry fixes MAC address, IP address and hostname (see MAC Address Assignment). Scaling workers up or down within the pool limit therefore never requires a gateway change.

Boot parameters (from boot.ipxe): 

kernel http://192.168.100.1/rhcos/rhcos-live-kernel \
  ip=enp2s0:dhcp ip=enp1s0:off rd.neednet=1 \
  coreos.inst.install_dev=/dev/vda \
  coreos.live.rootfs_url=http://192.168.100.1/rhcos/rhcos-live-rootfs.img \
  coreos.inst.ignition_url=http://192.168.100.1/rhcos/worker-hci.ign \
  ignition.platform.id=metal \
  coreos.inst.node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm= \
  coreos.inst.karg=rd.multipath=0 ...
initrd http://192.168.100.1/rhcos/rhcos-live-initramfs.img

enp2s0 is the internal NIC (DHCP), enp1s0 the pod-network NIC (left unconfigured).

Boot files: the kernel, initramfs and rootfs under /rhcos/ are downloaded by the gateway itself from the OpenShift mirror (rhcos-sync.timer, every 5 minutes), for the RHCOS stream requested by the operator. Scale-up is held back until the download is complete.

docs.title: Phase 3: OS Installation
docs.text:
RHCOS live image boots (kernel + initramfs + rootfs over HTTP)
        ↓
Fetch Ignition Config
  URL: http://192.168.100.1/rhcos/worker-hci.ign
        ↓
coreos-installer writes RHCOS to /dev/vda
        ↓
Reboot from disk
        ↓
Ignition stub on first boot contacts the Machine Config Server
  - https://api-int.cluster.example.com:22623/config/hci-vm
  - outbound traffic is routed (and NATed where needed) by the gateway VM

The ignition file is the stub described in Ignition Configuration; the actual machine configuration is pulled from the main cluster's Machine Config Server for the hci-vm pool.

Installation Progress: 

# Monitor from VM console
journalctl -u coreos-installer -f

docs.title: Phase 4: First Boot
docs.text:
VM Boots from Disk
        ↓
Ignition stub runs (first boot)
  - contacts the Machine Config Server of the main cluster
  - https://api-int.cluster.example.com:22623/config/hci-vm
  - merges the rendered configuration of the hci-vm pool
        ↓
Start kubelet (with the bootstrap credentials from that configuration)
        ↓
Kubelet submits a bootstrap CSR (client certificate) to the main cluster

Boot Process: 

# Key services
systemctl status kubelet
systemctl status crio

docs.title: Phase 5: Cluster Join
docs.text:
Two CSRs are involved. Both are approved automatically by the csr-approver sidecar of the hci-consumer-operator pod, and only for node names that match the worker name prefix (consumer.workers.namePrefix).

Bootstrap CSR (client certificate)
  - approved by csr-approver while the node object does not exist yet
        ↓
Node object registers in the main cluster
        ↓
Kubelet submits a serving CSR (server certificate)
  - approved by csr-approver once the node object exists
        ↓
Node Labeled by node-labeler
  - node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""
  - only if: arch amd64, InternalIP in the internal subnet, name matches prefix
        ↓
Node matches the MachineConfigPool nodeSelector (pool: hci-vm)
        ↓
machine-config-daemon applies the pool's MachineConfigs
        ↓
Node Ready

Manual fallback if a CSR stays pending: oc adm certificate approve <csr>.

Verification: 

# Check CSRs
oc get csr | grep Pending

# Check nodes
oc get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm

# Check MachineConfigPool
oc get mcp hci-vm

docs.title: DataVolume Creation
docs.text:
Purpose: Provides persistent storage for VM

Configuration: 

apiVersion: cdi.kubevirt.io/v1beta1
kind: DataVolume
metadata:
  name: worker-x86-1-rootdisk
spec:
  pvc:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 50Gi            # consumer.workers.resources.storage
    storageClassName: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization
    volumeMode: Block
  source:
    blank: {}

The disk is created blank; RHCOS is written to it by the installer during Phase 3.

Storage class: ocs-storagecluster-ceph-rbd-virtualization (Ceph RBD block storage optimised for virtualization) is used for all worker disks.

docs.title: Disk Layout
docs.text: The installer writes the standard RHCOS layout to the virtual disk (/dev/vda, 50Gi by default). The operators do not define a custom partitioning.

docs.title: Storage Performance
docs.text: Considerations: - IOPS - Ceph RBD provides good random I/O - Throughput - Network-attached storage limits - Latency - Typically 1-5ms for Ceph - Capacity - Plan for OS + container images + logs

docs.title: Network Attachment
docs.text:
Worker VMs attach to the router-internal-network UserDefinedNetwork that the hci-provisioner creates in provider.namespace (see Network Design). OVN-Kubernetes generates the matching NetworkAttachmentDefinition from it; none is written by hand. Each VM references it in a Multus annotation and a multus network.

IP Configuration: - DHCP - From the gateway VM, using a static per-slot reservation (MAC → IP → hostname)

docs.title: MAC Address Assignment
docs.text:
Fixed MAC Addresses:

MACs are derived as <macPrefix>:00:00:<hex> with hex = 0x10 + (index - 1). macPrefix is provider.networking.macPrefix from integration-setup.yaml (example: 52:54:01), so worker-x86-1 gets:

interfaces:
- name: internal
  macAddress: "52:54:01:00:00:10"
  bridge: {}

Why Fixed MACs? - The gateway's static DHCP reservations are keyed on the MAC - Predictable IP address and hostname per worker slot - Easier troubleshooting

docs.title: MachineConfig Application
docs.text:
Timeline (starts when the node has been labeled, see Platform Labeling): 

Node Labeled (t=0)
        ↓
Node matches the MachineConfigPool nodeSelector (t=0)
        ↓
machine-config-daemon takes over the node (t=0)
        ↓
Check rendered MachineConfig of the pool (t=0-30s)
        ↓
Apply Configuration (t=30s-2m)
  - Kernel arguments
  - System files
  - Systemd units
        ↓
Reboot if Required (t=2m)
        ↓
Verify Configuration (t=3m)
        ↓
Node Ready (t=3-5m)

docs.title: MachineConfigPool
docs.text:
Purpose: Group workers with common configuration

The pool name comes from consumer.machineConfigPool (default and example: hci-vm). If the pool and its kernel-argument MachineConfig (99-hci-vm-kargs) do not exist, the hci-consumer creates them; existing ones are never modified.

apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfigPool
metadata:
  name: hci-vm
spec:
  machineConfigSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role
      operator: In
      values:
      - worker
      - hci-vm
    - key: node-platform
      operator: NotIn
      values:
      - s390x
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""
  paused: false
  maxUnavailable: 1

Key Features: - Separate from main worker pool - Can pause updates independently - Allows HCI-specific configuration

docs.title: Platform Labeling
docs.text:
Automatic Labeling: the node-labeler sidecar of the hci-consumer operator adds node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: "" to a new node only if all of these hold:

  • the node's architecture is amd64
  • its InternalIP is within the internal worker subnet (provider.networking.internalSubnet)
  • its name matches the worker name pattern (consumer.workers.namePrefix)

The sidecar reads these values from the hci-node-manager-config ConfigMap, which the operator writes from the WorkerPool. Nodes of other architectures are never labeled, so the s390x nodes cannot be moved into the hci-vm pool by mistake.

Why Automatic? - Ensures correct pool assignment - Prevents configuration conflicts - Simplifies operations

docs.title: HCI Node Manager (sidecars)
docs.text:
Purpose: Automate node lifecycle tasks

Functions: 1. CSR Auto-Approval (csr-approver) — approves worker CSRs automatically via a Kubernetes watch stream 2. Node Labeling (node-labeler) — applies node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: "" so the node joins the correct MachineConfigPool

Deployment: The node manager runs as two sidecar containers inside the hci-consumer-operator Deployment. No standalone Deployment is required. Both sidecars read their config from the hci-node-manager-config ConfigMap, which the operator writes on every WorkerPool reconcile.

# Check sidecars
oc get pods -n hci-node-manager -l app.kubernetes.io/name=hci-consumer-operator

# Logs
oc logs -n hci-node-manager deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c csr-approver | tail -20
oc logs -n hci-node-manager deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c node-labeler | tail -20

docs.title: Operator Automation
docs.text:
Purpose: Declarative, self-healing VM lifecycle management

Features: - Observe/diff/act reconcile loop — continuously converges to desired state - Safe scale-down: cordon + drain gate before VM deletion - Status conditions and phase sub-states on the WorkerPool CR - Bootstrap (gateway VM, UDN, ignition) managed by hci-provisioner

Usage: generate-setup creates the initial WorkerPool with workers.count: 0. Scale by editing the live resource in the operator namespace (consumer.operatorNamespace, example hci-node-manager):

# Scale up
oc -n hci-node-manager patch workerpool hci-workers \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":4}}}}'

# Scale down
oc -n hci-node-manager patch workerpool hci-workers \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":2}}}}'

# Watch status
oc -n hci-node-manager get workerpool hci-workers -w

Re-running generate-setup rewrites the WorkerPool file with workers.count: 0; use oc get workerpool hci-workers -o yaml to keep the live state.

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text:
VM Creation: - Time to create VM: Target <2 minutes - Storage allocation time: Target <1 minute - Network attachment time: Target <30 seconds

Network Boot: - DHCP response time: Target <1 second - TFTP download of undionly.kpxe: Target <30 seconds - iPXE boot menu: 10 seconds, then installs automatically if the disk is empty

OS Installation: - Ignition fetch time: Target <5 seconds - RHCOS download time: Target 5-10 minutes - Installation time: Target 10-15 minutes - Total time: Target 15-20 minutes

Cluster Join: - CSR generation: Target <1 minute - CSR approval: Target <1 minute (auto) or manual - Node registration: Target <2 minutes - Node ready: Target <5 minutes

docs.title: Monitoring Commands
docs.text:
# Watch VM creation
watch oc get vm -n main-cluster-workers

# Monitor network boot (from VM console)
virtctl console -n main-cluster-workers worker-x86-1

# Check installation progress
oc logs -n main-cluster-workers virt-launcher-worker-x86-1-xxxxx

# Monitor cluster join
watch oc get csr
watch oc get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm

# Check MachineConfigPool
watch oc get mcp hci-vm

docs.title: VM Won't Start
docs.text:
Symptoms: - VM stuck in "Starting" state - VirtualMachineInstance not created

Checks: 

# Check VM events
oc describe vm worker-x86-1 -n main-cluster-workers

# Check DataVolume
oc get dv -n main-cluster-workers

# Check storage capacity
oc get pvc -n main-cluster-workers

docs.title: Network Boot Fails
docs.text:
Symptoms: - VM shows "No bootable device" - DHCP request times out - iPXE starts but cannot load boot.ipxe or the RHCOS kernel

Checks: 

# Check gateway VM (named hci-gateway)
oc get vmi hci-gateway -n main-cluster-workers

# Log in to the gateway (external IP = provider.gateway.ip)
ssh core@172.16.1.100

# On the gateway: DHCP/TFTP and HTTP services
sudo systemctl status dnsmasq nginx

# On the gateway: is the worker's MAC being offered an address?
sudo journalctl -u dnsmasq | grep -i dhcp | tail -20

# On the gateway: iPXE loader, boot script and RHCOS boot files
ls -la /var/lib/tftpboot/
ls -la /var/www/html/ /var/www/html/rhcos/
cat /var/www/html/rhcos/current-version.txt

If current-version.txt is missing, the gateway has not finished downloading the RHCOS boot files yet (systemctl status rhcos-sync.timer, journalctl -u rhcos-sync).

docs.title: Installation Fails
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Installation hangs - Cannot fetch ignition - Disk errors

Checks: 

# Check ignition availability (from the gateway or any host on the internal network)
curl -I http://192.168.100.1/rhcos/worker-hci.ign

# Check disk
virtctl console -n main-cluster-workers worker-x86-1
# In console: lsblk, fdisk -l

# Check logs
journalctl -u coreos-installer

docs.title: Node Won't Join
docs.text:
Symptoms: - CSR not generated - CSR pending forever - Node not appearing

Checks: 

# Check CSRs
oc get csr | grep worker-x86

# Check kubelet
oc debug node/worker-x86-1
chroot /host
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 100

# Check connectivity
ping api.cluster.example.com
curl -k https://api.cluster.example.com:6443/version

See Troubleshooting Guide for detailed solutions.

docs.title: VM Configuration
docs.text:
1. Use fixed MAC addresses - Ensures consistent networking
  2. Allocate sufficient resources - defaults are 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM, 50GB disk (consumer.workers.resources); size to your workload
  3. Use block storage - Better performance than file storage
  4. Enable virtio drivers - Optimal performance

docs.title: Provisioning
docs.text:
1. Test with one worker first - Verify process works
  2. CSR approval is automatic — the csr-approver sidecar in the operator handles it
  3. Monitor provisioning - Watch for failures
  4. Document custom configurations - Keep ignition changes tracked

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
1. Use operator CRs for management - Declarative and version-controlled
  2. Keep gateway VM updated - Security patches
  3. Backup configurations - CR manifests, ignition configs
  4. Plan for failures - Have recovery procedures ready

docs.title: HCI Cluster Configuration
docs.text:
This document describes, step by step, what is configured on the HCI cluster to host the x86 worker VMs that join the main OpenShift cluster.

This page describes the manual steps behind the scripted setup

The recommended way to set up the HCI side is the script-supported flow of the Setup Guide. Every step on this page is either a command from that guide or something its scripts do for you. Use this page to understand what each step does, to repeat a single step by hand, or to troubleshoot.

All values (cluster contexts, namespaces, addresses) come from workspace/integration-setup.yaml via generate-setup. The commands below use the variables from the generated setup_env.sh, for example ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} and ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}; source it first (see Workspace Setup). Example values in this page are those of templates/integration-setup.example.yaml.

Operator-managed

Gateway VM, internal UserDefinedNetwork, worker VM lifecycle and ignition distribution are managed by the hci-provisioner and hci-consumer operators. See operator/hci-consumer/ and operator/hci-provisioner/ for usage.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Manual step on this page Setup Guide step Scripted by Cadence Physical network mapping prerequisite, not scripted — once per HCI cluster Cluster-scoped external network A.2 oc apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml once per HCI cluster Integration namespace and label B.1 oc create namespace / oc label once per main cluster Consumer RBAC on the HCI cluster B.2 hci-cluster/setup-consumer-rbac.sh once per main cluster Operator credentials C.7 operator/setup-provider-credentials.sh once per main cluster WorkerPool CR C.9 generate-setup, then oc apply once per main cluster Verification Verify Integration — after each deployment

The HCI image registry (Setup Guide A.1) is not covered here.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before configuring the HCI cluster, ensure:

  • ✅ HCI cluster is operational (OpenShift 4.20 or later)
  • ✅ OpenShift Virtualization operator installed
  • ✅ Sufficient resources available (CPU, memory, storage)
  • ✅ Network connectivity to main cluster established
  • ✅ workspace/integration-setup.yaml completed and generate-setup run

See Prerequisites for detailed requirements.

docs.title: Cluster-Admin Setup
docs.text: Done once per HCI cluster, shared by all integrations. Setup Guide: Tier A.

docs.title: Step 1: Apply the Cluster-Scoped Network Resource
docs.text:
Purpose: Create the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork that gives every gateway VM its external connectivity.

Who: Cluster administrator (one-time setup)

Setup Guide: A.2

Command: 

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml

Resource created: 

apiVersion: k8s.ovn.org/v1
kind: ClusterUserDefinedNetwork
metadata:
  name: router-external-network
spec:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      hci-gateway-enabled: "true"
  network:
    topology: Localnet
    localnet:
      physicalNetworkName: localnet1
      role: Secondary
      mtu: 1500
      ipam:
        mode: Disabled

Verification: 

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get clusteruserdefinednetwork router-external-network
# router-external-network    Active

docs.title: Step 2: Physical Network Mapping
docs.text:
Purpose: Map the OVN network name localnet1 (the physicalNetworkName above) to the bridge that is connected to the physical network of the HCI nodes.

Who: Cluster administrator. This depends on how the HCI nodes are wired and is a prerequisite, not part of the scripted setup. Apply it before the namespace is labeled in step B.1 of the Setup Guide.

Example (requires the Kubernetes NMState Operator; adapt the bridge to your nodes): 

apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1
kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy
metadata:
  name: localnet1-bridge-mapping
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: ""
  desiredState:
    ovn:
      bridge-mappings:
      - localnet: localnet1   # must equal physicalNetworkName in the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork
        bridge: br-ex         # bridge connected to the physical network
        state: present

Verification: 

# Policy applied
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nncp localnet1-bridge-mapping

# Mapping present on a node
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/<hci-node> -- chroot /host \
  ovs-vsctl get open . external_ids:ovn-bridge-mappings
# "localnet1:br-ex,..."

docs.title: Namespace Setup
docs.text: Done once per main cluster you connect. Setup Guide: Tier B. The namespace name is provider.namespace in integration-setup.yaml (example: main-cluster-workers), available as ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}.

docs.title: Step 1: Create Integration Namespace
docs.text:
Setup Guide: B.1

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} create namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

docs.title: Step 2: Label Namespace for Network Access
docs.text:
Purpose: Let the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork create the router-external-network attachment in this namespace.

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} \
  hci-gateway-enabled=true

Verification: 

# Namespace label
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} --show-labels

# NetworkAttachmentDefinition created by the controller
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get network-attachment-definition \
  -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
# router-external-network

Expected: the attachment should appear within 1-2 minutes after labeling. It must exist before the gateway VM is created.

docs.title: Step 3: RBAC for the Operators
docs.text:
Setup Guide: B.2

./hci-cluster/setup-consumer-rbac.sh

The script requires the namespace from the previous steps and, in ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} on the HCI cluster, creates:

  • the hci-consumer-operator ServiceAccount with a namespace-scoped Role and RoleBinding (VirtualMachines, DataVolumes, PVCs, Secrets, ConfigMaps, UserDefinedNetwork)
  • a read-only ClusterRole for the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork existence check done by the provisioner
  • the registry-pusher ServiceAccount and token, used only by the cross-cluster registry model

Pass --delete to remove everything again before re-running it.

docs.title: Step 4: Secrets
docs.text: No other Secrets need to be created by hand on the HCI cluster. The gateway VM cloud-init Secret and the provisioner SSH keypair are generated by the hci-provisioner operator. The only credential handover is the provider kubeconfig Secret on the main cluster — see Operator Deployment below.

docs.title: Operator Deployment
docs.text:
The gateway VM, internal UserDefinedNetwork, ignition distribution and worker VM lifecycle are fully managed by the two operators. You apply one CR — the WorkerPool. Build and deployment of the operators themselves is described in Building and Deploying the Operators (Setup Guide C.8).

How the two operators interact

  1. You apply the WorkerPool CR.
  2. The hci-consumer operator creates the MachineConfigPool + MachineConfigs on the main cluster if absent, then gates on the pool being healthy.
  3. The hci-consumer creates the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR automatically and sets WorkerPool.status.phase = Provisioning.
  4. The hci-provisioner picks up the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR and runs the bootstrap steps (UDN → GatewayVM → Ignition) to Complete.
  5. The provisioner patches WorkerPool.status.phase = Ready.
  6. The hci-consumer immediately begins scaling up to workers.count.

docs.title: Step 1: Set Up Credentials
docs.text:
Setup Guide: C.7

Run the credential setup script once. It uses both cluster contexts from setup_env.sh, creates the ServiceAccounts and Roles on the HCI cluster, and writes the hci-provisioner-credentials and hci-provider-credentials kubeconfig Secrets to the operator namespace (${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}) on the main cluster:

./operator/setup-provider-credentials.sh

See operator/setup-provider-credentials.sh for the --consumer / --provisioner / --delete flags and environment overrides.

docs.title: Step 2: Apply the WorkerPool CR
docs.text:
Setup Guide: C.9

The WorkerPool CR is not written by hand. generate-setup renders it from integration-setup.yaml into workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml with workers.count: 0, so applying it provisions the gateway only. The provider values come from the HCI admin (provider.*), the consumer values from the main cluster admin (consumer.*). With the example file the generated CR contains:

apiVersion: hci-integration.openshift.io/v1alpha1
kind: WorkerPool
metadata:
  name: hci-workers
  namespace: hci-node-manager
spec:
  provider:
    apiEndpoint: "https://api.hci.example.com:6443"
    namespace: "main-cluster-workers"
    credentialsSecret: "hci-provisioner-credentials"
    maxPoolSize: 10
    gateway:
      ip: "172.16.1.100"
      prefixLength: 16
      defaultRouter: "172.16.0.1"
    networking:
      macPrefix: "52:54:01"
      internalSubnet: "192.168.100.0/24"
  consumer:
    machineConfigPool: "hci-vm"
    networking:
      topology: "mediated"          # or: direct
      dnsServer: "172.16.0.1"
      internalNetwork: "10.0.0.0/24"   # mediated topology only
      internalGateway: "172.16.0.1"    # mediated topology only
    workers:
      count: 0
      namePrefix: "worker-x86"

The field-by-field mapping is in Architecture Overview. The operator repository also contains an annotated sample: workerpool-sample.yaml.

Apply and watch: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml

# WorkerPool: Provisioning → Ready
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} get workerpool hci-workers -w

# WorkerPoolProvisioning: created automatically; shows per-step progress
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} get workerpoolprovisioning -w

Once the pool is Ready, add workers as described under Scaling Operations. The deployment is complete when PHASE=Ready and WORKERS, DEPLOYED and READY are equal with PENDING=0.

docs.title: Post-Deployment Verification
docs.text: Setup Guide: Verify Integration. The checks below look at the HCI side. The gateway VM is named hci-gateway; it is reached over SSH at its external address (provider.gateway.ip), the VMs are not pods.

docs.title: Step 1: Verify Gateway VM
docs.text:
Check VM status: 

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vm hci-gateway -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vmi hci-gateway -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
# PHASE=Running

Check inside the gateway VM: 

ssh core@172.16.1.100          # provider.gateway.ip

# 1. Network interfaces
ip addr show
# - eth1: 172.16.1.100/16   (external)
# - eth2: 192.168.100.1/24  (internal)

# 2. Routing
ip route show
# - default via 172.16.0.1 dev eth1
# - 10.0.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.1 dev eth1   (mediated topology only)
# - 192.168.100.0/24 dev eth2

# 3. Services (both active)
systemctl status dnsmasq nginx

# 4. DHCP log
sudo journalctl -u dnsmasq -n 50

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Worker VMs
docs.text:
Check VM status: 

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vm  -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -l app=worker-vm
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vmi -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -l app=worker-vm
# PHASE=Running for all

Check network boot: 

virtctl console -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} worker-x86-1

# Should show:
# 1. iPXE boot menu ("Worker VM Boot Menu")
# 2. RHCOS installation progress
# 3. Eventually: login prompt after installation

Monitor events: 

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get events -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} --watch

docs.title: Step 3: Verify Networks
docs.text:
# External network (from the ClusterUserDefinedNetwork) and internal network (UDN)
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get network-attachment-definition \
  -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
# router-external-network
# router-internal-network

# Details of one attachment
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get network-attachment-definition router-external-network \
  -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -o yaml

Connectivity test from the gateway VM: 

ssh core@172.16.1.100

ping -c 3 172.16.0.1                # bastion / DNS (consumer.networking.dnsServer)
ping -c 3 api.cluster.example.com   # main cluster API
ping -c 3 192.168.100.10            # first worker VM (once it has booted)

docs.title: Scaling Operations
docs.text: Scale by editing the live WorkerPool on the main cluster, in the operator namespace (${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}, example hci-node-manager). Workers can be added up to provider.maxPoolSize; DNS records and DHCP reservations exist for that many slots. See also Scaling the Worker Pool.

docs.title: Adding Workers
docs.text:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} patch workerpool hci-workers \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":5}}}}'

The hci-consumer operator creates the additional VMs and waits for them to join the cluster. WorkerPool.status.phase moves through ScalingUp → Ready.

docs.title: Removing Workers
docs.text:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} patch workerpool hci-workers \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":2}}}}'

The operator cordons and drains surplus nodes (highest-index first) before deleting the VMs. WorkerPool.status.phase reflects ScalingDown or ScalingDownBlocked (if live workloads are preventing drain) until the pool reaches the target size.

Regenerating the setup

generate-setup rewrites workspace/workerpool-hci-workers.yaml with workers.count: 0. To keep the current size of a live pool, save it with oc get workerpool hci-workers -o yaml.

docs.title: Updating Gateway VM Configuration
docs.text:
Gateway VM resources (CPU, memory, storage) are set in provider.gateway.resources of integration-setup.yaml and end up in the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR. The gateway VM is a one-shot provisioned resource, not continuously reconciled after Complete, so a change requires a teardown and re-bootstrap.

For in-place configuration changes on a running gateway VM (for example dnsmasq tuning), SSH directly:

ssh core@172.16.1.100          # provider.gateway.ip
sudo -i
# make changes, e.g.:
systemctl restart dnsmasq

docs.title: Updating Worker VMs
docs.text: Worker VMs run RHCOS from the main cluster — OS-level updates happen via the main cluster's MachineConfigPool. To change VM hardware resources (CPU/memory), scale the pool to 0 and back up; the hci-consumer operator will recreate the VMs with the updated WorkerPool spec values.

docs.title: Gateway VM Won't Start
docs.text:
Check: 

# VM events
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} describe vm hci-gateway -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# DataVolume status
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get dv -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# Storage capacity
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get pvc -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# Provisioner progress and errors
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} get workerpoolprovisioning -o yaml

docs.title: Worker VM Won't Network-Boot
docs.text:
Check: 

ssh core@172.16.1.100          # provider.gateway.ip

# DHCP/TFTP and HTTP services
sudo systemctl status dnsmasq nginx

# iPXE loader, boot script, RHCOS boot files
ls -la /var/lib/tftpboot/
ls -la /var/www/html/ /var/www/html/rhcos/

# Is the worker's MAC being offered an address?
sudo journalctl -u dnsmasq | grep -i dhcp | tail -20

See VM Provisioning for the full list of checks.

docs.title: Network Attachment Fails
docs.text:
Check: 

# Attachments exist
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get network-attachment-definition -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# Namespace carries the label
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} --show-labels

# ClusterUserDefinedNetwork status
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get clusteruserdefinednetwork router-external-network -o yaml

# OVN controller logs
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -l app=ovnkube-node --tail=100

See Troubleshooting Guide for detailed solutions.

docs.title: Resource Planning
docs.text:
1. Start small - Deploy 1-2 workers initially
  2. Monitor usage - Check CPU, memory, storage utilization
  3. Plan capacity - Ensure HCI cluster has sufficient resources
  4. Reserve resources - Don't overcommit HCI cluster

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
1. Version control - Keep integration-setup.yaml (without credentials) and an export of the live WorkerPool in Git
  2. Use separate CRs per consumer - One WorkerPool CR per LinuxONE tenant
  3. Document changes - Maintain changelog
  4. Test changes - Verify in dev before production

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Protect secrets - Use sealed secrets or external secret management
  2. Limit access - Use RBAC to control namespace access
  3. Network policies - Restrict traffic where possible
  4. Regular updates - Keep gateway VM OS updated

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
1. Monitor continuously - Watch WorkerPool.status phase and condition columns
  2. Backup CR manifests - Keep the exported WorkerPool YAML in Git
  3. Test recovery - Verify teardown and re-bootstrap procedures
  4. Document procedures - Maintain runbooks

docs.title: Kustomize Overlays Guide
docs.text:
This document explains the Kustomize structure in main-cluster/configuration/, which holds the main-cluster MachineConfigPool and MachineConfig resources for the two deployment variants.

Manual path behind the scripted setup

The overlays are what Setup Guide step C.4 – Apply MachineConfigs applies. The values inside the direct overlay are not written by hand: generate-setup renders the two route MachineConfigs from your integration-setup.yaml. The same resources are also created by the hci-consumer operator if they are absent (see Main Cluster Configuration).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The integration uses Kustomize to manage configuration variants:

  • Base — common configuration for all deployments
  • Overlays — variant-specific additions
    • mediated — mediated topology (private network, bastion routes traffic)
    • direct — direct topology (main-cluster nodes route to the HCI gateway themselves)

The overlay you apply follows consumer.networking.topology in integration-setup.yaml.

docs.title: Why Kustomize?
docs.text:
• DRY — common configuration is not repeated
  • Variant management — one overlay per deployment type
  • Native to OpenShift — oc apply -k, no extra tooling
  • Version-control friendly — clear separation of base and variant

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
main-cluster/configuration/
├── base/
│   ├── kustomization.yaml
│   ├── machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml
│   └── machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml
└── overlays/
    ├── mediated/
    │   ├── kustomization.yaml
    │   └── README.md
    └── direct/
        ├── kustomization.yaml
        ├── 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml   # generated by generate-setup
        ├── 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml   # generated by generate-setup
        └── README.md

docs.title: What generate-setup Writes
docs.text:
File Written when Source values in integration-setup.yaml overlays/direct/99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml consumer.networking.topology: direct provider.networking.internalSubnet, provider.gateway.ip overlays/direct/99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml consumer.networking.topology: direct provider.networking.internalSubnet, provider.gateway.ip

With topology: mediated (the value in the example file) nothing is written — the mediated overlay needs no per-installation values. The base files and both kustomization.yaml files are static and are never touched by generate-setup.

Do not edit the generated route files

They are overwritten on every generate-setup run. To change the route, change provider.gateway.ip or provider.networking.internalSubnet and re-run generate-setup.

docs.title: kustomization.yaml
docs.text:
Location: main-cluster/configuration/base/kustomization.yaml

apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

resources:
  - machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml
  - machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml

commonLabels:
  hci-integration: "true"
  • resources — the base manifests
  • commonLabels — hci-integration: "true" is added to every base resource

docs.title: 1. MachineConfigPool
docs.text:
File: machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml

Purpose: a separate pool for the HCI worker VMs

apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfigPool
metadata:
  name: hci-vm
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: hci-vm
spec:
  machineConfigSelector:
    matchExpressions:
      - key: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role
        operator: In
        values: [worker, hci-vm]
      # Exclude s390x platform-specific MachineConfigs (multipath storage)
      - key: node-platform
        operator: NotIn
        values: [s390x]
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""
  paused: false
  maxUnavailable: 1

Why in the base: required for every variant and has no variant-specific values. The pool name matches consumer.machineConfigPool (default hci-vm). The node-platform NotIn s390x rule keeps the s390x route MachineConfig (below) from being rendered into the x86 pool.

docs.title: 2. Kernel Arguments
docs.text:
File: machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml

Purpose: boot settings for the x86 worker VMs

apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  name: 99-hci-vm-kargs
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: hci-vm
    node-platform: hci-vm
spec:
  kernelArguments:
    - "root=/dev/disk/by-label/root"
    - "rd.multipath=0"      # no s390x multipath storage on VMs
    - "rd.neednet=1"
    - "ip=enp1s0:off"       # disable the HCI pod-network interface
    - "ip=enp2s0:dhcp"      # cluster network interface (static DHCP lease)
  config:
    ignition:
      version: 3.5.0

Why in the base: every worker VM needs these arguments, independent of the topology. Node role labeling is not done here — the node-labeler sidecar in the hci-consumer-operator pod labels the nodes.

docs.title: kustomization.yaml
docs.text:
Location: main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/kustomization.yaml

apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

namespace: openshift-machine-config-operator

bases:
  - ../../base

Characteristics: minimal — only references the base. The bastion routes the traffic to the HCI worker subnet (see Setup Guide C.2).

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use the mediated overlay when:

  • ✅ Main-cluster nodes are on a private network (example: 10.0.0.0/24)
  • ✅ The bastion (example: 172.16.0.1) routes all traffic to the HCI gateway
  • ✅ Common in z/VM and LPAR environments

docs.title: What It Provides
docs.text:
• The hci-vm MachineConfigPool
  • Kernel arguments for the worker VMs (including disabling enp1s0)
  • No additional routing configuration

docs.title: Application
docs.text:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

# Verify
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-hci-vm-kargs

docs.title: kustomization.yaml
docs.text:
Location: main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/kustomization.yaml

apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

namespace: openshift-machine-config-operator

bases:
  - ../../base

resources:
  - 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml
  - 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml

Characteristics: extends the base with two routing MachineConfigs — one for the masters, one for the s390x workers.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use the direct overlay when:

  • ✅ Main-cluster nodes can reach the gateway's external IP (example: 172.16.1.100) directly
  • ✅ No bastion routing is wanted
  • ✅ Common in KVM and bare-metal environments

docs.title: Additional Resources
docs.text: Both files are rendered by generate-setup. The examples below show the output for internalSubnet: 192.168.100.0/24 and gateway.ip: 172.16.1.100.

docs.title: 1. Master Node Route
docs.text:
File: 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml

Purpose: let the masters reach the HCI worker VMs (CSR handling, node status, scheduling, health checks)

apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: master
  name: 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route
spec:
  config:
    ignition:
      version: 3.5.0
    systemd:
      units:
        - name: hci-network-route.service
          enabled: true
          contents: |
            [Unit]
            Description=Add static route to HCI worker network
            After=network-online.target ovs-configuration.service
            Wants=network-online.target
            Requires=ovs-configuration.service

            [Service]
            Type=oneshot
            RemainAfterExit=yes
            ExecStartPre=/bin/bash -c 'until ip link show br-ex; do sleep 1; done'
            ExecStart=/bin/bash -c '/usr/sbin/ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 dev br-ex || true'

            [Install]
            WantedBy=multi-user.target

The master unit waits for ovs-configuration.service and the br-ex bridge, because the route is bound to br-ex.

docs.title: 2. S390x Worker Route
docs.text:
File: 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml

Purpose: let the dedicated s390x workers reach the HCI worker VMs (pod-to-pod traffic, service endpoints, multi-architecture applications)

apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: worker
    node-platform: s390x
  name: 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route
spec:
  config:
    ignition:
      version: 3.5.0
    systemd:
      units:
        - name: hci-network-route.service
          enabled: true
          contents: |
            [Unit]
            Description=Add static route to HCI worker network
            After=network-online.target
            Wants=network-online.target

            [Service]
            Type=oneshot
            RemainAfterExit=yes
            ExecStart=/bin/bash -c '/usr/sbin/ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 || true'

            [Install]
            WantedBy=multi-user.target

The worker route has no dev br-ex. The node-platform: s390x label is what keeps this MachineConfig out of the x86 hci-vm pool (see the pool's NotIn rule above).

Note: the worker route only applies to dedicated s390x workers. Compact clusters (master+worker roles) only need the master route.

docs.title: Application
docs.text:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

# Base resources
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-hci-vm-kargs

# Routing MachineConfigs
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route

# Master and worker pools roll out the route (10–30 minutes)
watch oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp master worker
# Wait for UPDATED=True, UPDATING=False

docs.title: Creating Custom Overlays
docs.text: Custom overlays are not part of the supported flow, but the structure allows them. Keep them outside the generated files so generate-setup does not overwrite your work.

docs.title: Use Case: Additional MachineConfig
docs.text:
1. Create the overlay directory: 

    mkdir -p main-cluster/configuration/overlays/custom

  2. Create kustomization.yaml: 

    apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

resources:
  - ../mediated          # or ../direct
  - custom-config.yaml

patches:
  - path: patch-kargs.yaml

  3. Add the custom resource: 

    # custom-config.yaml
apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: hci-vm
  name: 99-hci-vm-custom
spec:
  config:
    ignition:
      version: 3.5.0
    storage:
      files:
        - path: /etc/custom.conf
          contents:
            inline: |
              # Custom configuration

  4. Apply: 

    oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/custom/

docs.title: Use Case: Patching the Base
docs.text:
Example: add a kernel argument without changing the base files

# patch-kargs.yaml
apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  name: 99-hci-vm-kargs
spec:
  kernelArguments:
    - "root=/dev/disk/by-label/root"
    - "rd.multipath=0"
    - "rd.neednet=1"
    - "ip=enp1s0:off"
    - "ip=enp2s0:dhcp"
    - "custom.arg=value"     # added

A strategic-merge patch replaces the kernelArguments list, so repeat the existing entries and append yours.

docs.title: Overlay Design
docs.text:
1. Keep the base minimal — only truly common configuration
  2. Use overlays for variants — do not modify the base for specific cases
  3. Do not hand-edit generated files — change integration-setup.yaml instead
  4. Test each overlay independently

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
1. Version control — keep custom overlays in Git
  2. Tag releases — tag stable overlay versions
  3. Document changes — maintain a changelog

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
1. Descriptive names — mediated, direct, not variant1
  2. 99- prefix for high-priority MachineConfigs
  3. Clear labels — use labels to identify resources

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
1. Dry run first — oc apply -k <dir> --dry-run=client
  2. Test in dev — verify the overlay in a development cluster
  3. Validate output — oc kustomize <dir>
  4. Monitor — watch MachineConfigPool status

docs.title: Kustomize Build Fails
docs.text:
Symptoms: 

Error: accumulating resources: accumulation err='accumulating resources from '../../base': ...

Check: 

# Render the overlay
oc kustomize main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

# Verify the base path and referenced files exist
ls -la main-cluster/configuration/base/
ls -la main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

For the direct overlay, no such file ... 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml means the route files were not generated — check that topology: direct is set in integration-setup.yaml and re-run generate-setup.

docs.title: Resources Not Applied
docs.text:
Symptoms: oc apply -k succeeds but resources are missing.

# Preview what would be applied
oc apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/ --dry-run=client -o yaml

# Look for the resources
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc | grep hci

docs.title: Patches Not Working
docs.text:
Symptoms: a patch is defined but not applied.

# Build and inspect the output
oc kustomize main-cluster/configuration/overlays/custom/ | grep -A 20 "kind: MachineConfig"

# Verify the patch target (name and kind) matches the base resource

docs.title: Wrong Overlay Applied
docs.text:
Symptoms: the wrong variant was applied.

# Delete the resources of the wrong overlay
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} delete -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/<wrong-variant>/

# Apply the correct overlay
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/<correct-variant>/

# Verify
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc -l hci-integration=true

Deleting an overlay also deletes the base hci-vm pool and kernel-argument MachineConfig (they are part of both overlays). Re-applying the correct overlay recreates them; no workers should be running while you do this.
