docs.title: Main Cluster Configuration
docs.text:
This document describes the main-cluster side of the integration: what has to exist on the main OpenShift cluster (and its bastion) so that x86 worker VMs hosted on the HCI cluster can join it.

Manual steps behind the scripted setup

You normally do not perform these steps by hand. The Setup Guide – Tier C runs them for you with scripts, using the values from your integration-setup.yaml (rendered into setup_env.sh and workspace/ by generate-setup). This page documents what each step does, so you can understand, verify, or repeat a single step manually.

Manual step on this page Setup Guide step Done by Bastion routing and firewall C.2 main-cluster/scripts/01-add-route.sh, 02-firewall-setup.sh MachineConfigPool and MachineConfigs C.4 oc apply -k on the overlay (or the hci-consumer operator) Registry proxy C.5, C.6 main-cluster/bastion-registry/setup-registry-proxy.sh, setup-registry-access.sh HCI Node Manager C.8 Deployed with the hci-consumer operator Operator credentials, WorkerPool CR C.7, C.9 See HCI Cluster Configuration

DNS (C.1) and multi-architecture support (C.3) are covered only in the Setup Guide.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The main-cluster configuration consists of:

  1. MachineConfigPool and MachineConfigs — created automatically by the hci-consumer operator from the WorkerPool CR; kustomize overlays exist as an optional manual fallback
  2. Deployment variant — the mediated or direct overlay (the direct overlay adds static routes)
  3. Bastion routing — mediated topology only
  4. Registry configuration — only when registry.model: cross-cluster

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before configuring the main cluster, ensure:

  • ✅ Main cluster is operational (OpenShift 4.20+)
  • ✅ Cluster admin access available (${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT})
  • ✅ Network connectivity to the HCI cluster established
  • ✅ integration-setup.yaml written and generate-setup run (see Workspace Setup)
  • ✅ Topology (mediated or direct) and registry model chosen in integration-setup.yaml

See Prerequisites for detailed requirements.

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
main-cluster/
├── configuration/
│   ├── base/                    # Common configuration
│   │   ├── kustomization.yaml
│   │   ├── machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml
│   │   └── machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml
│   └── overlays/
│       ├── mediated/            # Mediated topology (no extra resources)
│       │   ├── kustomization.yaml
│       │   └── README.md
│       └── direct/              # Direct topology (adds route MachineConfigs)
│           ├── kustomization.yaml
│           ├── 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml   # generated
│           ├── 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml   # generated
│           └── README.md
├── scripts/                     # Bastion helper scripts
└── bastion-registry/            # Registry proxy (cross-cluster model)

MachineConfigs are operator-managed

The hci-consumer operator creates the MachineConfigPool, the kernel-argument MachineConfig and — for the direct topology — the two route MachineConfigs from the WorkerPool CR if they do not exist. The kustomize overlays are the equivalent manual path: apply them if you want the pool to exist before the operator first reconciles (Setup Guide step C.4 does exactly that).

Generated route MachineConfigs

The two 99-*-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml files in overlays/direct/ are generated by generate-setup from provider.networking.internalSubnet and provider.gateway.ip. They are only written for topology: direct. Do not edit them by hand — change integration-setup.yaml and re-run generate-setup.

docs.title: Bastion Routing and Firewall (Mediated Topology only)
docs.text:
Setup Guide: C.2

In the mediated topology the main-cluster nodes reach the HCI worker subnet through the bastion. The bastion needs a route to the internal subnet via the gateway VM's external IP, and a firewall rule that admits the internal subnet:

# Route: 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 (gateway external IP)
sudo ./main-cluster/scripts/01-add-route.sh
sudo ./main-cluster/scripts/02-firewall-setup.sh

ip route show | grep 192.168.100.0/24
# 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100

The scripts source the generated setup_env.sh from the repository root (INTERNAL_NETWORK, ROUTER_VM_EXTERNAL).

docs.title: MachineConfigPool and MachineConfigs
docs.text: Setup Guide: C.4

docs.title: MachineConfigPool
docs.text:
File: base/machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml

Purpose: Create a separate pool for the HCI workers

apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfigPool
metadata:
  name: hci-vm
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: hci-vm
spec:
  machineConfigSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role
      operator: In
      values:
      - worker
      - hci-vm
    - key: node-platform
      operator: NotIn
      values:
      - s390x
  nodeSelector:
    matchLabels:
      node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""
  paused: false
  maxUnavailable: 1

Key Features:

  • Separate from the main worker pool; the name is consumer.machineConfigPool (default hci-vm)
  • Selects nodes with the node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: "" label
  • Excludes MachineConfigs labelled node-platform: s390x, so the s390x route MachineConfig never lands on x86 VMs
  • Can be paused independently for maintenance

docs.title: Kernel Arguments
docs.text:
File: base/machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml (99-hci-vm-kargs; also created by the operator on first reconcile if absent)

Purpose: Configure HCI worker-specific boot settings

kernelArguments:
  - "root=/dev/disk/by-label/root"
  - "rd.multipath=0"    # Disable multipath — not needed for VMs
  - "rd.neednet=1"
  - "ip=enp1s0:off"     # Disable the HCI pod-network interface (prevents OVN conflicts)
  - "ip=enp2s0:dhcp"    # Cluster network interface via (static-lease) DHCP

Node role labeling is done automatically by the node-labeler sidecar in the hci-consumer-operator pod — no MachineConfig labeling is required.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose the Deployment Variant
docs.text: The variant follows consumer.networking.topology in integration-setup.yaml.

docs.title: Mediated Topology (Private Network)
docs.text:
When to use:

  • Main-cluster nodes sit on a private network (example: 10.0.0.0/24)
  • The bastion (172.16.0.1 in the example) routes all traffic to the HCI gateway
  • Common in z/VM and LPAR environments

What's included: the base MachineConfigPool and kernel arguments. No additional routing on the cluster nodes — the bastion handles it.

Apply: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

docs.title: Direct Topology (Public Network)
docs.text:
When to use:

  • Main-cluster nodes are on the same routable network as the HCI gateway's external IP (172.16.1.100 in the example)
  • Common in KVM and bare-metal environments

What's included: the base resources plus one static-route MachineConfig for the master nodes and one for the s390x worker nodes, each routing the internal subnet (192.168.100.0/24) via the gateway's external IP.

Apply: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

See Deployment Variants for a detailed comparison.

docs.title: Step 1: Apply Base + Overlay
docs.text:
For Mediated Topology: 

cd /path/to/fusion-hci-integration

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/mediated/

# Verify the MachineConfigPool
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm

# Expected output:
# NAME     CONFIG    UPDATED   UPDATING   DEGRADED   MACHINECOUNT   READYMACHINECOUNT
# hci-vm   rendered  True      False      False      0              0

For Direct Topology: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route

# The master and worker pools roll out the new route
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp master worker

docs.title: Step 2: Wait for MachineConfig Application
docs.text:
Mediated Topology: no node updates are required; the pool is ready immediately.

Direct Topology: master nodes and s390x worker nodes restart one by one. This can take 10–30 minutes.

watch oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp master worker

# Wait for UPDATED=True, UPDATING=False, DEGRADED=False

docs.title: Step 3: Verify Configuration
docs.text:
# Pool details
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm -o yaml
# - machineConfigSelector includes "hci-vm"
# - nodeSelector matches node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""
# - paused: false

# MachineConfigs for the HCI pool
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc | grep -E "hci"
# 99-hci-vm-kargs
# 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route   (direct topology only)
# 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route   (direct topology only)

Direct topology — verify the routes on a node: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/<master-node>
chroot /host
ip route | grep 192.168.100
# 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100 dev br-ex

# Same check on an s390x worker (no "dev br-ex")
# 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100

docs.title: HCI Node Manager
docs.text: Setup Guide: C.8 (deployed with the operator)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Automates the HCI worker node lifecycle:

  • CSR approval — approves the bootstrap and serving CSRs of the worker VMs
  • Node labeling — applies node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm: ""

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
The node manager runs as two sidecar containers (csr-approver and node-labeler) inside the hci-consumer-operator Deployment. It is deployed automatically as part of the operator — no separate build or deployment step is required.

The sidecars are configured via the hci-node-manager-config ConfigMap, which the operator writes on every reconcile from the WorkerPool CR:

ConfigMap key Source NODE_NAME_PATTERN spec.consumer.workers.namePrefix (example: worker-x86) TARGET_NETWORK spec.provider.networking.internalSubnet (example: 192.168.100.0/24)

The cluster domain is derived automatically from config.openshift.io/v1 DNS/cluster — no manual configuration is needed.

Both sidecars re-read the ConfigMap every ~30 s, so a pod that started before the first reconcile picks up the config by itself. The node-labeler labels a node only if its name matches <NODE_NAME_PATTERN>-<N>, its kubernetes.io/arch is amd64, and its InternalIP is in TARGET_NETWORK. This keeps s390x control-plane and compute nodes out of the hci-vm MachineConfigPool even if the networks overlap.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# The consumer operator pod (the sidecars are containers within it)
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get pods -n hci-node-manager \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/name=hci-consumer-operator

# csr-approver logs
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n hci-node-manager \
  deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c csr-approver | tail -20

# node-labeler logs
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n hci-node-manager \
  deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c node-labeler | tail -20

docs.title: Registry Configuration (Cross-Cluster Model only)
docs.text: Setup Guide: C.5 and C.6

docs.title: When Needed
docs.text: Only when registry.model: cross-cluster is set in integration-setup.yaml. With local-s2i or external, skip this section.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Location: main-cluster/bastion-registry/

  1. Bastion HAProxy and cluster insecure-registry entry — run as your normal user, not with sudo (the script uses sudo internally for HAProxy, firewall and certificates, and runs oc with your own login against ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT}):

    ./main-cluster/bastion-registry/setup-registry-proxy.sh

    The script generates a self-signed certificate, configures HAProxy to forward bastion.cluster.example.com:5443 to the HCI registry, and adds that address to image.config.openshift.io/cluster spec.registrySources.insecureRegistries on the main cluster. That change triggers a MachineConfigPool rollout (10–30 minutes).

  2. Registry push secret — reads the token of the registry-pusher ServiceAccount from the HCI cluster (created by setup-consumer-rbac.sh, see HCI Cluster Configuration) and stores it as a docker-registry Secret on the main cluster:

    ./main-cluster/bastion-registry/setup-registry-access.sh
# creates Secret hci-registry-push in namespace hci-node-manager

Verify:

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get image.config.openshift.io cluster \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.registrySources.insecureRegistries}'
curl -sk https://localhost:5443/v2/ && echo ok     # on the bastion
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get secret hci-registry-push -n hci-node-manager

See the Bastion Registry README for details.

docs.title: Helper Scripts
docs.text:
The scripts in main-cluster/scripts/ run on the bastion and source the generated setup_env.sh:

Script Purpose Setup Guide 01-add-route.sh Route to the internal subnet via the gateway external IP (mediated) C.2 02-firewall-setup.sh Verify/complete the bastion firewall configuration (mediated) C.2

The worker ignition file (worker-hci.ign) is produced by the hci-provisioner operator; no script is needed for it.

docs.title: Step 1: Verify the MachineConfigPool
docs.text:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm

# MACHINECOUNT: 0 (no workers yet)
# READYMACHINECOUNT: 0
# UPDATED: True   UPDATING: False   DEGRADED: False

docs.title: Step 2: Prepare for Worker Join
docs.text:
CSRs are approved automatically by the csr-approver sidecar in the hci-consumer-operator pod. No manual action is needed once the operator is deployed.

# Monitor csr-approver activity
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n hci-node-manager \
  deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c csr-approver -f

# Manual approval (e.g. operator not yet deployed)
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get csr | grep Pending
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get csr | awk '/Pending/ {print $1}' \
  | xargs -r oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} adm certificate approve

docs.title: Step 3: Monitor Worker Join
docs.text:
watch oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm
watch oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm

# As workers join, MACHINECOUNT and READYMACHINECOUNT increase

docs.title: Updating MachineConfigs
docs.text:
# Edit the MachineConfig
vi main-cluster/configuration/base/machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml

# Apply the change
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/<variant>/

# Workers restart to apply it
watch oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm

The hci-consumer operator only creates the MachineConfigs when they are absent; it never overwrites an existing one, so manual changes are preserved.

Pausing updates: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch mcp hci-vm --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"paused":true}}'
# Make changes ...
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch mcp hci-vm --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"paused":false}}'

docs.title: Switching Variants
docs.text:
Not recommended: switching the topology after deployment requires redeploying the workers.

If necessary: 

# 1. Scale the pool to 0 workers (edit spec.consumer.workers.count) and wait
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} -n hci-node-manager edit workerpool hci-workers

# 2. Delete the old route MachineConfigs (and the pool, if it is to be recreated)
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} delete mc 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route --ignore-not-found

# 3. Change consumer.networking.topology in integration-setup.yaml,
#    re-run generate-setup, then apply the matching overlay
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -k main-cluster/configuration/overlays/<new-variant>/

# 4. Scale the pool back up

docs.title: MachineConfigPool Stuck Updating
docs.text:
Symptoms: UPDATING: True for an extended period, or DEGRADED: True.

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm -o yaml
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[*].message}'

# machine-config-daemon logs on affected nodes
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n openshift-machine-config-operator -l k8s-app=machine-config-daemon

docs.title: Workers Not Joining the Pool
docs.text:
Symptoms: workers appear in the cluster but not in the hci-vm pool.

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get node worker-x86-1 --show-labels
# Should have: node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm

# The node-labeler requires: name matches worker-x86-<N>, arch amd64,
# InternalIP in 192.168.100.0/24.  Check its log first:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n hci-node-manager \
  deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c node-labeler | tail -30

# If you must label manually:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label node worker-x86-1 node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm=

docs.title: CSRs Not Being Approved
docs.text:
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get csr | grep Pending

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n hci-node-manager \
  deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c csr-approver | tail -30

docs.title: Routes Not Applied (Direct Topology)
docs.text:
# MachineConfigs exist
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route

# Applied to the pools
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp master -o yaml | grep 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp worker -o yaml | grep 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route

# Route on a node
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/<node>
chroot /host
ip route | grep 192.168.100

See the Troubleshooting Guide for detailed solutions.

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
1. Keep integration-setup.yaml as the single source of truth — regenerate rather than hand-edit generated files
  2. Version control — keep integration-setup.yaml and any customized MachineConfigs in Git (never the generated setup_env.sh/credentials)
  3. Test changes — verify in a dev environment before production
  4. Document customizations — maintain a changelog

docs.title: MachineConfigPool Management
docs.text:
1. Separate pools — keep HCI workers isolated
  2. Pause for maintenance — prevent automatic updates during changes
  3. Monitor status — watch for degraded state
  4. Plan updates — schedule during maintenance windows

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Limit access — use RBAC for MachineConfig management
  2. Audit changes — review MachineConfig modifications
  3. Protect credentials — secure ignition files, SSH keys and operator credential Secrets
  4. Regular updates — keep RHCOS updated

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
1. CSR approval is automatic — handled by the csr-approver sidecar in the consumer operator
  2. Monitor continuously — set up alerts for pool status
  3. Test recovery — verify disaster recovery procedures
  4. Document procedures — maintain runbooks

docs.title: Developer Notes
docs.text: This document captures key technical decisions, lessons learned, and best practices discovered during the development of this integration solution.

docs.title: 1. Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
Principle: Cluster-scoped resources should never be managed by namespace-scoped deployments.

Why: Multiple integration namespaces would conflict when trying to manage the same cluster-scoped resource (e.g., ClusterUserDefinedNetwork).

Implementation: - Cluster-admin applies ClusterUserDefinedNetwork once (Setup Guide Tier A) - Integration namespaces are labeled hci-gateway-enabled=true - Namespace-scoped UserDefinedNetwork and gateway/worker VMs are created automatically by the hci-provisioner operator - Clear separation between cluster-admin and integration-team responsibilities

Reference: See hci-cluster/ for cluster-scoped setup.

docs.title: 2. Network Interface Management
docs.text:
Principle: Disable unused network interfaces completely, don't just deprioritize them.

Why: Worker VMs have two interfaces: enp1s0 (HCI pod network) and enp2s0 (main cluster network / internal UDN). Having both active causes: - Dual default routes - DNS conflicts - Identity confusion - NetworkManager and OVN-Kubernetes bridge attachment conflicts

Implementation: - Completely disable enp1s0 via kernel arguments in the 99-hci-vm-kargs MachineConfig - Pass coreos.inst.karg=ip=enp1s0:off coreos.inst.karg=ip=enp2s0:dhcp during iPXE first boot / installation - Use only enp2s0 for all cluster communication and OVN br-ex mapping

Code: 

# 99-hci-vm-kargs
apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  name: 99-hci-vm-kargs
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: hci-vm
    node-platform: hci-vm
spec:
  kernelArguments:
    - "root=/dev/disk/by-label/root"
    - "rd.multipath=0"
    - "rd.neednet=1"
    - "ip=enp1s0:off"
    - "ip=enp2s0:dhcp"
  config:
    ignition:
      version: 3.5.0

Reference: main-cluster/configuration/base/machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml

docs.title: 3. Platform-Based Configuration Inheritance
docs.text:
Principle: Use labels to prevent architecture-specific config inheritance.

Why: HCI x86 workers were inheriting s390x multipath storage configs from the base worker pool, causing boot failures.

Implementation: - Label MachineConfigs with node-platform: s390x or node-platform: hci - MachineConfigPool selectors exclude incompatible platforms - Each platform gets appropriate storage/network configuration

Code: 

# MachineConfigPool selector
machineConfigSelector:
  matchExpressions:
    - key: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role
      operator: In
      values: [worker, hci-vm]
    - key: node-platform
      operator: NotIn
      values: [s390x]  # Exclude s390x-specific configs

Reference: main-cluster/configuration/base/machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml

docs.title: Static IP Assignment via Cloud-Init and DHCP
docs.text:
Decision: Use cloud-init with MAC address matching for the gateway VM, and static DHCP reservations on the gateway for worker VMs.

Why: - Gateway VM: Configured via cloud-init network configuration (gateway-vm-cloudinit.j2). MAC address matching configures static IPs on the physical interface (172.16.1.100/16) and internal UDN interface (192.168.100.1/24) without relying on OVN IPAM. - Worker VMs: Receive deterministic IPs and hostnames from dnsmasq on the gateway VM via static reservations in /etc/dnsmasq.d/pxe.conf based on MAC prefix 52:54:01. No cloud-init or ignition network injection needed on workers.

Gateway Cloud-Init Implementation: 

network:
  version: 2
  ethernets:
    external:
      match:
        macaddress: "52:54:01:00:00:01"
      addresses: [172.16.1.100/16]
      gateway4: 172.16.0.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [172.16.0.1]
    internal:
      match:
        macaddress: "52:54:01:00:00:02"
      addresses: [192.168.100.1/24]

docs.title: Kustomize for Deployment Variants
docs.text:
Decision: Use Kustomize base + overlays for mediated vs direct topologies (with generate-setup providing automated rendering).

Why: - DRY principle - base configs defined once - Clear visibility of variant differences - Easy to add new variants (ARM, Power) - GitOps-ready - Industry standard

Structure: 

main-cluster/configuration/
├── base/                    # Common MachineConfigs
│   ├── kustomization.yaml
│   ├── machineconfig-pool-hci-vm.yaml
│   └── machineconfig-hci-vm-kargs.yaml
└── overlays/
    ├── mediated/            # Mediated Topology (private network)
    │   └── kustomization.yaml
    └── direct/              # Direct Topology (shared/public network)
        ├── kustomization.yaml
        ├── 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml
        └── 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml

docs.title: OVN Networking Topology
docs.text:
Decision: Use OVN localnet (external) + layer2 (internal) topologies.

Why: - Localnet: Direct physical network access without overlay encapsulation - Layer2: Complete isolation for internal worker network - Performance: No double encapsulation overhead - Security: Internal network completely isolated from HCI pod network

Alternatives Rejected: - Pure overlay networks - Too much encapsulation overhead - Physical bridge - Requires node-level configuration - Router VM with NAT - Adds complexity, breaks cluster networking

docs.title: 1. NAD Namespace References
docs.text:
Problem: NetworkAttachmentDefinition references pointing to wrong namespace.

Symptom: VMs fail to start with "failed to get pod annotation" errors.

Solution: Always use fully qualified NAD references: 

# Wrong
networks:
  - name: router-external-network

# Correct
networks:
  - name: <namespace>/router-external-network

Prevention: The operator automatically formats the network attachment as <namespace>/router-external-network.

docs.title: 2. ClusterUserDefinedNetwork Conflicts
docs.text:
Problem: Multiple deployments trying to manage the same ClusterUserDefinedNetwork.

Symptom: Second deployment fails or overwrites the cluster-scoped network.

Solution: - Cluster-admin creates ClusterUserDefinedNetwork once - Integration namespace must be labeled: hci-gateway-enabled=true - Provisioner operator references the generated NAD and manages only namespace-scoped resources

docs.title: 3. Master and Worker Node Routing (Direct Topology)
docs.text:
Problem: Master and s390x worker nodes cannot reach HCI internal network in direct topology deployments.

Symptom: CSR approval fails, cross-architecture pod communication fails.

Solution: Add static routes on master and worker nodes via MachineConfigs: 

# Master route
ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via <gateway-external-ip> dev br-ex

# Worker route
ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via <gateway-external-ip>

Implementation: main-cluster/configuration/overlays/direct/99-master-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml and 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route.yaml

docs.title: 4. DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Problem: Workers using wrong DNS server (HCI cluster instead of main cluster).

Symptom: Can't resolve main cluster API, etcd endpoints.

Solution: - Gateway VM dnsmasq serves main cluster DNS (172.16.0.1) via DHCP - Disable enp1s0 via kernel arguments to prevent HCI Pod network DNS from taking precedence - Verify with: oc debug node/<worker> -- chroot /host cat /etc/resolv.conf

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
1. Use single source of truth: integration-setup.yaml processed by ./generate-setup
  2. Never commit credentials: Use .gitignore and example files
  3. Validate before apply: Check generated artifacts in workspace/
  4. Test both topologies: Mediated (private network) and Direct (shared network)

docs.title: Deployment Workflow
docs.text:
1. Gateway first: The operator provisions and boots the gateway VM before worker VMs
  2. Verify gateway: Ensure RHCOS boot files are downloaded and services are active
  3. Enable workers gradually: Start with 1 canary worker, verify Ready state, then scale
  4. Monitor MachineConfigPool: Watch oc get mcp hci-vm for UPDATED: True

docs.title: Troubleshooting Approach
docs.text:
1. Check MachineConfigPool status: oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm
  2. Verify network attachments: oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nad -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
  3. Inspect VM status: oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vmi -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
  4. Debug node: oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/<worker-name>
  5. Check gateway status: ssh core@<gateway-ip> (or virtctl console)

docs.title: Network Performance
docs.text:
• OVN localnet: Near-native performance (no overlay encapsulation)
  • MTU: Ensure consistent MTU across all networks (typically 1500)
  • Gateway VM resources: 2 vCPU, 4GB RAM sufficient for 10-20 workers

docs.title: Storage Performance
docs.text:
• Worker VMs: Use fast storage for etcd-heavy workloads
  • Gateway VM: Standard storage sufficient (mostly network I/O)
  • Avoid multipath: HCI virtual disks don't need multipath

docs.title: Network Isolation
docs.text:
• Internal worker network (192.168.100.0/24) completely isolated via OVN layer2
  • No direct access from HCI pod network to workers
  • Gateway VM provides controlled routing

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
• Cluster-admin required for ClusterUserDefinedNetwork
  • Namespace-level RBAC for VM deployment
  • SSH key from main cluster required for VM access

docs.title: Firewall Rules
docs.text: Gateway VM implements defense-in-depth: - Explicit allow rules for cluster traffic - NAT for internet access - Drop all other traffic

docs.title: Operator Development
docs.text:
See Operator Roadmap and Build & Deploy Operators.

Key benefits: - Declarative configuration via WorkerPool and WorkerPoolProvisioning CRDs - Automated lifecycle management (gateway, UDN, worker VMs, CSRs, node labeling) - Self-healing capabilities - Multi-cluster and multi-namespace support

docs.title: Additional Architectures
docs.text:
Structure supports: - ARM-based main clusters - Power-based main clusters - Additional HCI platforms

Implementation: Create new Kustomize overlay for architecture-specific needs.

docs.title: Building and Deploying the Operators
docs.text:
The integration relies on two Ansible operators that run on the main cluster:

Operator CRD watched Responsibility hci-consumer WorkerPool Scale worker VMs up/down; CSR approval and node labeling via sidecars hci-provisioner WorkerPoolProvisioning Bootstrap/teardown: UDN, gateway VM, ignition, MachineConfig validation

Both operators must be built and deployed before you create a WorkerPool CR. This page covers everything from configuring the registry to verifying the running pods.

Prerequisite

You must be logged in to the main cluster with cluster-admin and have kustomize on your PATH.

Reconnecting an existing cluster?

If the operators were previously deployed on this main cluster:

  • Step 2 (BuildConfigs) — skip unless the BuildConfig definitions changed
  • Step 4 (CRDs) — skip unless the CRD schemas changed
  • Step 1 (registry config) — verify config.env still matches your setup_env.sh values (rendered from integration-setup.yaml); confirm the push secret exists with oc get secret ${REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME} -n ${OPERATOR_NAMESPACE}

For a code-only rebuild the minimum is: Step 3 → Step 5 (add make rollout if the image tag did not change — see Updating the Operators).

docs.title: Step 1 — Configure the Registry
docs.text:
All image coordinates live in a single file: operator/build/config.env. Open it and fill in the values that match your environment:

# Namespace where everything lives (BuildConfigs, ImageStreams, operator Deployments)
OPERATOR_NAMESPACE ?= hci-node-manager

# ── Push target (build output) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Leave REGISTRY_PUSH empty to use the cluster's internal registry (default).
# Set it to an external / bastion-proxy registry hostname + project if needed.
REGISTRY_PUSH        ?=
REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME ?=

# ── Pull source (Deployment image references) ────────────────────────────────
# Internal registry — the namespace is added as a path segment automatically:
REGISTRY_PULL ?= image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/hci-node-manager

REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME is the single push+pull secret — the same credential used by the BuildConfig (push) and the operator Deployments (pull). It matches the variable of the same name exported by setup_env.sh (rendered from integration-setup.yaml), so if your shell environment is already set up, no manual editing of this file is needed.

docs.title: Registry strategy
docs.text:
Internal registry (default)External / bastion-proxy registry

Leave REGISTRY_PUSH empty and keep the REGISTRY_PULL default. The build writes directly into the cluster's ImageStream and the Deployment pulls through the in-cluster registry service.

No push secret is required.

Set your bastion coordinates in config.env — or just export them in your shell before running make and the ?= defaults will be overridden automatically:

REGISTRY_PUSH        = bastion.example.com:5443/myproject
REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME = hci-registry-push
REGISTRY_PULL        = bastion.example.com:5443/myproject

The push+pull secret (REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME) must already exist in ${OPERATOR_NAMESPACE} on the main cluster. It is created by setup-registry-access.sh (Getting Started step C.6) — if you have completed that step, the secret is already in place.

You can override any variable on the make command line without editing the file:

make build IMAGE_TAG=v1.2.3
make deploy IMAGE_TAG=v1.2.3

docs.title: Step 2 — Apply BuildConfigs (one-time)
docs.text:
cd operator/
make apply-buildconfigs

This single command:

  1. Creates the hci-node-manager namespace (if absent)
  2. Creates ImageStream objects for both operator images (internal-registry mode) or generates the external push patch (external-registry mode)
  3. Applies both BuildConfig objects to the cluster

You only need to re-run this step when the BuildConfig definition itself changes.

Day-to-day rebuilds of the operator images skip straight to Step 3.

docs.title: Step 3 — Build the Images
docs.text:
make build

This runs oc start-build --from-dir for both operators. The build executes on a cluster node (s390x architecture), so no local container toolchain is needed.

Build a single image if only one operator changed:

make build-consumer     # hci-consumer only
make build-provisioner  # hci-provisioner only

Monitor a running build:

oc logs -f bc/hci-consumer-operator   -n hci-node-manager
oc logs -f bc/hci-provisioner-operator -n hci-node-manager

docs.title: Step 4 — Install the CRDs
docs.text:
make install

Applies the WorkerPool and WorkerPoolProvisioning CRD manifests to the cluster. Run this once per cluster, or again after a CRD schema update.

Verify:

oc get crd | grep hci
# workerpoolprovisionings.hci.openshift.io
# workerpools.hci.openshift.io

docs.title: Step 5 — Deploy the Operators
docs.text:
make deploy

make deploy generates deploy/overlays/active/kustomization.yaml (git-ignored) from your shell environment and runs oc apply -k against it. There is nothing to edit — the active overlay is produced entirely from the variables already set in your environment.

To inspect what will be applied before committing:

make print-config

If REGISTRY_SECRET_NAME is set, make deploy automatically adds an imagePullSecrets patch for both Deployments. No OVERLAY flag is needed.

make deploy does not restart running pods on its own

make deploy is a declarative oc apply: it only changes the cluster if the rendered manifests differ from what is already there. imagePullPolicy: Always only takes effect when a pod is (re)created. If you rebuilt the :latest image and re-run make deploy, the Deployment spec is identical, so nothing happens and the old image keeps running. Run make rollout afterwards (or deploy with a new IMAGE_TAG, which changes the spec and triggers a rollout automatically).

MAIN_CLUSTER_DOMAIN — no action required

The csr-approver sidecar derives the cluster domain automatically at startup by querying the DNS/cluster config object on the main cluster. No env var or patch file needs to be set before deploying. MAIN_CLUSTER_DOMAIN exists only as a fallback if that API call fails.

What gets deployed

  • Deployment/hci-consumer-operator — three containers: operator, csr-approver, node-labeler
  • Deployment/hci-provisioner-operator — one container: operator
  • ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for both operators (RBAC)

docs.title: Step 6 — Verify
docs.text:
oc get pods -n hci-node-manager
# NAME                                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# hci-consumer-operator-xxxx-yyyy         3/3     Running   0          2m
# hci-provisioner-operator-xxxx-yyyy      1/1     Running   0          2m

Inspect individual container logs:

# hci-consumer — three containers
oc logs deployment/hci-consumer-operator   -c operator      -n hci-node-manager
oc logs deployment/hci-consumer-operator   -c csr-approver  -n hci-node-manager
oc logs deployment/hci-consumer-operator   -c node-labeler  -n hci-node-manager

# hci-provisioner — one container
oc logs deployment/hci-provisioner-operator -c operator     -n hci-node-manager

Both operators start idle (no WorkerPool CR exists yet). Once you apply the WorkerPool CR, the operators begin their automated reconcile loop.

docs.title: All Make Targets
docs.text:
Run make help inside operator/ for a quick reference at any time.

Target What it does apply-buildconfigs Create namespace, ImageStreams, BuildConfigs in-cluster (one-time) build Build both operator images in-cluster via oc start-build build-consumer Build hci-consumer image only build-provisioner Build hci-provisioner image only install Apply both CRDs to the cluster uninstall Remove both CRDs (deletes all CRs) deploy Generate active overlay from config.env, then oc apply -k (does not restart unchanged Deployments) rollout oc rollout restart both operator Deployments and wait for completion (use after make build with an unchanged tag) undeploy Delete operator Deployments (CRDs and namespace kept) print-config Show resolved image references and overlay path

docs.title: Updating the Operators
docs.text:
To roll out a code change to either operator:

# 1. Build the new image (no need to re-apply BuildConfigs)
make build                 # or build-consumer / build-provisioner

# 2. Restart both Deployments to pull the new :latest image, wait until ready
make rollout

make rollout runs oc rollout restart followed by oc rollout status for both operators (timeout via ROLLOUT_TIMEOUT, default 300s). To restart only one operator:

oc rollout restart deployment/hci-consumer-operator -n hci-node-manager
oc rollout status  deployment/hci-consumer-operator -n hci-node-manager

For a tagged release:

make build IMAGE_TAG=v1.2.3
make deploy IMAGE_TAG=v1.2.3

docs.title: Tearing Down
docs.text:
# Remove Deployments (leaves CRDs and namespace intact)
make undeploy

# Also remove CRDs (WARNING: deletes all WorkerPool and WorkerPoolProvisioning objects)
make uninstall

# Remove the namespace entirely
oc delete namespace hci-node-manager

Removing CRDs while WorkerPools exist

Running make uninstall while active WorkerPool CRs exist bypasses the finalizer that drains nodes and deletes VMs. Always scale down / delete all WorkerPool objects first: 

oc delete workerpool --all
# wait for finalizer to complete, then:
make uninstall

docs.title: Local Debug Workflow (No Image Build)
docs.text:
Each operator directory contains a run-local.sh that runs the Ansible role directly on the bastion against a live cluster — useful for iterating on role logic without a full image build cycle:

# Test hci-consumer reconcile against a live WorkerPool CR
cd operator/hci-consumer
./run-local.sh

# Test hci-provisioner reconcile against a live WorkerPoolProvisioning CR
cd operator/hci-provisioner
./run-local.sh

See the individual operator READMEs for prerequisites.

docs.title: Operator Optimization and Go Migration Guide
docs.text: This document captures architectural analysis, performance tuning recommendations for the current Ansible-based operators, and the roadmap for migrating to native Golang operators.

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text:
The Fusion HCI integration currently runs two Ansible-based operators built with the Operator SDK Ansible plugin: * hci-consumer: Watches WorkerPool CRs on the main cluster, scales worker VMs on the HCI cluster, and manages node join operations. * hci-provisioner: Watches WorkerPoolProvisioning CRs, orchestrating UDN creation, gateway VM deployment, SSH readiness probes, and ignition generation.

While functional and verified end-to-end, the Ansible implementation exhibits latency during state transitions due to synchronous playbook execution and timer-based reconciliation loops.

docs.title: 2. Immediate Optimizations for Ansible Operators
docs.text: The following improvements can be implemented directly within the existing Ansible operator architecture without rewriting the codebase in Go.

docs.title: 2.1 Enable Event-Driven Dependent Resource Watches
docs.text:
In operator/hci-consumer/watches.yaml and operator/hci-provisioner/watches.yaml, watchDependentResources is currently set to false. Reconcile loops rely almost entirely on the timer tick (reconcilePeriod: 60s).

Recommended Configuration: 

- version: v1alpha1
  group: hci-integration.openshift.io
  kind: WorkerPool
  role: hci_consumer
  reconcilePeriod: 30s
  manageStatus: false
  watchDependentResources: true
  watchClusterScopedResources: true
  gatheredFacts: false

  • Mechanism: Because WorkerPoolProvisioning CRs carry an ownerReference pointing to the owning WorkerPool, enabling watchDependentResources: true triggers an instant reconcile on WorkerPool when provisioning step statuses change (e.g. from Pending → InProgress → Complete).
  • Impact: Eliminates up to 60 seconds of idle wait time when bootstrap completes.

docs.title: 2.2 Disable OS Fact Gathering (gatheredFacts: false)
docs.text:
Both operators currently set gatheredFacts: true in watches.yaml solely to obtain ansible_date_time timestamps.

  • Problem: Ansible executes the complete setup module inside the container on every single reconcile cycle, gathering host/container hardware, network, and disk metrics. This adds 1 to 3 seconds of CPU overhead per reconcile pass.
  • Fix: Set gatheredFacts: false in watches.yaml and generate timestamps on-demand in tasks: 
    lastTransitionTime: "{{ lookup('pipe', 'date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ') }}"

docs.title: 2.3 Cascade Sequential Steps in advance_steps.yml
docs.text:
In hci-provisioner, each step transition currently terminates the playbook via ansible.builtin.meta: end_play. When Step 1 (UserDefinedNetwork) completes, the operator waits for the next 60s timer tick before evaluating Step 2 (GatewayVM).

  • Fix: Allow advance_steps.yml to evaluate downstream steps whose dependencies are immediately met, executing them in the same reconcile pass if no asynchronous external wait is required.
  • Impact: Shaves 1 to 2 minutes off the initial bootstrap flow.

docs.title: 2.4 Server-Side API Filtering in observe_world.yml
docs.text:
In observe_world.yml, listing all cluster nodes and iterating through pods on cordoned nodes produces multiple sequential API queries.

  • Fix: Add label_selectors directly to k8s_info calls so filtering occurs on the Kubernetes API server rather than across large Jinja2 lists in the Ansible runner: 
    - name: "Observe | List pool worker nodes"
  kubernetes.core.k8s_info:
    api_version: v1
    kind: Node
    label_selectors:
      - "node-role.kubernetes.io/{{ consumer.machine_config_pool }}"
  register: _obs_all_nodes

docs.title: 2.5 Operator Runner Environment Tuning
docs.text: Configure runtime environment variables in operator/deploy/base/ deployments: * WORKERS: "2" or MAX_CONCURRENT_RECONCILES: "2" — Prevents queue blockages across multiple CR events. * ANSIBLE_VERBOSITY: "0" — Reduces runner JSON parsing and disk I/O in the container during steady state. * ANSIBLE_RETRY_FILES_ENABLED: "0" — Disables retry file creation.

docs.title: 3. Comparison: Ansible vs. Golang Operators
docs.text: Metric / Feature Ansible Operator Golang Operator (controller-runtime) Event Reaction Time Seconds (sequential playbook execution) Milliseconds (informer work queues & event filters) Memory Footprint ~400 MB – 800 MB per pod (ose-ansible-operator + Python) ~30 MB – 60 MB per pod (single static binary) Sidecar Containers Requires 3 containers (operator, csr-approver, node-labeler) Single container; approver & labeler run as integrated informers Type Safety Runtime YAML string interpretation; Ansible 2.9 quirks Compile-time Go type safety for KubeVirt, CDI, and OpenShift APIs Cross-Cluster Auth Writes temporary kubeconfig files to /tmp per reconcile In-memory client.Client instances with pooled HTTP/2 connections External Operations Python scripts, shell-outs for SSH/SCP Native Go packages (golang.org/x/crypto/ssh, crypto/ed25519) Testing Live cluster or bastion runner (run-local.sh) Fast unit/integration tests with envtest (no live cluster required) Ecosystem Support Standalone ansible-operator binary deprecated in SDK v1.38+ First-class, standard Kubernetes & OpenShift operator ecosystem

docs.title: 4. Golang Operator Migration Blueprint
docs.text:
When migrating to Go, the architecture simplifies into a single controller binary managing multiple controllers and informers:

cmd/main.go
├── WorkerPoolReconciler (replaces hci-consumer role)
│   ├── Remote HCI KubeVirt / CDI Client Manager
│   └── Local Node Lifecycle & Drain Manager
├── WorkerPoolProvisioningReconciler (replaces hci-provisioner role)
│   ├── State Machine Engine (UDN -> GatewayVM -> Ignition -> Bootfiles)
│   └── Native SSH/SFTP Client (gateway file transfer & probes)
├── CSRAutoApproverInformer (replaces node-auto-approver.py sidecar)
└── NodeLabelerInformer (replaces node-labeler.py sidecar)

docs.title: Key Migration Steps
docs.text:
1. Scaffold Project:
  2. Initialize using operator-sdk init --plugins=go/v4 --domain=openshift.io.
  3. Create APIs for WorkerPool and WorkerPoolProvisioning.
  4. Implement Multi-Cluster Client Cache:
  5. Implement a manager that reads the credentials Secret and instantiates/caches a remote client.Client using clientcmd.RESTConfigFromKubeConfig.
  6. Port Reconciliation Logic:
  7. Use typed KubeVirt (kubevirt.io/api/core/v1) and CDI (cdi.kubevirt.io/v1beta1) client packages.
  8. Replace manual node drain logic with the standard k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/drain package.
  9. Integrate Node Manager Sidecars into Informers:
  10. Add a CertificateSigningRequest controller that approves kubelet and bootstrap CSRs matching the pool naming pattern.
  11. Add a Node controller that applies role labels based on internal IP subnet checks.
  12. Multi-Architecture Builds:
  13. Leverage Go cross-compilation (GOARCH=s390x go build) to produce LinuxONE binaries directly from standard CI build pipelines.

docs.title: 5. Trade-offs and Recommendation
docs.text:
• Trade-offs: Rewriting in Go requires Go/controller-runtime expertise and an upfront development investment (~20–25 story points), temporarily diverting focus from upcoming functional epics (such as Epic 3: HCI Provider Operator).
  • Recommendation:
  • Phase 1 (Immediate): Apply the Ansible optimizations in Section 2 (watchDependentResources: true, gatheredFacts: false, cascading step execution) to achieve immediate responsiveness gains with minimal effort (~4 points).
  • Phase 2 (Production Hardening): Transition to Go when preparing for multi-tenant production deployments or publishing to OperatorHub.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text:
Goal: Fully automated, declarative lifecycle management of multi-architecture worker nodes.

An operator administrator applies one WorkerPool CR; the system: 1. Provisions UDN, gateway VM, and ignition via the hci-provisioner operator (Bootstrap) 2. Continuously reconciles workers.count → VMs on HCI and nodes on the LO cluster (Steady-state) 3. Handles scale-up and scale-down safely, with drain timing controlled by LOOps 4. Tears down all infrastructure cleanly on CR deletion

HCI-side provisioning (namespace, network, quota, ticket generation) will be automated by the HCI Provider Operator (Epic 3, future work).

Target Users: Platform administrators, SREs, DevOps teams Key Principles: Declarative, self-healing, observable, privilege-minimal

docs.title: Operator Framework
docs.text:
Choice: Ansible Operator (operator-sdk Ansible plugin)

Rationale: - Most of the existing integration work already uses Ansible and kubernetes.core modules - Ansible roles map directly to the observe/diff/act reconcile structure - Low barrier to contribution from the existing team - Excellent kubernetes.core.k8s and k8s_info modules for both clusters - No Go cross-compilation concern for s390x (runs on bastion natively)

ansible-operator binary: standalone download removed in operator-sdk v1.38+. Development uses ansible-runner directly on the cluster bastion.

Note: For performance tuning recommendations and the planned roadmap to migrate to native Golang operators, see Operator Optimization and Go Migration Guide.

docs.title: Cross-Cluster Communication
docs.text:
Choice: Direct API calls with kubeconfig (stored as Kubernetes Secret)

Rationale: Simple, standard, no additional infrastructure. The kubeconfig is written to a temp file per reconcile and cleaned up after. The namespace-scoped SA limits blast radius.

docs.title: CRD API Group
docs.text:
Choice: hci-integration.openshift.io

Used for WorkerPool, WorkerPoolProvisioning, and all future CRDs in this project.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Steady-State Core ✅ COMPLETE
docs.text:
Delivered: - WorkerPool CRD with CEL admission validation - Observe/diff/act reconcile loop - Scale-up and scale-down with set-difference logic (gap-fill correct) - ScaleDownBlocked + CountExceedsMaxPoolSize + ProviderCredentialsReady conditions - Status counts: deployedWorkers, readyWorkers, pendingWorkers - Phase sub-states: ScalingUp, ScalingDown, ScalingDownBlocked, Ready, Deprovisioned - Drain gate: cordon + no non-system pods before VM deletion - Local-storage node protection via annotation - Finalizer/cleanup role with workload-safety gate - Minimal RBAC ServiceAccount - Bastion-based dev workflow with run-local.sh

Confirmed e2e on a live test cluster pair: full lifecycle (create → scale-up → scale-down → delete) verified including status counts and phase transitions.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Bootstrap Operator (Epic 2) ✅ LARGELY COMPLETE
docs.text:
Delivered: - WorkerPoolProvisioning CRD with step-based state machine (wpp) - WorkerPool CRD split into spec.provider + spec.consumer (BS-00b refactor) - UDN step: create/delete UserDefinedNetwork router-internal-network on HCI (BS-03) - Gateway VM step: full cloud-init stack (DHCP, PXE/iPXE, nginx, ignition, RHCOS sync) (BS-04) - Ignition step: generate worker-hci.ign, SCP to gateway nginx root (BS-06a) - Bootfiles version gate: desired-version.txt drift detection, scale-up gate (BS-06b) - MachineConfig step: validate MachineConfigPool exists and is healthy (BS-02) - Workers teardown step: delete all consumer VMs before UDN teardown (BS-08) - Single credential secret (hci-provisioner-credentials) via setup-provider-credentials.sh - BS-05 deliberately descoped: manual script remains the documented handover tool

Confirmed e2e: apply one WorkerPool CR → gateway provisions → workers PXE-boot and join cluster → scale up/down → delete CR → full teardown. See CURRENT-STATUS.md.

docs.title: Worker VM Has Dual Network Conflict
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Worker VM has two active interfaces (enp1s0 and enp2s0) - Dual default routes causing routing conflicts - DNS resolution fails or returns wrong results - Node cannot reach main cluster API

Root Cause: The worker VM has two network interfaces: - enp1s0: Connected to HCI cluster's Pod network (should be disabled) - enp2s0: Connected to main cluster network (should be active)

Both interfaces receive DHCP configuration, creating conflicts.

Solution:

The 99-hci-vm-kargs MachineConfig (and the iPXE boot command) disables enp1s0 and configures enp2s0 via kernel arguments:

# 99-hci-vm-kargs (created automatically by the hci-consumer operator)
apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata:
  name: 99-hci-vm-kargs
  labels:
    machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: hci-vm
    node-platform: hci-vm
spec:
  kernelArguments:
    - "root=/dev/disk/by-label/root"
    - "rd.multipath=0"
    - "rd.neednet=1"
    - "ip=enp1s0:off"
    - "ip=enp2s0:dhcp"
  config:
    ignition:
      version: 3.5.0

During installation, the iPXE boot command on the gateway also supplies coreos.inst.karg=ip=enp1s0:off coreos.inst.karg=ip=enp2s0:dhcp so that RHCOS installs and boots with the correct interface active.

Verification: 

# Debug worker node
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/worker-x86-1
chroot /host

# Check interface status
ip link show enp1s0  # Should be DOWN or unconfigured
ip link show enp2s0  # Should be UP

# Check IP addresses
ip addr show enp1s0  # Should have no IP
ip addr show enp2s0  # Should have 192.168.100.x

# Check routes
ip route show  # Should only show routes via enp2s0 (192.168.100.1 gateway)

# Check DNS
cat /etc/resolv.conf  # Should show main cluster DNS (172.16.0.1)

docs.title: OVN-Kubernetes br-ex Bridge Conflict
docs.text:
Symptoms: - OVN-Kubernetes creates br-ex bridge on wrong interface (enp1s0) - Default route appears on br-ex instead of enp2s0 - Worker cannot reach main cluster API - DNS resolution uses wrong DNS server

Root Cause: OVN-Kubernetes automatically selects the first available network interface for the external bridge (br-ex). In HCI workers, it incorrectly chooses enp1s0 instead of enp2s0.

Solution:

Force OVN to use enp2s0 for br-ex:

# In MachineConfig
storage:
  files:
    - path: /etc/systemd/system/ovs-configuration.service.d/override.conf
      mode: 0644
      overwrite: true
      contents:
        inline: |
          [Service]
          Environment="OVN_KUBERNETES_EXTERNAL_INTERFACE=enp2s0"

Verification: 

# Check OVN interface selection
systemctl cat ovs-configuration.service | grep OVN_KUBERNETES_EXTERNAL_INTERFACE

# Check br-ex is using enp2s0
ovs-vsctl show | grep -A 5 br-ex

# Should show enp2s0 as port, not enp1s0

docs.title: Gateway VM Gets Wrong IP Address (IPAM Issue)
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Gateway VM receives a dynamic IP (e.g. 172.16.0.2) instead of the requested static IP (172.16.1.100) - Network conflicts or routing mismatches with bastion - Workers cannot reach main cluster through the gateway

Root Cause: ClusterUserDefinedNetwork with Localnet topology does not honor static IP addresses specified in pod annotations. OVN's IPAM for localnet networks assigns IPs sequentially from the subnet.

Solution:

The gateway VM configures its static IP via cloud-init network configuration (handled automatically by the hci-provisioner operator using gateway-vm-cloudinit.j2):

# Inside gateway-vm-cloudinit Secret (rendered by operator)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: gateway-vm-cloudinit
stringData:
  networkdata: |
    version: 2
    ethernets:
      external:
        match:
          macaddress: "52:54:01:00:00:01"
        addresses:
          - 172.16.1.100/16
        gateway4: 172.16.0.1
        nameservers:
          addresses:
            - 172.16.0.1
      internal:
        match:
          macaddress: "52:54:01:00:00:02"
        addresses:
          - 192.168.100.1/24

Why This Works: - Cloud-init configures the static IP and MAC matching directly inside the VM - No dependency on OVN IPAM for the external physical interface - Standard approach for physical network attachment - Gateway has full control over its external and internal routing

Verification: 

# Check gateway VM status
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vmi -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} hci-gateway

# SSH to gateway VM
ssh core@172.16.1.100

# Inside VM: check IP addresses
ip addr show
# Should show 172.16.1.100 on external interface (eth1)
# Should show 192.168.100.1 on internal interface (eth2)

docs.title: VM Stuck in ContainerCreating
docs.text:
Symptoms: - virt-launcher pod stuck in ContainerCreating for hours - VM never starts - Pod events show network attachment errors

Possible Causes:

docs.title: 1. Wrong NetworkAttachmentDefinition Reference
docs.text:
Error Message: 

failed to get pod annotation: timed out waiting for annotations: context deadline exceeded

Check: 

# Get NAD configuration
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nad router-external-network -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -o jsonpath='{.spec.config}' | jq .

# Check netAttachDefName field
# Should be: "${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}/router-external-network"
# NOT: "other-namespace/router-external-network"

Solution: See Multi-Namespace Deployment Issues

docs.title: 2. Missing ClusterUserDefinedNetwork
docs.text:
Check: 

# Verify ClusterUserDefinedNetwork exists on HCI
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get clusteruserdefinednetwork router-external-network

# Verify namespace is labeled
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} --show-labels | grep hci-gateway-enabled

Solution: 

# Apply cluster-admin network setup (Setup Guide A.2)
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml

# Label namespace (Setup Guide B.1)
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label namespace ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} hci-gateway-enabled=true

docs.title: 3. OVN Controller Issues
docs.text:
Check: 

# Check OVN controller logs on HCI
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -l app=ovnkube-node --tail=100 | grep -i error

# Check for NAD creation
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nad -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

Solution: Wait for OVN controller to create NAD (usually 1-2 minutes after namespace labeling).

docs.title: VM Fails to Boot from PXE
docs.text:
Symptoms: - VM starts but doesn't PXE boot - Console shows "No bootable device" or iPXE timeout - DHCP requests not answered

Possible Causes:

docs.title: 1. Gateway VM Not Running
docs.text:
Check: 

oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vmi -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} hci-gateway
# Should show "Running"

Solution: 

# Check virt-launcher pod logs
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -l kubevirt.io/domain=hci-gateway

# Restart if needed
virtctl restart hci-gateway -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

docs.title: 2. DHCP/PXE Service Not Running
docs.text:
Check: 

# SSH to gateway VM
ssh core@<gateway-external-ip>

# Check dnsmasq and nginx
systemctl status dnsmasq nginx
journalctl -u dnsmasq -n 50

Solution: 

# Restart services
sudo systemctl restart dnsmasq nginx

# Check static DHCP reservations
cat /etc/dnsmasq.d/pxe.conf

docs.title: 3. Network Connectivity Issue
docs.text:
Check: 

# From gateway VM, test internal network
ping 192.168.100.10  # Worker IP

# Check firewall rules
sudo iptables -L -n -v | grep 192.168.100

docs.title: 4. RHCOS Boot Files Missing or Downloading
docs.text:
Check: 

# SSH to gateway VM
ssh core@<gateway-external-ip>

# Verify boot files exist in webroot
ls -lh /var/www/html/rhcos/

# Check sync timer status
systemctl status rhcos-sync.service

docs.title: Worker Node Doesn't Appear in Cluster
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Worker VM boots successfully - RHCOS installed - Node doesn't appear in oc get nodes

Diagnostic Steps:

# 1. Check if node is trying to join
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get csr | grep Pending

# 2. Access worker node (via debug or SSH from bastion)
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/worker-x86-1  # If visible
# Or: ssh core@192.168.100.10 (from bastion)
# Or: virtctl console worker-x86-1 -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# 3. Check kubelet status
chroot /host
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 100

# 4. Check machine-config-daemon
systemctl status machine-config-daemon
journalctl -u machine-config-daemon -n 100

Common Issues:

docs.title: 1. CSR Not Approved
docs.text:
The csr-approver container in the hci-consumer-operator pod automatically approves both bootstrap and node-serving CSRs for nodes matching the configured prefix, internal subnet, and amd64 architecture.

Manual Approval (if approver is not running): 

# Approve pending CSRs
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get csr -o name | xargs oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} adm certificate approve

docs.title: 2. Cannot Reach API Server
docs.text:
Check: 

# From worker node
curl -k https://api.cluster.example.com:6443/version

Solution: - Verify DNS resolution - Check routing (see DNS and Routing Issues) - Verify gateway VM is routing correctly

docs.title: 3. Stale kube-apiserver-lb-signer CA Bundle (MCP Created Long Before First Worker)
docs.text:
Symptoms:

  • Worker installs RHCOS and boots successfully
  • kubelet cannot register with the API server
  • SSH to the worker (ssh core@worker-x86-<n> from the bastion) shows:
journalctl -b | grep -i "22623\|mcs\|ignition\|tls" | tail -30
# x509: certificate signed by unknown authority (possibly because of
# "crypto/rsa: verification error" while trying to verify candidate
# authority certificate "kube-apiserver-lb-signer")

Root cause:

The rendered-hci-vm MachineConfig is generated by the MCO when the hci-vm MachineConfigPool is first created. It bakes in the current kube-apiserver-lb-signer CA bundle at that point in time. If a significant amount of time passes between MCP creation and the first worker actually joining the pool, the cluster's lb-signer certificate rotates — but the MCO does not re-render an empty pool (no nodes = no trigger). Workers that boot and receive the stale rendered-hci-vm apply the old CA bundle and kubelet can no longer verify the API server certificate.

Once the MCP is current, additional workers can join at any later time: the MCO keeps the rendered MC up to date for pools that have at least one node, so the bundle stays current going forward.

Fix:

# 1. Scale the WorkerPool down to zero (removes all worker VMs cleanly)
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch workerpool hci-workers -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":0}}}}'

# Wait for all VMs to be gone
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get vm -n ${HCI_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -w

# 2. Delete the MCP and its source MachineConfig
#    The hci-consumer operator recreates them on the next reconcile,
#    causing the MCO to render a fresh rendered-hci-vm with the current
#    kube-apiserver-lb-signer bundle.
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} delete mcp hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} delete mc 99-hci-vm-kargs

# 3. Wait for the operator to recreate the MCP and for the MCO to render
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc -w | grep rendered-hci-vm          # wait for new rendered-hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm -o jsonpath='{.status.configuration.name}'  # must be non-empty

# 4. Verify the MCS now serves the config without error
curl -sk https://api-int.${MAIN_CLUSTER_DOMAIN}:22623/config/hci-vm \
  | jq .ignition.version

# 5. Scale back up — start with one canary worker to confirm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch workerpool hci-workers -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":1}}}}'

# Once worker-x86-1 is Ready, scale to the desired count
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch workerpool hci-workers -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"consumer":{"workers":{"count":3}}}}'

docs.title: 4. Machine Config Daemon Stuck
docs.text:
Check: 

journalctl -u machine-config-daemon-pull.service -f

Common causes: - Cannot pull images (check internet connectivity) - Cannot reach image registry - Disk space issues

Solution: 

# Check disk space
df -h

# Test image pull
podman pull quay.io/openshift-release-dev/ocp-release:latest

# Check registry connectivity
curl -v https://quay.io

docs.title: Node Stuck in NotReady State
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Node appears in cluster - Status shows NotReady - Pods cannot be scheduled

Check: 

# Get node details
oc describe node worker-x86-1

# Look for conditions
oc get node worker-x86-1 -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[*].message}'

Common Issues:

docs.title: 1. CNI Not Ready
docs.text:
Solution: 

# Check OVN pods on node
oc get pods -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -o wide | grep worker-x86-1

# Check logs
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes <ovn-pod-name>

docs.title: 2. Container Runtime Issues
docs.text:
Solution: 

# SSH to node
oc debug node/worker-x86-1
chroot /host

# Check CRI-O
systemctl status crio
journalctl -u crio -n 100

docs.title: WorkerPool Stuck in ScalingUp Although All Workers Are Ready
docs.text:
Symptoms: - oc get workerpool -n hci-node-manager shows phase: ScalingUp indefinitely - status.deployedWorkers equals spec.consumer.workers.count, but status.readyWorkers: 0 - All worker-x86-* nodes are Ready and report kubernetes.io/arch=amd64 - The x86 nodes do not carry the node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm label - oc get mcp hci-vm shows MACHINECOUNT 0; the x86 nodes are counted in the worker pool instead - The WorkerPool may still show the stale condition WorkerReconcileActive=False / BootstrapInProgress, even though the WorkerPoolProvisioning CR is Complete. This condition is left over from the first reconcile and does not mean anything here.

Background:

The operator counts a node as ready only when the node name matches <namePrefix>-* and the node has the MCP role label node-role.kubernetes.io/<machineConfigPool>. The node-labeler sidecar in the hci-consumer-operator pod adds this label. It reads its config from the hci-node-manager-config ConfigMap, which the operator writes on its first WorkerPool reconcile.

Root cause in older images (fixed by OPS-08):

Older node-labeler versions read TARGET_NETWORK only once, at startup. If the operator pod started before a WorkerPool CR existed, which is the normal order on a fresh install, the ConfigMap was missing. The labeler then fell back to 192.168.100.0/24 and kept that value for the lifetime of the pod.

Current images re-read the ConfigMap every ~30 s and fix themselves. If the symptom still shows up with a current image, the most likely cause is a mismatch between TARGET_NETWORK / NODE_NAME_PATTERN and the actual node IPs/names. Check the labeler's debug output and compare the ConfigMap with the node list.

Check: 

# Check node-labeler logs
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} logs -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} deploy/hci-consumer-operator -c node-labeler | grep -E "fallback|Target network|Labeling"
# Healthy output:
#   Labeling active: network=192.168.100.0/24, name pattern=worker-x86-.*, arch=amd64

# Network the labeler should be using
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get cm hci-node-manager-config -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE} -o jsonpath='{.data.TARGET_NETWORK}{"\n"}'

# Nodes missing the role label
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nodes -l 'kubernetes.io/arch=amd64,!node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm'

Solution:

# Option A (preferred): restart the operator pod to force a re-scan
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} rollout restart deployment/hci-consumer-operator -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} rollout status deployment/hci-consumer-operator -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}

# Option B: label the nodes manually
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label node <worker-x86-N>.<cluster-domain> node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm= --overwrite

Note: Once labelled, the nodes move from the worker MCP to the hci-vm MCP. HCI workers boot from /config/hci-vm and already run the rendered-hci-vm-* config. Check this with the node annotation machineconfiguration.openshift.io/currentConfig. If it already shows rendered-hci-vm-*, labelling triggers no MCO update and no reboot. If it shows rendered-worker-*, MCO applies the hci-vm config and reboots the nodes one at a time (maxUnavailable: 1).

⚠️ Never put hci-vm on s390x nodes. The hci-vm config carries x86-VM kernel arguments and would make them unbootable. Current labeler images enforce this through a name + arch guard.

Verify: 

oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/hci-vm
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp hci-vm                       # MACHINECOUNT == worker count
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get workerpool -n ${MAIN_INTEGRATION_NAMESPACE}   # phase: Ready, readyWorkers == count

docs.title: DNS Resolution Fails
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Cannot resolve cluster hostnames - Cannot resolve internet hostnames - Intermittent resolution failures

Diagnostic Steps:

# From worker node
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/worker-x86-1
chroot /host

# Check DNS configuration
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# Test DNS resolution
dig api.cluster.example.com
dig quay.io

# Test DNS server directly
dig @172.16.0.1 api.cluster.example.com

Common Issues:

docs.title: 1. Wrong DNS Server
docs.text:
Expected: 

nameserver 172.16.0.1
search cluster.example.com

Solution: Verify the DHCP server (dnsmasq) on the gateway VM is advertising dhcp-option=option:dns-server,172.16.0.1 and dhcp-option=option:domain-search,cluster.example.com.

docs.title: 2. DNS Server Not Allowing Recursion
docs.text:
Check: 

# On bastion/DNS server (172.16.0.1)
# Check named configuration
grep -r "allow-recursion" /etc/named*

# Should include internal worker network and mediated network
allow-recursion { localhost; 10.0.0.0/24; 192.168.100.0/24; 172.16.0.0/16; };

Solution: Update DNS server configuration to allow recursion from worker network.

docs.title: Routing Issues
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Cannot reach main cluster API - Cannot reach internet - Packets not being forwarded

Diagnostic Steps:

# From worker node
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/worker-x86-1
chroot /host

# Check routing table
ip route show

# Test connectivity
ping -c 3 192.168.100.1  # Gateway
ping -c 3 api.cluster.example.com
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8  # Internet

# Trace route
traceroute api.cluster.example.com

Common Issues:

docs.title: 1. Missing Default Route
docs.text:
Solution: 

# Check if default route exists
ip route show default

# If missing, check DHCP
journalctl -u NetworkManager | grep DHCP

docs.title: 2. Gateway Not Routing (Mediated Topology)
docs.text:
Check: 

# On bastion
ip route | grep 192.168.100

# Should show route to HCI internal network via gateway external IP

Solution: 

# Add route on bastion (Setup Guide C.2 / 01-add-route.sh)
sudo ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 172.16.1.100

# Make persistent
sudo nmcli connection modify <conn-name> +ipv4.routes "192.168.100.0/24 172.16.1.100"

docs.title: 3. Master Nodes Cannot Reach Workers (Direct Topology)
docs.text:
Symptoms: - CSRs not being approved - Node status updates delayed - Pods cannot be scheduled

Check: 

# From master node
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/<master-node>
chroot /host

# Check route to HCI network
ip route | grep 192.168.100

# Test connectivity
ping -c 3 192.168.100.10

Solution: Verify MachineConfig for master route is applied (Setup Guide C.4):

# Check MachineConfig
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-master-s390x-hci-network-route

# Check if applied to masters
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp master

# If not applied, apply from workspace rendered by generate-setup
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f workspace/main-cluster-machineconfigs/

docs.title: 4. S390x Workers Cannot Reach HCI Workers (Direct Topology)
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Cross-architecture pod communication fails - Services spanning both worker types don't work - Network policies fail

Check: 

# From s390x worker
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} debug node/<s390x-worker>
chroot /host

# Check route
ip route | grep 192.168.100

# Test connectivity
ping -c 3 192.168.100.10

Solution: Verify MachineConfig for s390x worker route is applied (Setup Guide C.4):

# Check MachineConfig
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mc 99-worker-s390x-hci-network-route

# Check if applied to workers
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get mcp worker

# If not applied, apply from workspace rendered by generate-setup
oc --context ${MAIN_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f workspace/main-cluster-machineconfigs/

docs.title: Gateway VM NAT Issues
docs.text:
Symptoms: - Workers can reach main cluster but not internet - Or vice versa

Check: 

# SSH to gateway VM
ssh core@172.16.1.100

# Check NAT rules
sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v | grep 192.168.100

# Check IP forwarding
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward  # Should be 1

Expected NAT Rules: 

# Transparent routing (no NAT) for mediated private network
ACCEPT all -- 192.168.100.0/24 10.0.0.0/24

# Transparent routing (no NAT) for external network
ACCEPT all -- 192.168.100.0/24 172.16.0.0/16

# Masquerading (NAT) for internet
MASQUERADE all -- 192.168.100.0/24 0.0.0.0/0

Solution: Check gateway VM cloud-init configuration and redeploy if needed.

docs.title: Second Namespace Deployment Fails
docs.text:
Symptoms: - First namespace deployment works fine - Second namespace VMs stuck in ContainerCreating - Network attachment errors in pod events

Root Cause: ClusterUserDefinedNetwork is cluster-scoped. Only the cluster-admin should create it; each integration namespace gets the resulting NAD automatically via the namespace label.

Error Message: 

network cluster_udn_router-external-network NAD main-cluster-workers/router-external-network
failed to get pod annotation: timed out waiting for annotations

Solution:

  1. Cluster admin applies cluster-scoped resources once (Setup Guide A.2): 

    oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml

  2. Label each namespace (Setup Guide B.1): 

    oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label namespace <namespace> hci-gateway-enabled=true

  3. Apply WorkerPoolProvisioning CR — the hci-provisioner operator creates the namespace-scoped UserDefinedNetwork and gateway VM automatically.

Quick fix for existing deployments:

# 1. Apply cluster-admin setup
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} apply -f hci-cluster/cluster-network-setup.yaml

# 2. Label all namespaces
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label namespace main-cluster-workers hci-gateway-enabled=true
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} label namespace main-cluster-workers-2 hci-gateway-enabled=true

# 3. Stop gateway VMs
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch vm hci-gateway -n main-cluster-workers --type merge -p '{"spec":{"running":false}}'
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch vm hci-gateway -n main-cluster-workers-2 --type merge -p '{"spec":{"running":false}}'

# 4. Delete incorrect NADs
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} delete nad router-external-network -n main-cluster-workers
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} delete nad router-external-network -n main-cluster-workers-2

# 5. Wait for controller to recreate NADs (1-2 minutes)
watch oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nad -A

# 6. Verify NAD configuration
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} get nad router-external-network -n main-cluster-workers -o jsonpath='{.spec.config}' | jq .netAttachDefName
# Should show: "main-cluster-workers/router-external-network"

# 7. Start VMs
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch vm hci-gateway -n main-cluster-workers --type merge -p '{"spec":{"running":true}}'
oc --context ${HCI_CLUSTER_CONTEXT} patch vm hci-gateway -n main-cluster-workers-2 --type merge -p '{"spec":{"running":true}}'
